title: ABC News Daily with Samantha Hawley - ABC listen
description: ABC News Daily is the podcast that helps you understand the issues affecting your world. Every episode, host Samantha Hawley walks through one story with the help of an ABC colleague or expert in under 15 minutes. When you want coverage you can trust, listen to ABC News Daily.

episodes.title: Will anyone get a refund for Trump’s illegal tariffs?
episodes.description: The US Supreme Court has ruled that most of Donald Trump’s tariffs are illegal. So, will President Trump give back to Australian companies the millions of dollars they’ve already lost?
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more. episodes.title: What are AI agents and can they be trusted?
episodes.description: They used to be known as personal assistants, now you can just get an AI agent to plan your day, answer your emails and organise your life.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Hi, I'm Patricia Carvellas, the host of the Politics Now podcast. 2026 is already shaping up to be another huge year in politics, with inflation remaining persistently high, lingering housing challenges and now a Royal Commission getting underway. So join me and the sharpest minds of the ABC to cut through the political spin and bring you what politics means for you. That's Politics Now and you can hear it on the ABC Listen app. They used to be known as personal assistance or PAs. Now you can just get an AI agent to plan your day and to your emails and well organise your life and the agents can even talk to each other. Bush is the latest wave of artificial intelligence really safe to use yet. Today computer security expert at Melbourne Uni, Shanan Kony, on how it works and whether we're a step closer to AI taking our jobs. I'm Sam Hawley on Getting All Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Shanan, the so-called AI agents are here. Now just tell me first of all, have you got an AI bot handling your life? If I look at the computer screen in front of me right now, I can see four different agents already working on things that I've sent them to do over the last 30 minutes. They don't have access to my emails but they've got access to a lot of other things. Okay, so just give me an example of what they're doing for you right now. There's one that is looking at the website for my class and making sure that all the tutors are on there with all their personal details to send to the rest of the class. Mary Ellen, you are retired, of course, from the FBI now, but just before we launch into the details of the case of Nancy Guthrie, just tell me about the high-profile cases that you worked on. So some of the cases that are high-profile that I worked on over the years would include the Unibomber case, the Natalie Holloway case, the Zodiac case in San Francisco, Polyclass kidnapping case, multiple kidnapping cases. So those are just a few of the ones that I've worked. So you are, Mary Ellen, the perfect person to talk to about this case. The first major breakthrough came when footage showed a masked man tampering with a security camera on her front door, leading to thousands of public tips. So Mary Ellen, Nancy Guthrie, was last seen on the 31st of January. And on February the 1st, she was reported missing. Now two days later, a ransom note arrives. Just tell me about that because it went to a TV outlet, didn't it? Not directly to the Guthries. Is that a usual thing to occur? But for something like this, where a note is submitted by allegedly by the kidnappers, and then it goes to a third party entity, which in this case was TMZ, is not typical. We received an email at TMZ from somebody purporting to basically issue a ransom demand. They are asking for money a lot. They are asking for it in the form of Bitcoin, and they are putting an or else on this. That is pretty unusual, at least in my experience to see that happen. All right, well then, on February the 4th, Savannah and her siblings Annie and Cameron issue a video plea for their mother's safe return. Our mom is a kind, faithful, loyal, fiercely loving woman of goodness and light. Mama, if you're listening, we need you to come home. We miss you. Now, tell me would police have advised them to do that? I think the police would have had a role in encouraging them to do that. And the reason that they would is to establish communication, hopefully with the kidnapper, but if not with that person who took their mom, was someone close to the kidnapper that would be able to recognize the kidnappers' behavior. Maybe the kidnapper had talked about the kidnapping before, as they were preparing for the kidnapping. And they want that mother, that wife, that relative, next door neighbor to come forward with information. We too have heard the reports about a ransom letter in the media. As a family, we are doing everything that we can. We are ready to talk. Well, Mary Ellen, a few days later, on the 10th of February, a surveillance video is released. Just tell me about that video and how significant it was. Well, the video is extremely significant. First of all, it was retrieved from a disabled door camera, which a lot of people did not think would be retrievable. So it produced actually some very clear video. It shows the individual, one person, who is dressed with a mask on and wearing the infamous gloves that we're hearing so much about now, walking onto the porch and looking at the camera, and picking up a plant, apparently rubbing it, maybe against the camera. But it shows this person on the camera for a pretty good amount of time. And what's so interesting to me is that you have the offender coming across as not being overly nervous or jittery or uncertain, or even angry or even inebriated or possibly on drugs, you see a moving slowly, you see almost a confidence about this person, which is very telling to a profiler in terms of the mindset and the personality of this person. So this is pretty useful vision then at this point for the FBI and for police. It's very useful. Yes, it's very useful in terms of the comfort level with which this offender seems to have had. And the only way you can have that kind of comfort level is planning, planning ahead, and that planning could have included going to the house before the night of the abduction. Of course, there's been some speculation if it was a robbery going wrong. I mean, can we tell anything about that from that vision? Yeah, I've heard that on a number of cases over the years. And a robbery going wrong would suggest something that I have never seen in my career. Not that that makes it impossible. But a robbery or a burglary is described as taking property that belongs to another person. And most burglaries, at least those here in the United States, occur at a time when the burglar doesn't think somebody will be at home because what their intent is is to go in, take things of value, and then to leave. But if you go into somebody's home at one or two o'clock in the morning, you're pretty guaranteed you're going to run into somebody. And burglares don't want to do that. So if you're a burglar and you go into somebody's home and now you're confronted with the person that lives there, now it requires that you morph in to this violent kidnapper. Because burglarry and kidnapping are very different crimes. And so when I hear people say that this was a burglary that has gone wrong, this does not have the elements of that kind of crime, whatsoever, at least to me. All right, so this is vital vision retrieved actually by Google from a disabled camera. Now the FBI also found these gloves that you referred to before. So at this point, they're obviously throwing everything they have at this case. They are using the most current state-of-the-art technology that they can to using things like DNA. That's me is extremely important. We need to draw on every piece of technology that we can't even if it's a long shot at the end. So the pacemaker and being able to possibly track the pacemaker, if it works, it's great. If it doesn't work, at least they tried. Right, and at this time, you know, the family has posted a number of videos saying it's never too late to return their mother to do the right thing. It's been two weeks since our mom was taken and and I wanted to say to whoever has her, it is never too late to do the right thing. And we are here. They have, haven't they, been cleared by police. Chris Nanos is the sheriff in charge and he says they have been completely gracious victims. We really put them through the ringer. We not just interview them. We take their cars, we take their houses, we take their phones, all this stuff. They have been 100% cooperative with us. Yes, when you work at Kidnapping Case and we learn this the hard way, especially with child Kidnapping cases, you always, always have to clear the immediate family. And you have to do that as soon as you can to rule out people that are closest to the victim. Well, let's consider Mary Ellen whether this huge amount of attention and these thousands of leads given to police are a help or actually a hindrance because surely the sheer number of tips that the FBI has received would take a massive amount of resources to analyse. You can, you're right, it absolutely can but the FBI is really used to going into what we call a command centre which is where all the officers of the investigation are and this is where all the leads would be coming in there or to other field offices around the country. And they have a lot of experience in being able to go through these leads and being able to rule out leads that may be generated by somebody's opinion about the case and then they can prioritise leads as well and leads have to be actionable. We have field offices all over including in Australia and so we can handle leads internationally and we can do that pretty quickly. Mary Ellen, let's look then at what comes next. The FBI would be under huge pressure to solve this case. What sort of job do you think they're doing because I suppose there will be criticism that it's too slow, that a resolution is too slow? Unfortunately, it's not like TV where cases resolved in 45 minutes on television or in a movie. So it does take much longer to be able to bring resources to the case and analyse the forensic evidence and get a resolution and I think what's important is this offender, this kidnapper, if he's still alive and you always have to consider that possibility, this offender more than likely doesn't want to be caught. And if the more planning and offender puts into a crime ahead of time, the more they've put into their post-offense behaviour, that means their behaviour after the crime. And when a crime is not spontaneous where a person decides in 10 minutes, I'm going to rob a bank. When a crime has some planning to it and sometimes a lot of planning to it, that can really make it challenging. But I think in this case, this offender, he has no competition for the forensics that are probably being collected and analysed as we speak. And that includes the DNA evidence. As you say, it's clear a lot of planning went into this. From all you've learned as a former FBI profiler, what attributes would you be expecting in a perpetrator in a case like this? One of the tenants that we learn in the FBI's behavioural analysis unit or the profiling unit is the perpetrator or the offender brings their personality with them to the crime scene. So you don't switch personalities just because you're committing a violent crime. So when we see what your personality traits are as they're exhibited during the crime, then we're able to tell the investigators, this is the kind of person that you are looking for in their normal everyday life. And I'll just give you an example here. If this person appeared to be relaxed and comfortable as he was on Nancy's porch, knowing that within minutes he was going to commit a very violent crime, this is somebody who doesn't get stressed out in high-risk situations. This is probably also someone who had very low empathy for Nancy. And probably viewed her more as an object. This person probably also has a sense of grandiosity because this crime has a certain flare of grandiosity to it. When I start to see those kinds of traits, you're starting to put together the profile of somebody that displays traits of a personality disorder that we know as psychopathy. It's not a mental illness. People just don't care about others, and you see people with these traits responsible for a larger percentage of violent crimes. Interesting. And the motive is it just money. I have never seen a crime, especially one that is complex, where there is a single motive. But in this case, it certainly could be money. Sex is always considered in a kidnapping crime, although here I think it's less so based on the age of the victim. The motives could include something like wanting to commit a crime where you get a lot of attention, and another motive can be actually a sense of revenge. And these are people that blame others for how badly screwed up their life is. All right, well, Mary Ellen, as the days roll on, what are the chances in your view that Nancy will be found alive? I know what the investigators, the agents, and the sheriff's deputies are feeling, and that is that they are motivated to find her and bring her home alive. And you can't rule that out. I've had cases where the victims were missing for a year, and they will return home alive. So you always operate from that perspective. It's difficult because you know what the reality is, she's 84 and in real health, but it's not impossible that that could happen. Mary Ellen O'Toole is a former FBI profiler and currently director of the forensic science program at George Mason University. This episode was produced by Sydney Pete and Cinnamon Nippard, Audio Production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Coney. I'm Sam Hawley, ABC News Daily. We'll be back again on Monday. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: Will Coles go ‘Down Down’ in court?
episodes.description: When Coles told you that prices were “Down Down”, were they really? That’s a matter now before the Federal Court with the competition watchdog, the ACCC, arguing consumers have been misled and it needs to end.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Killed with a drug overdose, then cut up and put in a wheelie bin. That is what prosecutors alleged Sheree Glasston breed did to our partner, 55-year-olds Jeffrey McLean. On the case of the wheelie bin murder, we'll follow the murder trial of Sheree Glasston breed and three co-accused as they defend charges relating to Jeffrey's death. Search for the case of podcasts on ABC Listen or wherever you get your podcasts to make sure you don't miss an episode. When Coles told you that prices were down down, were they really? Well, that's a matter now before the federal court. The competition watchdog arguing consumers have been misled and it needs to end. Today, Consumer Affairs reporter Michael Atkin, on what we've heard in the case so far and how Coles defends its practices. I'm Sam Hawley on Gadigal Land in Sydney. This is ABC News Daily. Michael, this court case is really intriguing because it goes to how Coles will market things and gets us to buy certain products with slogans like down down. I'm not a damn down to just what already. I call. Land down. Yes, so we're in the middle of this 10-day trial. It's Coles versus the Consumer Watchdog in the federal court. And the A-Triple C is accusing Coles of something very serious saying that they've been utterly misleading over discounts on products between February 2022 and March 2023. Really important staple items that everybody buys each week, toothpaste, soft drinks, cheese, yoghets. And the allegations are that they increased their prices artificially. So they jack them up for a very short period of time and then put it down on a down-down discount and say you're getting a saving essentially is what they triple-sea ledges. The Coles has been disguising these price rises as price discounts when in fact they're not. Yeah, and you can still see those down-down labels on shelves around Coles, can't you? I notice them all the time. That's correct. It's still a staple part of their supermarket campaigning. They've been around since 2010. And what was interesting is they actually played the ads to the court to a few chuckles from the gallery. The A-Triple C has said as part of the court case, well, Coles should have been levelling with consumers like the customers in its stores should have been told while prices are going up. You didn't have to say your marketing tagline down down because prices weren't going down. That's what they claim. Can they prove it? Okay, so the A-Triple C, the Consumer Watchdog, it's taken Coles to court this week. So let's now Michael consider what the court has heard. Now, one example that's been spoken about is dog food. Yes, so it was nature's gift at wet dog food as a product and it was charged at $4 for almost 300 days, so nearly a year before the price rose. It rose to $6 for a week, so that's an increase of 50% before falling to $4.50 on a down-down discount. And the A-Triple C says a reasonable consumer would think seeing that price tag in the store that they were getting a discount. But if they knew the full picture that actually it had been $4 for 300 days before the seven-day price increase, that actually they would think, well, I'm not getting a discount here at all. I'm paying 50 cents more than it was. Interesting. All right. And there was other examples, of course, as well. A box of strepses was one put forward, those throat lozenges, of course. And also who doesn't love a shape biscuit, Michael? Indeed. So in the strepses case, it was a regular price for a box of them for $5.50. And the price remained that for 640 days before it was increased to $7 for 28 days. And then it was reduced on a down-down promotion. And the sales ticket that people saw when they purchased it for a down-down price was a was price of $7. However, what you were paying was actually 9% higher than the regular price of $5.50 according to the A-Triple C. So this is at the heart of why they say it's just utterly misleading. With the shapes, they put that example out in court earlier this week, that the shapes were sold for $5 a box in 2021, then got as high as $6.50 before going back to $5.50, all part of the down-down promotion cycle. All right. But overall, Michael, the court is looking at more than 200 products. That's right. This is not a case over one or two products. They're saying that this was more than 200 products for over a year. So they're saying that there was a massive amount of revenue generated for Coles and its suppliers using this misleading conduct. And what was really interesting is that they quoted from some internal emails, the A-Triple C, saying that Coles was actually looking very closely at the discounting we're worse was offering, and that they saw that we're worse was very sharply increasing the price of a product for a short period before discounting, much faster than Coles was. And so Coles staff were agitating internally to change their internal policies. And they eventually did that for the period that covers this conduct, and the A-Triple C ledges that in almost all of the cases, the discounting that followed, wouldn't have been allowed under Coles' previous internal policies. And one of the staggering bits of evidence, one of the Coles' internal emails, you know, mueson, whether they should actually report the conduct of Woolworths to the A-Triple C, and the A-Triple C Council said, well, that's exactly what Coles should have done, but instead it didn't. You know, lawyers from the Consumer Watchdog have labeled Coles' price discounts utterly misleading. They say it was a planned campaign. So this goes to intent. This wasn't something that just happened. If the A-Triple C can land that intent, that's a significant win for the A-Triple C, but they don't need to prove that outright. It's just whether the average consumer in the shops were misled. All right, well, Michael, this court case, it's not necessarily about how much things actually cost, but really how they're marketed, and then what consumers take away from that. Now, Coles rejects the A-Triple C's allegations that it's down, down, ads were misleading, and of course, they're defending it in court. What has Coles been saying to the court? Yeah, Coles has unfolded its defense over a couple of days now, and they vehemently reject the A-Triple C's allegations. And I guess there's two parts to the Coles' defense. So they say that customers were really offered genuine discounts. So this A-Triple C allegations that they were fake discounts, they say that's wrong, because if you have a look at the price tag, well, Coles really did charge $6 for the item before discounting it to $4.50, and it showed clearly what the saving was on that price tag. Now, that may have been only the price for a very short period of time, as little as seven days, but that doesn't make it a fake discount. Coles says it was still a genuine discount from that previous price. And it also says, well, we've had this period of massive rampant inflation. Our costs were increasing far more than we'd seen in the past. So were our suppliers, and suppliers were banging down our door, pushing for price increases. And they say that this first price that was charged, that's often for 300 days or more, that was no longer relevant because time had moved on. And it's its right to increase prices. And that has been a key part of the argument here. There was this great line from the Coles Council saying, in the end, all prices are temporary. Nothing lasts forever. You can tell he'd been mulling that one over in front of the mirror, I think. That's... And isn't it so true? The top executives at Coles, Michael, they're not actually fronting up to this. Are they? Why not? Well, that's a good question. When I interviewed Alan Fels, the former A-triple C-boss ahead of the case, he thought they should, because if they wanted to have the best chance of defending the case, he thought that would be important. Obviously, Coles disagrees. We don't know exactly who is going to be called yet, but from information they've submitted to the court, but it seems like it's likely to be people who are in charge of pricing or individual products or negotiations with suppliers. You know, it's Coles' right to choose what it wants to do in terms of defending the case. It's really harping on this point of, well, they, Triple C, hasn't established what a reasonable period is for us to charge a price before we discount. And they think they're onto a winning argument there, I think, in defending the case. Well, Michael, of course, most, if not all Australians have shopped at Coles at one point or another. And I know we've talked about this before, but the biggest problem we have is that we just don't have much option. We can't really just shop around because there's not that many supermarkets to shop at. Yes, I think this is the big white elephant hanging over this entire court case. It's still Coles and Woolworth dominating about two thirds of the market. And so really, the desperate need for more competition is what would make a difference to everybody in terms of driving down price and having intense competition. The supermarkets do say they're getting a lot of competition on certain items from players like Amazon. But when I ask people like Alan Fels about that, he says it's a drop in the ocean compared to the overall market and it's not making a meaningful difference. Well, Alan Fels, who you mentioned there, the former atriple-sea boss, he says this is the case of the century. And, you know, Michael, it could be really costly for Coles, couldn't it, if it loses this case? But on the flip side of that, if it doesn't and it wins, it won't be great for the atriple-sea. Yeah, this makes a massive for everybody, which is why Alan Fels calls it the case of the century because Coles faces the possibility of a massive penalty of it loses, you know, north of $50 million. Alan Fels thinks it could be much more than that. The specs are enormous. For Coles, the behaviour affects millions of customers, potential finds in hundreds of millions of dollars, and reputation affects. You know, we saw Quantus find $100 million for misconduct, opt as the same. And so there could be something in that ballpark if the case succeeds. And not only that, there's another case against Woolworth's for almost identical conduct waiting in the wings. So whatever happens in this case is going to impact that. There's a class action waiting. But I think from a big picture perspective, if Coles loses, then it could change this area of was now pricing, it's called. So this is discount pricing that happens basically in every area of retail where you see an original price with a big cross through it, and then a discount price, and you meant to feel really great about how much money you're saving. Well, if there's new rules or boundaries put around how long a price needs to be offered before a discount is seen as valid, that could really shake up the retail sector and a lot of consumer advocates think that would be really good for consumers. Right. Now, but just to put that $50 million fine into this perspective, Coles did report a net profit last year of 1.08 billion. Didn't that Michael? Yes, that's right. So I think in terms of the fine, you know, they won't want to pay that fine if it does come to fruition, but it's really the reputational damage that people think makes the real difference. You know, it will be able to handle that in the ballot sheet, as you've just talked about with the profit margin. But it's, it's the loss of face that these corporations really worry about. And what's so interesting about this case is they have chosen to defend it because when the consumer watchdog comes knocking with a lawsuit, quite often the big companies choose to settle because they don't want the damaging headlines that come from weeks of a court case like Coles is going through now. But they obviously think they have a chance to win, and so they're fighting back and they're fighting back hard. Michael Atkin is the ABC's consumer affairs reporter. This episode was produced by Sydney Pete, audio production by Sam Dunn. Our supervising producer is David Cody. I'm Sam Wally. Thanks for listening.

episodes.title: Long Read | How social media algorithms decide who you are
episodes.description: This week, Prianka Srinivasan arms herself with a burner phone and a fake name, and sets out to learn how Instagram’s algorithm really works.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music, and more. Hi, Corbin Middleman here. What's going on with the cricket? Well, that's what the ABC cricket podcast is for, with me and my sparring partner Ed Cowan. Who's been selected? Who's been rejected? Who has the best grade cricket salad roll? What's the key of quality of the cheese or the bun? The diet is always fresh or the salad and so on. Search for the ABC cricket podcast on the ABC Listen app, or wherever you get your podcasts. The background briefing team are working hard on fresh episodes. In the meantime, we've collaborated with ABC Longreads to bring you some of the best pieces of journalism read by the people who've written them. Armed with a microphone and a fake name, I set out to learn how Instagram's algorithm really works. I'm Priyanka Srinivasan, and this is a piece I wrote for the ABC's Longread, called How Social Media Algorithms Decide Who You Are. At some point, let's say a Wednesday night, around 8.40pm, too late to work, but far too early to sleep. I find myself watching someone spread toothpaste and butter on a cracked phone screen. Scroll. A pigeon with a hole in its neck pecs at a plastic water bowl. Scroll. A woman, her face and hands coated in a shiny paste, the color of Vegemite, runs the back of a butter knife along her left cheek, revealing a patch of clear, poor, it's looking skin underneath. There's something strangely intimate about sharing the content of your social media feed with others. It feels like exposing a secret part of yourself, your idle curiosities, guilty pleasures, the things you like to click on when no one else is watching. Our feeds can often feel like private mirrors, reflecting a version of ourselves that others just rarely get to see. On this particular occasion, though, it wasn't exactly my reflection I was staring at. These clips belonged to a sock puppet account. I had created on Instagram using a factory reset benefit. It was part of a month and a half long experiment I was running to figure out how social media apps curate the unique digital worlds we occupy. The motivation to run the experiment came to me on a separate evening while I was mindlessly scrolling through my genuine Instagram feed. I was struck by this feeling that the videos are poor and sometimes shameful representation of who I really am. As a journalist, with what I hope are diverse interests in world politics, arts and culture, my feed ripples with banal videos of celebrities, makeup tutorials and puppy hijinks. Put another way, if my Instagram feed were a diet, it would be one riddled with ultra-processed junk food, accompanied by almost no vegetables or greens, all pleasure, zero nutrition. I know I'm not alone with my anxieties. I want to understand why do social media apps show a certain content over others? Are they a true reflection of the unique interests and values that define us or are the algorithms driving our social media feed? Somehow, penicious, drip feeding us an endless slurry of addictive brain rot. Can we wrestle back control? My social media experiment attempted to answer these questions. By tracking how my fake feed responded to deliberate behaviour on and off the platform, I wondered if I could unravel how apps like TikTok, Instagram and YouTube decide what to show us and how they ensnare us in a loop of provocative or misinformed content. Maybe I could even coax my account into reflecting a more nourishing version of myself. So I built a sterile digital environment untethered for my real life. I wiped the contents of an old phone clean, randomly generated an alias called tank promotion and created a matching email account. After buying a new SIM card to verify the device, I downloaded Instagram, my platform of choice to run the experiment since I was most familiar with its interface. Other apps like Google, YouTube and others I downloaded would serve as tools to more subtly manipulate the signals Instagram uses to curate its feed. Stage one of the experiment could begin. I started scrolling. The content seemed random, unpredictable. With no existing accessive information, my page was a menagerie of interest. Videos of gooey sources being mixed into steaming pasta, of men holding fish, of kittens, of idyllic landscapes. Instagram operates with a basic motive. To ensure you stay on its app as long as possible. Finding out what holds our attention also keeps social media companies profitable. Most users enter their accounts with existing friends and networks, allowing the platform to guess their likes with decent accuracy. But faced with a blank profile like mine, Instagram acts like a parent, feeding a fussy child, serving up a plethora of tastes, until it strikes the one that's gobbled up with glee. A former meta intern named Mohammed Haroon told me, when you start with a vanilla profile, you have this diverse content pool, and the algorithm is trying to gauge what this user is interested in. Haroon is now a doctoral student in computer science from UC Davis, researching how content is recommended to you online. He says, they have a bunch of different feedback mechanisms, like if you watch a reel a second longer than you watch something else. At this early stage of the experiment, I was determined to limit my feedback. I made sure not to linger on any one piece of media. I watched each video in its entirety and quickly scroll to the next. I kept my movements steady and rhythmic. Despite my attempts, Instagram kept unlocking parts of me I tried to keep hidden. A steady mix of AFL content and hyper-local news stories suggested the app knew I lived in Melbourne. I checked my phone's location settings, and sure enough, Instagram had recently accessed this information. Other additions to my feed were harder to explain. One video featured a woman in a sari, called South Indian Dumplings called Creepaniyata, an obscure dish my mom would make when I was growing up. On another occasion, photos of kittens suddenly overtook my page. Some of them eerily similar to my friends cat. He'd just come over for dinner days earlier. Were these just coincidences, or did this phone actually know who my family and friends were? Professor Daniel Angus from Queensland University of Technology introduced me to this one possibility that gives me chills. With access to our location data, social media platforms suggest profiles and content to us based on not just where we are, but who we are with. He says, it's going to be using that geolocation to profile you and your tastes and likes and wants. It's not individual targeting, it's associative logics now. Your tastes, behaviors and connections mapped as coordinates with in a larger field of data relations. A sociative logic works like this. Social media systems see your phone as one node in a vast network of devices. When you spend time in the same place with certain other people, say at work at home or at with friends, these connections are reinforced. The system begins associating your account with theirs. This information shapes the content you see online. Angus advises, think less of what you were doing individually on the device and more about what everybody else around you is doing on theirs. This model may explain the spooky experiences many of us have on social media. Meeting a stranger at a party and finding their profile appears on your suggested friends list. Or seeing an ad for a product your partner recently purchased. Or in my case, finding content on Tank Promotions Instagram account that relates to parts of my personal life. Angus says, you need to remove the idea of you being one single isolated point in a space. You are the product of not just you, but every other phone and device in your environment. I will never know for sure why certain videos turned up in my feed. But the experiment was already making clear that the media we see online is tied to the people and places we see offered. Faced with this reality, Australia's social media ban offers the comfort of action. Shielding users under the age of 16 from the omnipresence of targeted content. But as Angus warns, it may also distract us from answering deeper issues. Like, will such a ban address how social media companies harvest data, including that of their youngest users? Will the online behavior of adults or older siblings still shape what children see on their devices? And are these models inherently harmful to young people? If they simply mirror a world, that's all ready around them. In social media's early days, some 20 years ago, only the posts from accounts you followed appeared chronologically in the order they were shared. You could quickly reach the end of your feed, a place where there was nothing more to see. The result was a more user controlled, though restrictive, experience. As social media companies looked to include more advertising, they began curating our feeds without us actively looking for content. They adopted recommended systems, now called the algorithm, that act like invisible strings pulling us towards certain content. The so-called collaborative model, pioneered by Netflix, was one of the earliest recommended systems. If you use a one, liked movies A, B, and C, and user two, liked movies A, B, C, and D, the algorithm would suggest movie D to use a one. As the models became more sophisticated, social media companies designed systems that learned directly from an individual's behavior. Every deliberate action on a post acted like a weighted vote for content you wanted to see more of. Most of us understand that if you consistently like comment or share videos of puppies, for example, the algorithm will rank puppy videos higher, and they will show up more regularly in your feed. But we're not always reliable reporters of our own preferences. To appeal to our deepest desires, social media companies started trekking how long you gaze at a video when you close the app, and how quickly you scroll through your page. This all feeds the ranking system, helping predict what will keep you scrolling. Haroon says TikTok is particularly advanced in interpreting the so-called implicit signals. No surprise then, that this platform is also particularly addictive. Modern platforms use AI and deep learning methods where systems are trained on masses of data, and programmed to optimize our feeds for high engagement. Haroon calls these systems a sort of black box, where it's hard to understand exactly why this model spits out something at you. He says even experts on the inside are finding it increasingly hard to understand what's happening. And that's where we're left today. A recommendation system that's almost entirely data and engagement driven, without reliable methods to automatically block harmful content. Many of us now feel stuck on a conveyor belt of content intricately designed to appeal to our specific interests, and no one can fully explain how it happens. My experiment was a chance to pull back the kin. To examine the power of these systems, I wanted to see if I could convince my new Instagram account that I was someone else. Say a mother with a newborn baby. I tested a popular conspiracy that your phone's microphone listens in. I opened my laptop, typed in new mother into YouTube search engine, and it ought to play a variety of associated videos. I took advantage of YouTube's own recommendation system by allowing it to cycle through suggested videos while I was at work. I put my banner phone right up against my laptop speaker and left. Once I returned home, I eagerly checked my Instagram feed. No new baby-related content appeared. On its website, Meta says it does not listen to our conversations through the microphone. Perhaps it doesn't need to. Perhaps our behavior on the devices speaks loudly enough. Time to ramp up my signals. I downloaded a suite of pregnancy and baby tracking apps. I added fake data. I pretended to track the rituals and schedules of my fake baby, who I christened tanky. A few days later, the first video waiting for me in my Instagram timeline was a cartoon of a woman in labor. Over the next week, I noticed more videos in thumbnails of infants and moms. By no means was my account flooded with baby content, so I introduced new variables to see if I could magnify the results. I googled best baby carriers. I joined new mother's groups on Facebook. I followed subreddits called new mom stuff and pregnancy underscore care. My account continued to shift, but in more unexpected ways. I began to get semi-pornographic content. Busty women rolling around their beds. Animations of maids, gyrating suggestively back and forth alongside a green hot dog-like character. At times, my suggested friend's profile pictures consisted of several women with their heads cropped out. Their curvaceous bodies pouring out of lingerie. Even the motherhood content seemed somehow salacious. A man squeezing a woman's breast to fill his mug with milk. I suspect two reasons. I first noticed this change while I was using the free Wi-Fi in a London cafe. Was there something about my location or others in the cafe that prompted the algorithm to serve me adult content? Alternatively, a simpler reason. Sex sells. Porn is ubiquitous online. It's estimated that one in three young Australians encounters pornography unintentionally before they turn 13 and often through social media. I was about three weeks into my experiment and I hadn't clicked, liked, or interacted with any content. Perhaps in an act of desperation, the platform was sending me the posts that kept many of its users engaged. Muhammad Haroon finds this theory plausible. He says, when you optimize for engagement, you start seeing content that could be misinformation, controversial, or shocking, that keeps you engaged because of morbid curiosity. After a few more days of watching my feed slide into filth, alongside some motherhood and other content, I decided to give Instagram a more obvious push. I selected a few thumbnails on my expo page that looked vaguely child-oriented. Photos of toilet rolls crafted into animals, a cake shaped like the number six, and an infant's walker. Within seconds, the account bloomed with baby gear and motherhood content. My real feed became a constant stream of chubby infants. In under eight minutes, Instagram had reimagined me as a parent. The behavior that may have led me to being classified as a new mother was relatively benign, and I imagined useful for someone who really had a new baby. But soon, that same profiling logic would push me towards something far more toxic. A few weeks later, my phone began insisting I follow an all-meat diet and massage my husband every night. As a single woman and a lifelong vegetarian, this was an odd development. I wanted to push my feed away from the motherhood content that now dominated into corners of Instagram linked to young men. I searched for the popular podcast to Joe Rogan. On YouTube, I subscribed to Rogan's channel and commented on his videos. I did the same to other accounts in YouTube's recommended list, namely Fox News and Sky News Australia. My Instagram feed didn't budge, not yet anyway. The next day, I watched Rogan's videos directly on Instagram. I returned to my reals feed. What I found there shocked me. In three swipes, I landed on a video from TopG inspired. It featured controversial internet personality Andrew Tate talking to a blonde woman. In the video, Tate implored men as being, quote, good at suffering. He calls women spiteful sufferers. I had not searched for Tate, a man who's been accused of rape and inspiring a generation of misogynists. I wasn't following his accounts or any for that matter. Yet here he was. Tate wasn't the only bigoted commentator I met that day. Sean Strickland, a mixed martial artist, appeared shortly after, wearing a t-shirt that said, woman in every kitchen, gun in every hand. He was talking to a man off screen who called himself an ally of the gay community. Strickland responded, saying there are two genders and calling the man weak and an infection. Over the next week, my feed entered a universe of anti-vaccine screeds, oads to all meat diets, information on how to increase testosterone and why nicotine is good for you, alongside more clips of Tate railing against feminism. These videos seem to carry a distinct ideological tilt, and I'm stunned that a handful of actions, both on and off the platform, were enough to trigger a wave of hyper-masculine conspiratorial content. Herun and his colleagues found that recommendation engines can funnel users towards progressively more extreme and polarizing content. They ran an experiment with 100,000 sock puppet accounts on YouTube, each with an assigned political ideology. More than 36% of these accounts received extremist video recommendations, for right-leaning accounts, that number was closer to 40%. Herun says, these more extremist channels, which are usually white nationalist, anti-work, anti-feminism, appear more often for people who are not necessarily watching these channels explicitly, but they are engaging with right-leaning content. He also says this study showed some degree of radicalisation was happening because of the recommendation systems used by social media companies. He says his experiment showed that personalisation is causing you to be in an ideological filter bubble. The question is, how do you escape? On a grey Melbourne afternoon, I clicked on a Zoom meeting for Internet and Technology Addix Anonymous, a gallery of boxes filled my screen, some blank with just their first names, others with faces from around the world. Internet and Technology Addix Anonymous is a support group for people struggling with Internet addiction. For many of its members, social media has become a vice, trapping them in an addictive bubble that they can't escape alone. This group follows a 12-step recovery model based on mutual support and spiritual guidance. Several spoke about their compulsion to scroll. Others about how online addiction has had serious consequences on their work and personal lives. Many expressed gratitude for being part of the group and their journey to recovery. A young man from Melbourne described to me how his entire nights were lost surfing YouTube and other platforms, falling deeper down the rabbit hole of recommended content. Even while signed out or in different devices, he felt pulled back in. Piers' support through this group helped him. He now uses special programs on his phone that block social media platforms and the other sites he finds particularly addictive. My experiment showed we can take deliberate steps to develop a healthier relationship with social media. We can spend time with people in places that reflect the content we want to see, engage with posts that uplift us and actively block those that don't. Algorithms reward engagement, so the more consciously we participate, the more consciously our feed responds. I tried following accounts on my experimental Instagram account that better reflected my interests. The bands I liked, the hobbies that excited me, the new sites I trusted. But often, I found myself drifting back to the extreme and conspiracy-laden videos that now littered my feed. And I was hesitant to give up the access. Yes, escaping these worlds curated by engagement-hungry algorithms takes effort. But after this experiment, I feel like I have a few more tools available to outsmart them. Maybe I'll do that later. episodes.title: Encore: the life and legacy of author John Marsden
episodes.description: Growing up, John Marsden found school incredibly difficult and, as a teenager, spent time in hospital after a breakdown. This difficult early life profoundly shaped his work as a writer and educator of young people.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Today is my conversation with the late John Marsden. John was a beloved children's author and a visionary educator who started his own school called Candle Bark in Victoria. I spoke with John in 2018. John Marsden was a high school English teacher when he wrote his first novel so much to tell you. John's writing took teenagers seriously. And right from that first book, they loved his novels. Tomorrow when the war began was the start of a series of books that imagined the invasion of Australia, resisted by a small band of teenagers waging guerrilla war. Long before the Hunger Games, John made young people the heroes of stories that had real consequences. But even as he became an internationally best-selling author, John never lost his love for teaching. In 1998, he bought a giant swag of natural bush on the northern edge of Melbourne, and eventually started his own school there called Candle Bark. It's a school that John's described as somewhere between Steiner and The Simpsons. Hi, John. Good day, sir. What works about that combination, Steiner and The Simpsons? Well, I shouldn't take too literally. So I think I like the subversiveness of The Simpsons and the way that it causes you to challenge your question or most every aspect of society. But I also like the fact that Steiner was on about being reflective and about big issues and profound thinking. There's stuff about the Steiner system I don't like, and stuff about systems I don't like. But between the two is some sort of worthwhile area to explore, I think. Let's go back into your childhood. What's your earliest memory, John? What comes to mind? Well, this is embarrassing being toilet trained. I remember sitting on the toilet and screaming in terror, thinking I was going to fall in. And I could hear my father and siblings playing outside. So the toilet must have been in the backyard, in the traditional manner. And I was, I think I was angry that they were having a good time while I was about to drop into this bottomless pit. The darkness didn't smell good, either. So who else was in your family? How many siblings do you have? Three others, yeah, boy, boy. Well, I can't say, boy anymore. He's nearly 70. Yeah, two sisters and one brother. You unspent some of your time growing up in Devon Port in Tasmania. What was that like as a place for you? It was idyllic for a kid. I mean, we just wandered and explored and adventure all day long. There was a ferry you could catch across the river and go to North Devon Port, which we did quite often. We loved the town tip. That was always a great playground. The town tip? What would you find? Oh, just anything from old stoves to the brick and things, broken plates. If they weren't broken, we'd break them. Or if they were broken already, we'd break them again. And we'd go through the bush, we'd go through the town. And the library was ever small, but it was my kind of safe place, I guess. How much time would you spend at the local library? This is sounds a bit like self-agrandism, but I'd go down after school and borrow three books, which was the maximum allowed to fiction and one nonfiction. And because rules were strict in those days. And take them home and try to read them before the library closed at whatever 6 p.m. or something. What would you do with the three books? And then race back and get three more. So I was an avid reader. And what were you getting from those books? Was it a kind of a competition if you were trying to get them read or was it where they were? No, it was the fear that I wouldn't have anything to read after about 9 o'clock if I didn't get three more books. It was an escape. It was disappearing into a different world. And so in everyone from England to Blighten to Nan Shaw and C to Geoffrey Trees, mostly British writers with quite a lot of Australian and a few American and not much else. There was a few European novelists that read, but it was just going into a world where things were so different. And I felt completely detached from reality, which seemed to be desirable to me. Why what was reality like at home? I was a bit grim, I have to say. I don't want to defame my parents after their deaths, but they were themselves, I suppose they mirrored what their parents had done. So my father had a tyrannical father. And I guess that made him quite a severe person himself. And my mother had a very manipulative and really quite negative mother. And I think she echoed some of those behaviors herself. So although they did their best as parents, they were forever changed. But their own childhood experiences, this is my best guess anyway. And that then meant that they weren't, it wasn't a very safe house to be in. As a kid, did you feel that your parents were interested in you? Interested, say, in your love of reading? No, they were interested in our achievements, which had to be of the highest order. And they were extremely critical of us at home, but very angry if anyone could have s-this outside the home. So if we got a bad school report, they'd be angry at the teacher and angry at us. It created conflict intention, which meant that by the start of adolescence or early in my adolescence, I stopped being the conformist child who was trying to achieve the highest possible standards in order to satisfy the unsatisfiable parents. And I became the rebel and went to the other extreme and started listening to Bob Dylan, God help me. That was the beginning of the end. I do remember the first time I heard a Bob Dylan song, it was lent to me by an amazing guy called Rob Bilby who I was at school with. And it was Mr. Tambourine man. And from the first notes and the first syllables of that voice, I was transfixed and transformed. And I remember almost consciously thinking, is this legal? You're allowed to do this? It just sounded like something so much the voice of the outlaw that I couldn't believe you were allowed to do it. And reading the catcher in the rye had the same effect on me. I was like, God, this isn't Thomas Hardy. This seems like our voice. And that seemed extraordinary to me that you could express that voice openly and publicly and even get paid and recognised for doing it. You're right. In Dylan's voice, there's so much attitude, isn't there? There's an identity in that voice. There's a message that's coming across regardless of what he's singing. There's a posture there. Yeah, it's like he's torn up the rule book even though he knows the rule book. I was talking at a conference organized by Griffith University about creativity and saying to teachers who are at the conference that as a teacher you need to teach kids what's in the rule book, and then they teach them to tear it up and how to tear it up and when to tear it up. And Dylan, he knows music as well as anybody. He's got an extraordinary knowledge of folk music and blues and gospel, but he's chosen to go his own way. But nevertheless, you can see the elements of those influences in his work. Why did your family leave Tasmania, John? My father was a bank manager and they had an inflexible policy that every four years people were transferred. And the way you'd find out that you were transferred was to get the Fortnite Lee Starve Bulletin and the last perhaps four or five pages was a list of the transfers for this fortnight. So you'd look up the list and if your name was on it you'd bring your partner and say start packing. We're off to Calgouli or Devonport or Brisbane or whatever. Yep, that's the way the system worked. Do you remember how you felt about moving from Devonport to Sydney? I was torn. I was excited about the big smoke going to the big city, but also had very strong feelings about leaving my friends and just walking away from a place where I'd just gradually established my own kind of territories and did feel safe when I was roaming around the countryside and the town. What was the drive up to Sydney like? It was a marathon. We took two nights staying in Golden and County Liberty, have a place along the way, Aubrey. And yeah, it was a massive road trip to us and it was hot. It was January and then we came to Sydney and it was just mind-boggling to go through suburb after suburb after suburb and being a car from Tasmania with Tasmania number plates made us an instant object of curiosity. And so crowds would gather when we stopped anywhere or when the people would point to the car and look at it with amazement as we drove around the city or the suburbs. Because I saw one other car from Tasmania during those early months before we got the number plates changed. Once you got to Sydney, John, where did you go to school? Well, I started at Castle Hill Primary and then went to Eastwood Primary and then ended up at the King School, which is for people who don't know it in all boys school, Anglican, very conservative with a military bent military philosophy or ideology. We had to wear military uniforms all day every day and a lot of marching and saluting and... Who did you have to salute? Our teachers, if we met them down the street or if anyone stopped to let us cross the road, we had to salute the driver of the car. We had to stand to attention when we spoke to prefects. Yeah, it was all down along Victorian lines and I mean Queen Victoria, not the state of Victoria. But it was pretty anachronistic. As a bookish kid or kid into Dylan and into Catherine the Rye, how did you find this environment? There was a small number of teachers who were quite liberal and I guess I could use a word. It's not used much in Australia and said that there were intellectuals and they were the people who kind of kept me sane, but they were in a minority and I don't know how they survived because it was a pretty rigid and authoritarian atmosphere. And I copped it big time because it was, as I was saying earlier, the start of my kind of adolescent rebellion against parents and that rebellion extended to the school and to the university really. I remember this moment. I don't know where this is common, but I was 4 to 1. I was standing outside my lockers after school one afternoon and I could take you to the spot today if you had time. And there was a kind of lightning strike through my brain and I suddenly thought, what if my parents aren't perfect and what if the school isn't right in all these rules and regulations and what if there is no God and what if all the politicians are not telling the truth and this all happened in the space of it seems to me. I don't know, 8 seconds. And it was like a lightning bolt and earthquake. The world was turned upside down to mix my metaphors and I was never the same again. I just, from then on, I questioned everything and challenged everything and started to see that appearances did not tell the truth and that there were other worlds which were difficult to find sometimes little and explore, but it was very worthwhile to try to get inside them. It's amazing that you can remember that in a, like, a road to Damascus moment were there are the kids that you kind of had shared sensibility with the talk to this stuff about. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, kids had a little prep school at Mosfail called Tudor House, which was a very idiosyncratic school and the students from there skipped the first year of secondary school at Tudor House and then came on to Kings in Year 8. And they were quirky, funny, engaging and challenged everything and rebelled happily at every opportunity. And I found great kinship with that group and again, they helped keep me sane to, well, not that I was particularly sane, but it was a lifeline really. Did that moment feel liberating or terrifying? Ah, both, but probably certainly terrifying. I wouldn't say liberating, but just incredibly powerful. I just sort of felt that I was now in a state of chaos or a limbo and I didn't know what was true anymore. I mean, Kings was very good and what I say about Kings now refers to 1968. I'm sure it's a very different school in 2018, but it was very good at appearances. And so the school looked wonderful, the campus looked beautiful, the buildings were spectacular, and the sight of aspirating around all day was apparently impressive. And yes, it was more like the heart of darkness. There was a tremendous amount of violence and bullying. And I think that was very important for me to realize that Western society was too much into illusion and appearances. You had a letter published in the School magazine in 1967, John, tell me about it. I wrote a letter just challenging the idea that the prefix should have so much power. It's that old adage which applies to anyone in a position of authority. Are you yourself, honourable enough to use an old fashioned word to tell other people how to behave and to punish them when they don't behave according to your criteria. So there were prefects who were obviously corrupt and were spectacularly corrupt and usually in the way in which they exercised their power, which was violently. So I wrote a letter just suggesting that this wasn't a very good system which caused outrage among some and the light among others, I guess. What was expected of you after finishing school? Well, I think just to follow the traditional career path, and so I got into Arts Law at Sydney University and didn't really think twice about doing that course, I had little interest in science or maths through my secondary schooling and I have to say that's largely due to inadequate teaching. I think that's a fair and objective comment. The science department in particular was really weak. And I don't know how you can make science boring but they managed to do it. And so that meant the very few paths were open to me and going to university was definitely expected. So I signed up but I was just lost at university. I think there were 23,000 students there in that era. And the psychology lectures I remember in particular because there were just giant video screens all through this massive auditorium. And the lecturer was sort of a distant figure at the front of the hall and so you'd watched the video screens. So the whole thing was incredibly impersonal. What about all that freedom and that meaning that you were wanting or hungering after as a high school student, wouldn't that have been everywhere on the campus in the late 60s? It possibly was but I'd gone badly off the rails but then by January had enough of life at home and I did the traditional thing of leaving a note on the pillow and nicking off it. It was meant to be a three o'clock in the morning and a friend was going to pick me up by stealing his mother's car, but he didn't arrive. And luckily I had a plan B which was a taxi driver who'd heard me talking about my plans one day when I was with a mate in the back of his cab. And he said, every shoulder, are you doing a midnight flip? I didn't even know what that meant. But sort of gave an evasive or ambiguous answer and he said, oh, you know, I'll come and pick you up for a count remember there. There is 20 bucks or 50 bucks any time 24 seven just ring this number. There was a sympathetic song. Well, he was it. It's a turned out. I wasn't sure what his motives were but I rang the number at about 5 a.m. And he came burning out to Paramatta so fast that his radio had boiled and we had to wait a while till it calmed down. And then took off again like where were you going? Where did he take you? Well, I found a room in Kings Cross. This sounds incredibly sorted and unlikely but it's all true. I'd been checking out rooms via estate agents, just little rental bed sitters. And I noticed that the window in one was open at the top to allow ventilation and it was on ground level in Kellogg Street.
