This episode of Conversations was produced by Nicola Harrison and the executive producer was Pam O'Brien. I'm Sarah Kanozki. Thanks for listening. ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more.

segments.text: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more.
Today is my conversation with the late John Marsden.
John was a beloved children's author and a visionary educator
who started his own school called Candle Bark in Victoria.
I spoke with John in 2018.
John Marsden was a high school English teacher when he wrote his first novel
so much to tell you.
John's writing took teenagers seriously.
And right from that first book, they loved his novels.
Tomorrow when the war began was the start of a series of books
that imagined the invasion of Australia,
resisted by a small band of teenagers waging guerrilla war.
Long before the Hunger Games,
John made young people the heroes of stories that had real consequences.
But even as he became an internationally best-selling author,
John never lost his love for teaching.
In 1998, he bought a giant swag of natural bush
on the northern edge of Melbourne,
and eventually started his own school there called Candle Bark.
It's a school that John's described as somewhere between Steiner and The Simpsons.
Hi, John.
Good day, sir.
What works about that combination, Steiner and The Simpsons?
Well, I shouldn't take too literally.
So I think I like the subversiveness of The Simpsons
and the way that it causes you to challenge your question
or most every aspect of society.
But I also like the fact that Steiner was on about being reflective
and about big issues and profound thinking.
There's stuff about the Steiner system I don't like,
and stuff about systems I don't like.
But between the two is some sort of worthwhile area to explore, I think.
Let's go back into your childhood.
What's your earliest memory, John? What comes to mind?
Well, this is embarrassing being toilet trained.
I remember sitting on the toilet and screaming in terror,
thinking I was going to fall in.
And I could hear my father and siblings playing outside.
So the toilet must have been in the backyard, in the traditional manner.
And I was, I think I was angry that they were having a good time
while I was about to drop into this bottomless pit.
The darkness didn't smell good, either.
So who else was in your family? How many siblings do you have?
Three others, yeah, boy, boy. Well, I can't say, boy anymore.
He's nearly 70. Yeah, two sisters and one brother.
You unspent some of your time growing up in Devon Port in Tasmania.
What was that like as a place for you?
It was idyllic for a kid.
I mean, we just wandered and explored and adventure all day long.
There was a ferry you could catch across the river
and go to North Devon Port, which we did quite often.
We loved the town tip. That was always a great playground.
The town tip? What would you find?
Oh, just anything from old stoves to the brick and things, broken plates.
If they weren't broken, we'd break them.
Or if they were broken already, we'd break them again.
And we'd go through the bush, we'd go through the town.
And the library was ever small, but it was my kind of safe place, I guess.
How much time would you spend at the local library?
This is sounds a bit like self-agrandism, but I'd go down after school
and borrow three books, which was the maximum allowed to fiction and one nonfiction.
And because rules were strict in those days.
And take them home and try to read them before the library closed
at whatever 6 p.m. or something.
What would you do with the three books?
And then race back and get three more.
So I was an avid reader.
And what were you getting from those books?
Was it a kind of a competition if you were trying to get them read
or was it where they were?
No, it was the fear that I wouldn't have anything to read after about 9 o'clock if I didn't get three more books.
It was an escape.
It was disappearing into a different world.
And so in everyone from England to Blighten to Nan Shaw and C to Geoffrey Trees,
mostly British writers with quite a lot of Australian and a few American
and not much else.
There was a few European novelists that read, but it was just going into a world
where things were so different.
And I felt completely detached from reality, which seemed to be desirable to me.
Why what was reality like at home?
I was a bit grim, I have to say.
I don't want to defame my parents after their deaths, but they were themselves,
I suppose they mirrored what their parents had done.
So my father had a tyrannical father.
And I guess that made him quite a severe person himself.
And my mother had a very manipulative and really quite negative mother.
And I think she echoed some of those behaviors herself.
So although they did their best as parents, they were forever changed.
But their own childhood experiences, this is my best guess anyway.
And that then meant that they weren't, it wasn't a very safe house to be in.
As a kid, did you feel that your parents were interested in you?
Interested, say, in your love of reading?
No, they were interested in our achievements, which had to be of the highest order.
And they were extremely critical of us at home, but very angry if anyone could have s-this outside the home.
So if we got a bad school report, they'd be angry at the teacher and angry at us.
It created conflict intention, which meant that by the start of adolescence or early in my adolescence,
I stopped being the conformist child who was trying to achieve the highest possible standards in order to satisfy the unsatisfiable parents.
And I became the rebel and went to the other extreme and started listening to Bob Dylan, God help me.
That was the beginning of the end.
I do remember the first time I heard a Bob Dylan song, it was lent to me by an amazing guy called Rob Bilby who I was at school with.
And it was Mr. Tambourine man.
And from the first notes and the first syllables of that voice, I was transfixed and transformed.
And I remember almost consciously thinking, is this legal? You're allowed to do this? It just sounded like something so much the voice of the outlaw that I couldn't believe you were allowed to do it.
And reading the catcher in the rye had the same effect on me.
I was like, God, this isn't Thomas Hardy. This seems like our voice.
And that seemed extraordinary to me that you could express that voice openly and publicly and even get paid and recognised for doing it.
You're right. In Dylan's voice, there's so much attitude, isn't there? There's an identity in that voice.
There's a message that's coming across regardless of what he's singing. There's a posture there.
Yeah, it's like he's torn up the rule book even though he knows the rule book.
I was talking at a conference organized by Griffith University about creativity and saying to teachers who are at the conference that as a teacher you need to teach kids what's in the rule book,
and then they teach them to tear it up and how to tear it up and when to tear it up.
And Dylan, he knows music as well as anybody. He's got an extraordinary knowledge of folk music and blues and gospel, but he's chosen to go his own way.
But nevertheless, you can see the elements of those influences in his work.
Why did your family leave Tasmania, John?
My father was a bank manager and they had an inflexible policy that every four years people were transferred.
And the way you'd find out that you were transferred was to get the Fortnite Lee Starve Bulletin and the last perhaps four or five pages was a list of the transfers for this fortnight.
So you'd look up the list and if your name was on it you'd bring your partner and say start packing. We're off to Calgouli or Devonport or Brisbane or whatever.
Yep, that's the way the system worked.
Do you remember how you felt about moving from Devonport to Sydney?

I was torn. I was excited about the big smoke going to the big city, but also had very strong feelings about leaving my friends and just walking away from a place where I'd just gradually established my own kind of territories and did feel safe when I was roaming around the countryside and the town.
What was the drive up to Sydney like?
It was a marathon. We took two nights staying in Golden and County Liberty, have a place along the way, Aubrey.

And yeah, it was a massive road trip to us and it was hot. It was January and then we came to Sydney and it was just mind-boggling to go through suburb after suburb after suburb and being a car from Tasmania with Tasmania number plates made us an instant object of curiosity.
And so crowds would gather when we stopped anywhere or when the people would point to the car and look at it with amazement as we drove around the city or the suburbs.
Because I saw one other car from Tasmania during those early months before we got the number plates changed.
Once you got to Sydney, John, where did you go to school?

Well, I started at Castle Hill Primary and then went to Eastwood Primary and then ended up at the King School, which is for people who don't know it in all boys school, Anglican, very conservative with a military bent military philosophy or ideology.
We had to wear military uniforms all day every day and a lot of marching and saluting and...
Who did you have to salute?
Our teachers, if we met them down the street or if anyone stopped to let us cross the road, we had to salute the driver of the car.
We had to stand to attention when we spoke to prefects. Yeah, it was all down along Victorian lines and I mean Queen Victoria, not the state of Victoria.
But it was pretty anachronistic.
As a bookish kid or kid into Dylan and into Catherine the Rye, how did you find this environment?
There was a small number of teachers who were quite liberal and I guess I could use a word.

It's not used much in Australia and said that there were intellectuals and they were the people who kind of kept me sane, but they were in a minority and I don't know how they survived because it was a pretty rigid and authoritarian atmosphere.
And I copped it big time because it was, as I was saying earlier, the start of my kind of adolescent rebellion against parents and that rebellion extended to the school and to the university really.
I remember this moment. I don't know where this is common, but I was 4 to 1. I was standing outside my lockers after school one afternoon and I could take you to the spot today if you had time.

And there was a kind of lightning strike through my brain and I suddenly thought, what if my parents aren't perfect and what if the school isn't right in all these rules and regulations and what if there is no God and what if all the politicians are not telling the truth and this all happened in the space of it seems to me.
I don't know, 8 seconds.
And it was like a lightning bolt and earthquake. The world was turned upside down to mix my metaphors and I was never the same again.

I just, from then on, I questioned everything and challenged everything and started to see that appearances did not tell the truth and that there were other worlds which were difficult to find sometimes little and explore, but it was very worthwhile to try to get inside them.
It's amazing that you can remember that in a, like, a road to Damascus moment were there are the kids that you kind of had shared sensibility with the talk to this stuff about.

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, kids had a little prep school at Mosfail called Tudor House, which was a very idiosyncratic school and the students from there skipped the first year of secondary school at Tudor House and then came on to Kings in Year 8.
And they were quirky, funny, engaging and challenged everything and rebelled happily at every opportunity.
And I found great kinship with that group and again, they helped keep me sane to, well, not that I was particularly sane, but it was a lifeline really.
Did that moment feel liberating or terrifying?
Ah, both, but probably certainly terrifying. I wouldn't say liberating, but just incredibly powerful.
I just sort of felt that I was now in a state of chaos or a limbo and I didn't know what was true anymore.
I mean, Kings was very good and what I say about Kings now refers to 1968. I'm sure it's a very different school in 2018, but it was very good at appearances.
And so the school looked wonderful, the campus looked beautiful, the buildings were spectacular, and the sight of aspirating around all day was apparently impressive.
And yes, it was more like the heart of darkness. There was a tremendous amount of violence and bullying.
And I think that was very important for me to realize that Western society was too much into illusion and appearances.
You had a letter published in the School magazine in 1967, John, tell me about it.
I wrote a letter just challenging the idea that the prefix should have so much power. It's that old adage which applies to anyone in a position of authority.
Are you yourself, honourable enough to use an old fashioned word to tell other people how to behave and to punish them when they don't behave according to your criteria.
So there were prefects who were obviously corrupt and were spectacularly corrupt and usually in the way in which they exercised their power, which was violently.
So I wrote a letter just suggesting that this wasn't a very good system which caused outrage among some and the light among others, I guess.
What was expected of you after finishing school?
Well, I think just to follow the traditional career path, and so I got into Arts Law at Sydney University and didn't really think twice about doing that course,
I had little interest in science or maths through my secondary schooling and I have to say that's largely due to inadequate teaching.
I think that's a fair and objective comment. The science department in particular was really weak.
And I don't know how you can make science boring but they managed to do it.
And so that meant the very few paths were open to me and going to university was definitely expected.
So I signed up but I was just lost at university. I think there were 23,000 students there in that era.
And the psychology lectures I remember in particular because there were just giant video screens all through this massive auditorium.
And the lecturer was sort of a distant figure at the front of the hall and so you'd watched the video screens.
So the whole thing was incredibly impersonal.
What about all that freedom and that meaning that you were wanting or hungering after as a high school student,
wouldn't that have been everywhere on the campus in the late 60s?
It possibly was but I'd gone badly off the rails but then by January had enough of life at home and I did the traditional thing of leaving a note on the pillow and nicking off it.
It was meant to be a three o'clock in the morning and a friend was going to pick me up by stealing his mother's car, but he didn't arrive.
And luckily I had a plan B which was a taxi driver who'd heard me talking about my plans one day when I was with a mate in the back of his cab.
And he said, every shoulder, are you doing a midnight flip? I didn't even know what that meant.
But sort of gave an evasive or ambiguous answer and he said, oh, you know, I'll come and pick you up for a count remember there.
There is 20 bucks or 50 bucks any time 24 seven just ring this number.
There was a sympathetic song.
Well, he was it. It's a turned out. I wasn't sure what his motives were but I rang the number at about 5 a.m.
And he came burning out to Paramatta so fast that his radio had boiled and we had to wait a while till it calmed down.
And then took off again like where were you going? Where did he take you?
Well, I found a room in Kings Cross. This sounds incredibly sorted and unlikely but it's all true.
I'd been checking out rooms via estate agents, just little rental bed sitters.
And I noticed that the window in one was open at the top to allow ventilation and it was on ground level in Kellogg Street.
And I thought, yeah, I could come in through that window and get into this place.
And I just gambled that it would still be empty when I arrived with my few mega possessions.
I had a couple of days later that's what I did. It was the Australia day weekend. It was a public holiday.
So Monday morning we arrived at this place and luckily the window was still open.
So I said to the taxi driver, I've lost my key. I'll go in through the window and let myself in through the door.
And I squatted in there for a few weeks until I had enough money to pay the rent.
And then went back to the real estate agent and said, I want to rent that room that you showed me a few weeks ago.
And they asked for the rent in advance, which I had. So that was fine. And then they asked for something called a bond.
And I said, what's a bond? And they said, well, it's what you explained what it was.
And I was just dumbfounded because I didn't have any more money.
And I guess this wouldn't happen now, but the two women there looked at each other and one said to the other, he seems like a nice boy.
The other one agreed and they decided that I wouldn't have to pay a bond.
So I moved in legally.
I hope you took very good care of that room.
I did. I didn't do anything to damage it at all. I vacuumed it occasionally even.
And I was there for about eight months, I think.
And what did you have any contact with your parents who just left a note on the pillow?
Yeah.
Yeah, I had friends whose family's three friends in particular whose parents helped me in different ways.
One gave me a lot of crockery and cutlery and cooking stuff and one lent me 50 bucks.
And the other one helped me find a job. So, yeah, there was a big factor.
And so when you were there at Sydney Uni and feeling overwhelmed by the numbers and the impersonality of it, I guess,
were you seeing a kind of future for yourself when you looked around at the other students, the people who were there? What did it look like?
Yeah, I didn't really think about that much. I was mainly interested in earning money to keep myself afloat.
And so I had a mantra which was take any job you're offered. And so at times I was working three different jobs,
cleaning job on weeknights, working at Sydney Hospital on weekends and just picking up casual work occasionally as well.
So I wasn't giving much time or effort to study.
And the time came when I had actually some couple of years down the track, I'd got as far as the second year law.
And I'd landed articles with a very good firm. But towards the end of second year, I was in the cafeteria at the law school in Phillips Street.
And the final year students were all coming in for their evening classes and they were all doing articles.
So in apprenticeship effectively. And they all had these grey pinstripe suits, three-piece suits.
And I just saw this army of pinstripe suited men mostly.
Coming through the doors of the cafe and I thought I can't do this assist. I can't join that army.
And I got up and left and went back a couple of days later to clear up my locker. But that was the last time I entered the doors.
The hall of doors of the law school.
How were things going for you emotionally at this time, John?
Oh, badly as you'd expect. I ended up in a psych hospital for about six weeks, I think.
What was going to end up in the psych pool? I was suicidal. And I thought in a very rational way, I haven't ever seen a psychiatrist.
And I think psychiatry sounds like a load of bunking. And I'd seen American comedies about psychiatrists, which made them all sound like nutcases.
But I thought it'd be pretty silly to kill myself without at least trying this path because obviously you must have something to offer.
And so I went and saw one and I think that was the turning point really. I think what I learned in that hospital was immensely valuable.
And although it was a painful time, it was also a time of discovery. And so I'm very grateful to the staff there. It was a positive experience.
When you took that, you know, very courageous and smart decision to check into a hospital, could you name what you were feeling?
And you'd even have the language to talk about what you were experiencing?
No, there was something that slowly dawned on me while I was in there that I didn't have the language of emotions.
I looked back on that and think how weird that is. But it was true that they'd get me to talk about things that had happened to me.
And I'd do that. And then they'd say, but how did you feel when that happened?
And I'd just look at them completely unable to answer and look at them quizzically and say, what do you mean? How did I feel?
I'd say, well, you must have felt something. And I'd think, God, I don't know what I felt. And I had to develop, I had to learn of vocabulary for feelings.
I was 19 when this was going on and a bit late to be learning those words. But that's essentially what happened.
And that stood me in good stead since I think I learned a lot there about honesty and emotions.
How do you go about learning that language if you haven't learned it from your family or your teachers?
Well, I guess because they were good at their job and they kept probing and saying, and they'd prompt me, they'd say, did you feel anger?

And I think, yeah, I guess I did. Yeah, yeah. And I remembered, for example, looking into a mirror when I was about nine and using all the bad words I could think of against my parents who weren't in the room at the time, of course.
But I was saying them out loud to the mirror that you are beep, beep, beep. And I was a bit horrified at that age that I was doing it. And I didn't know why I was doing it.
But when I looked back at that at the age of 19, I could see that, yeah, that's anger. So there was just recalling all the aspects of those experiences, I guess.
Was there one therapist or one psychiatrist in particular that you made a connection with?

Yeah, there was a young social worker there. They had a team to look after each patient. And so there'd be the psychiatrist and the psychiatric registrar and a couple of nurses and so on under social worker.
And something about this social worker meant this about her ability to listen and respond seemed to work for me. So I asked if I could sort of make her the person I talked to most.
And then when I was discharged, I kept seeing her and she became a psychotherapist, a psychoanalytic called psychotherapist, not even sure what that means, even to the state.
But I kept seeing her intermittently for 40 years. She moved to Melbourne eventually and later I moved to Victoria and resumed the connection.
So that became an extremely long relationship, obviously, which meant that I was seeing her for many years, it was five days a week.
Sometimes four days a week or three during other periods, depending on which decade you're talking about, yeah, until she retired, that was an incredibly important relationship.
What was it about the way that she listened to you that was so helpful?
She never gave me advice and she never talked about herself and she was completely scrupulous and honest and ethical in every respect.
I'd never met anyone like that, but I sort of needed that. I needed someone objective because I'd been surrounded by people who were emotionally very caught up in their own lives.
And I didn't want to take on someone else's emotions again. It was too taxing.
So what was it like when she retired?
She gave me plenty of warning and we sort of meant this, we could sort of prepare for it, but yeah, I was very tearful for the last couple of sessions.
And I still, if she went back into business tomorrow, I'd be there on the doorstep. So it was life sustaining.
I think without that, I think I probably would have ended up taking my own life to be blunt. I was pretty desperate.
So I'm very grateful to her, but yeah, there's no magic cure. I don't think that I'm now completely happy, healthy, fulfilled person.
Not sure if anyone is, but it's a lot to ask for or hope for.
But it has given me strength to cope with crises and to deal with difficult situations and running a school. You certainly need some sort of inner strength.
But how did teaching enter the picture?
Partly for negative reasons. I think I was so angry at the schooling that I'd been subjected to.
For 13 years, I'd had two inspiring teachers and another one who was pretty good, but I wouldn't say inspiring.
And the rest varied from mediocre to just appalling. And really, for 13 years, that's not much.
And yet people I met nowadays, young people nowadays seem to have a similar strike rate.
So I don't think anything much has changed. So I was angry about the way I was taught. I felt that it could be done better.
And having dropped out of four university courses, which you could do in those days, in five years, I'd lost all confidence.
So I thought I'd choose the easiest tertiary course that I could find. If I failed that, I dropped out of that, that would prove to me that I was a completely useless student.
So I chose a primary teaching course at a country, C-A-E, because I figured that you can't get anything easier.
And I got to say, from the first day, I was utterly energized and excited, but of course, because they were quite overtly teaching us to be subversive.
And they were saying, get out there and change the system and don't accept the practices and traditions that you'll find, but instead turn them upside down and change everything.
So John, when you began your teaching degree and found it invigorating and exciting, you then moved out into actual teaching in a school. How did that compare?

It was good in many ways. It was a school at Bathurst in New South Wales, or St. College, and they'd had an extraordinary few years under the leadership of a guy called Peter Gebhard, who later went on to run Jolong College in Victoria.

And I think he was appointed principal at 28, or some extraordinary age like that. But he gathers around him the most exciting group of teachers that anyone could possibly find, and the place just took off as far as cultural and spiritual and artistic and aesthetic kind of issues went.
And unfortunately, he just missed that because he'd left and a new person had come, a very conservative person. But so many of his staff remained that it was a really exciting place to work.
And I learned more about teaching from those colleagues in those first couple of years than I have ever done before or since.
How big a part was sport of that school culture?
Oh, yeah, it was, I was a sports master for the first year.
You were a sports master.
Who was?
We'll call it back for that role.
Not at all. But I was desperate to get a job and tried to make myself, I've been getting a free board in exchange for helping supervise borders and coached sporting teams and so on.
Well, I did my university course on my CAE course. And so I already was at the school for two years before I got a job there.
And I could see that unemployment in teaching was a problem. So I decided to make myself indispensable.
So that that half of me a job and they did. But the only vacancy they have was sports master and PE teacher.
So there I was. And I mean, when I said Kings, they ranked rugby teams by ability and rugby was compulsory.
But you could be in the under 16 A's B C's all the way down to H's. I was reserved for the H's for my whole school career.
So the end up as a sports master was certainly something paradoxical.
But I quite enjoyed it. And then gradually I got to teach more and more English and enjoyed that even more.
I'd have to say.
When did you first have the idea of starting your own school? Was it way back then?
Yeah, absolutely. And about my first or second year of teaching in Bethesda. I put an ad in the Sydney Morning Herald.
And we got about 18 or 20 replies from people who were interested, but it wasn't enough. And we didn't have any money or location or anything.

There's a couple of teachers at all Saints and I who put the ad in. And it was, yeah, it was certainly enough to wet my interest and to make me think, yeah, there is a response that's possible to generate for something like this.
But I didn't try again until many years later, the mid 80s when I tried for Wager. And in a very rational way, picked Wager as the 17th biggest city in Australia.
And the highest one on the list that didn't have an independent school. So that's the only criterion that I used.

And again, it's fizzled out. We got much closer. I've made the decision then that the only way to do it was to get enough money to do it yourself without having to go around sort of with cap in hand begging for money and trying to squeeze
a dollar here and a dollar there. And I thought, today it becomes when I get enough money to do it myself. I'll do it, but otherwise it's just a waste of time and energy.
So did you start writing fiction as a way to make money? No, I don't think that was, I bought lottery tickets, but that didn't work, funnily enough.
I don't think that was connected. Writing with something that always done and loved and it was just my creative outlook.
When you started though writing the book that led to being published your first novel, did you have a particular reader in mind or what were you trying to do with that book?
I just wanted to write something that modern adolescence would respond to because having studied Thomas Hardy at school and other writers like him, the society had changed, but the literature hadn't.
And although a couple of American writers were just emerging who wrote for teenagers, it was an unknown field, an unknown genre.
But I read those American writers, Paul Zindale and Judy Bloom and I thought these guys are onto something.
And then at about the same time the year 9 students started asking me for books that I could recommend.
And I went into the school library and combed the shelves and came out empty handed and feeling very depressed and feeling that I'd failed them.
And I thought, bugger this, I'll write one myself. And so I did write so much to tell you and gave it to six students to read.
And they all responded positively. One girl wept as she talked about the effect that it had on her.
And I don't know, maybe she just wanted to know in English or something, but she's saying very sincere and I was very moved by her response.
And so I kept going.
What was it about the way that you were writing that you think connected with those six readers and then all the readers after?
Was it different language? Was it the story? What was it that you were doing?
Well, it was certainly different language and different story. I had in mind that at age of W.H. Eldens that you should marry the highbrow with the lowbrow.
So I wanted to write a story that would be accessible and engaging, but at the same time have more profound, I don't know, debts to it than end of life and God rest her soul.
And I think you said in your introduction something about treating young people is important.
I totally respect their feelings and their thoughts. So if they fall in love, I'm not going to mock it or make condescending comments about puppy love or tell them, oh, yes, we all get a hug.
When we're 14, it's the love that you feel at any age is intense and incomparable.
And I respect that whether it's a 10 year old or a 15 year old or a 50 year old.
What did you understand teenagers to be interested in to care about from your experience with them as a teacher?

Relationships in the world, they're at that age where they still have the egoism of young children in that they are concerned about their own lives and so on, but they also can take a global perspective.
And so they're deeply interested in the environment and issues like that. Many of them are interested in politics, many of them are interested in history and philosophy.
So we are pretty patronizing in the way we treat them. Like I've been to schools where they set role dial books for year seven or eight students.
And I really admire role dials books, but not for studying in a year seven or eight English class. They've written for primary age children.
And I think it's incredibly patronizing to give them stuff like that.
So secondary school, when I teach year seven English, I start most years that I've done it. The very first lesson is Shakespeare.
We dive straight into Hamlet because I want to give them a shock and realize, okay, we're in the big world now.
But also they're ready for that. They can handle that and they can take on that challenge.
After your first novel so much to tell you was published, how quickly did you start hearing from readers?
Oh, yeah, pretty quickly. It was kind of what you dream of as a writer that people will write to you these letters.
And they were heartbreaking. Many of them, 10 ages writing about their lives and the difficulties they encountered.
Some of those became quite long correspondences that went on for some years, including one with the girl who died essentially of psychological problems that she was experiencing.
And yeah, it was pretty heart-rending stuff. How do you know how to respond to those letters?
I guess just because I'd been through therapy myself. And so I wrote back in the same kind of style.
Really, I just respond sympathetically without getting mushy or emotional.

episodes.title: Losing three mothers in one lifetime—Layne Beachley's drive to win
episodes.description: The legendary surfer has grieved the deaths of her adoptive mother, stepmother and birth mother. Only later in life did she realise her drive to win came from a place of loss, and Layne needed to look inward to find her place off the podium.
episodes.transcript: Corbin Middlemas here, the Ashes were awesome, but they are over. The good news is, the cricket keeps rolling, as the focus shifts to the T20 World Cup. Search for ABC cricket podcast, wherever you get your podcasts. ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music, and more. When Lane was a little girl, her dad Neil, told her she was adopted, and from that moment, Lane questioned where she really belonged. But I think also he acknowledged that at a population level, not every Australian voter will necessarily be feeling confident enough to go further down that path with the Americans. But we're in the Asia region. Our geography is different. Big Chinese diaspora here in Australia. Very successful migrant communities from all over Southeast Asia. This changes the shape and even the psychology and the mentality of a nation. What it does is it prepares us to be able to do so if we choose to.
And in the process, hopefully, will deter conflict.
So I understand it's difficult, of course, now a lot of questions about the commitment of the United States.
Does Australia want to deepen its partnership with the United States in this moment?
What it does is we already have an alliance together.
The United States already has an alliance with Australia.
What this is actually about more than commitments with the United States is commitments with each other for Australia and Japan, for instance, to integrate with each other.
And not just have the existing prevailing system, which is something that's often referred to as a hub and spoke model with the United States in the middle and separate alliances.
So it brings those allies together, such that Australia and Japan could operate more seamlessly with each other.
You're here, obviously speaking, to foreign policy, experts and officials, defense experts.
But there is a public that has very strong views about these matters.
Is it a strange time to be talking about building stronger American relationships in the world, talking about multilateralism?
When it seems from the outside that America wants to go in the opposite direction, Trump's walking all over existing alliances, degrading NATO.
That is true to a certain degree, but I will tell you here in the Indo-Pacific, America's alliances have been moving forward in deepening over the last year in near continuity.

I was recently out at a defense conference in Honolulu. You wouldn't have known anything had changed in international politics if you were out there listening to military leaders from the United States, but also from Australia, from Japan, from other partners describing their ambitions, their trajectories, their plans for 2026.
We're going to have our biggest exercises ever. We're going to have more partners there than ever.
So we're going to have more capabilities than ever. So defense and security quality has been siloed off, I think.
What's the difference then for this region compared with Europe? Like, why does this US administration take a kind of full-stem ahead approach here, and yet it in Europe it's so different?
Yeah, well, I'm not here as a spokesman for the Trump administration, so I don't know the answer to that for sure, but there clearly has been a difference.
And the animus that has been directed at the Europeans and the consequences of that, we have not seen thankfully here in the Indo-Pacific.
I think that's in part because the Asian allies have responded in a very positive way in areas that are important to the Trump administration on defense spending, on things like critical minerals.

And also the nature of the China challenge is growing and severe, and the imperatives of that are that the United States is, in fact, working with its allies, whereas I think in Europe, the perception is Russia and the European continent is something for the Europeans to deal with on their own.
You don't hear that about the Indo-Pacific American strategist saying, hey, it's up to Australia and Japan to keep China at bay. That's not America's approach.
You used an interesting word earlier. You said that you think that China is seeking to revise the way it operates in the Indo-Pacific.
What is the revision? What is the nature of the revision? And what is it that you're fearful of?
Well, I think we actually have a relatively clear sense of what China's military ambitions and security ambitions are in the Indo-Pacific.
They want to unify with Taiwan. They want to seize Taiwan through force if necessary. They want to control the South China Sea.
They want to weaken U.S. alliances, and they want to dominate the East Asian littoral all the way up from the East China Sea down through the South China Sea.

I think that would be part of a broader effort of Beijing to control the economics and the politics of the Indo-Pacific in ways that would have very negative effects on U.S. national interest from a security.
And prosperity perspective, and potentially from a political perspective as well. I think it would be really corrosive to our societies and our way of life.
Can I ask what you mean by that? Because let's just take the South China Sea trade routes. Let's say there's a conflict and China ends up in control or dominates that space.
Presumably, they want it to operate peacefully and effectively. How does that damage the United States long ago?
They've given them coercive leverage over America's ability to access the most important economic and political region of the world in the 21st century.

And what we saw over the last year was Xi Jinping absolutely willing to use co-lors of leverage over the United States, for instance in the area of China's dominance in rare earths, to get the Trump administration to change its foreign policy and its politics.
And we will just see versions of that. I think we've seen a micro...
When are we doing similar things to them? We microchips onto the Biden administration?

We were, but for different reasons. And I think I would not draw moral parallelism between the Communist Party and the Trump administration as frustrated as folks are with the United States of America right now.

I read in the paper over the last couple days, as you probably know, that there's been an incident here in Australia where Chinese national drivers, delivery food drivers who are potentially going to be part of some kind of labor action.
Their families are being threatened back in China because the Chinese government doesn't want to see them organizing around politics and labor in a way that may reflect back on Beijing.
So these things are driving into our domestic politics. It's affecting labor disputes. It's affecting your universities. It's affecting your media.

And I think the question is, do you want the people's Republic of China and the Chinese Communist Party to have co-lors of leverage over Australian society in areas where you really value and probably assume that your freedoms are not at risk.
And I just think we are so used to an era in which those things aren't contested. We have not seen our countries be under military coercive leverage in a very long time.
I think that would be a real wake-up call and we ought to prevent that.
Do you think Australians are naive about the power of China wields? I mean, in other interviews you've talked about warning Australians against co-zying up with China.
It's not a zero-sum game. Australia has surely the sophistication to be able to navigate this.

Absolutely. Look, for countries here in the Indo-Pacific and I travel across and work across the region here in Asia, China is a political, economic, geographic, and cultural reality for countries in the region.
And what I'm proposing is not to make that go away. But maybe I'll talk about my own country rather than making a judgment about Australians.
I don't think the United States government has yet to approach the China challenge with the attention, urgency, and resources that it warrants.
I think we've been distracted on other issues. I think we've assumed a level of military primacy, assumed a level of technological leadership that frankly is not how things are playing out right now.
The time is running out for the United States and its partners to maintain areas that we want to maintain control and at least an advanced lead-in like technology and military.
The scenario you're describing where China influences more of the domestic politics of countries like Australia and presumably the region as well.
I wonder if America is aware of the fact that we're always calibrating these big, great power relationships.
And we have experienced economic coercion, particularly during COVID, many of the countries in this region, Southeast Asia, particularly have experienced that recently but also historically.
And at the moment, America issues trade barriers and tariffs that will remove them, can you understand why these arguments that you're making are viewed with a bit more nuanced today?

Of course, and I don't support those policies. I think treating particularly allies in a core of sufficient, levying tariffs against countries like Australia that are not guilty of the kind of economic and balance.
And unfair trade practices that do exist in other contexts does not make strategic sense. And it's undermining US influence and interest around the world.

I think that's widely recognized in Washington. So I agree with you. I don't think that's the permanent state of US foreign policy. And there's a lot of people arguing that well, we're not going to be able to rewind the clock and go backwards that we ought to be taking a much different approach to international economics and to our alliances.

And that we ought to particularly in the context of the China challenge, which presents itself in many instances as a challenge of scale that America will fundamentally need to be working with allies and partners to continue advancing its interest.
So I agree it is strategically counterproductive and doing things that require allies to stick their neck out and take risk is going to be less likely in that context.
You're listening to global roaming on radio national as we talk with former US defense official doctor Eli Ratner.

And if you're one of these people that has been thinking to yourself, you know, maybe Australia needs to look elsewhere away from the United States. Well, Eli Ratner has got a message for you and it may involve looking in the mirror.
I wonder what you envisage the path back to some kind of more normal American foreign policy and foreign economic policy is.

We hear countless Americans say this is an aberration. But then, you know, we're kind of, I guess talking about, look, do we just have to accept that this is America and it will be America in the future and Trump is not some blip that America is going down a different path.
Not Connie certainly thinks so.

Well, I think there may be threads of President Trump's approach to the world that do outlast his presidency, for instance, some of the tariffs, some of the efforts to rebalance economic relationships with partners which frankly have historically been quite unfair and quite imbalanced as opposed to America's more open market.
And the desire of the Trump administration to see allies and partners taking on more responsibility within alliance relationships is long overdue.

I think that will likely continue. But the excesses we're talking about here, I think are likely to be corrected. Some of that may happen as soon as the midterm elections where I think we're likely to see Republicans starting to distance themselves a little bit more from Trump Democrats, maybe taking over one or both houses of Congress and we're going to have another presidential election before we know it.
So that doesn't mean somehow again we're going to be able to go back to exactly the way things were before.

But I don't think Donald Trump's foreign policy represents the center of American public opinion and foreign policy and the public opinion polls show that he's quite unpopular now and his excessive actions and rhetoric in places like Greenland are very unpopular in the United States.

I think what we're seeing in response to some of his actions, we're seeing millions of people out in the streets of the United States and peaceful protest of what the Trump administration is doing. Are we seeing any mass gatherings in his favor or marches or not.

So what I'm seeing now is already a process of recalibration. Trump's still president. He's going to be for another three years and that has major consequences and we ought to not downplay the effects of that. But I also think it would be a misinterpretation to say everything's different.

America has changed. American foreign policy is now somehow again some moral equivalents to Chinese aggression and assertiveness and that's a new fact of life. I hope that's not the case. And I think the trend lines are not pointing in that direction.
Do you think some of your allies and out the point of almost wanting Trump's America to fail?

Well, I think it's been it is interesting watching the responses of allies to this context and you mentioned because I think your your reference of sort of moral equivalents of China and Trump's America. I see and hear that.

People saying, well, maybe we can tolerate some of what China does because Trump's no better. And you know, you might dismiss it and say that's an unreasonable comparison. But it exists to clearly exist in people's minds.

It does. Look, I guess what I would say here is for folks who are having this reaction of I really hate what Trump is doing. I'm done with you. I'm done with America. I'm going somewhere else. I mean, maybe take a look in the mirror.

What does it mean about your country and your leadership if the minute that there's an American president doing something that you don't like you want to sever your relationship with the United States?
What does that mean about your own understanding of your country's cultural historical economic ties with the United States? How deep they are and how important they are?

So in some ways, I think the not that President Trump's actions haven't been totally unacceptable. I fully agree with that. So I'm not making excuses for them. But I do think the way that countries are responding to President Trump are as much a reflection of them and their beliefs and their their commitment.
I will just say generally they are commitment to the United States and the US relationship as it is about Donald Trump. So I would recommend or I wouldn't even say I recommend.

I am encouraged by countries particularly in this region, including the government here in Japan and elsewhere who are looking a little bit more broadly on the horizon about the broader relationship with the United States and seeing that as something that's deeper and bigger and longer lasting and much more fundamental than just Donald Trump.
Like you're going to pick up your ball from the playground and go home if you don't like what you're experiencing.

You're going to be spending more focus on, you know, how can I protect myself? Do I have the level of autonomy and independence that I need?

I think that's all natural and acceptable. I guess I'm making a different point, which is as you do all that, don't take steps that make it a self-fulfilling prophecy of breaking these relationships in a way when maybe

folks are getting a little too wound up in what's the latest outrage on social media and reacting to something that feels very important and very significant, but I think in the long run not that it's a blip, but that we're going to get through this and we ought to looking on the future and we ought to look at what's important.
And to my earlier point, there's a reason why we have been together and working together and trading together and operating militarily together for a long time.

There's a foundation there and we ought to keep that in mind as we're considering these near term actions to adjust to the reality of Trump's America, but not in the process, break up much more fundamental, more important set of relationships.

We've just had Democrat Senator Tim Cain on the show and he says that he's confident Australia actually will spend more on defense. Do you think that's inevitable given the cost of these submarines in this project?
Well, my interesting is we'll know the answer to that in a few months about exactly what kind of increase may occur within the expectation.

Well, I think my expectation is there may be some increase. I'm not convinced we're going to see the level of increase that is necessary to provide for all of the requirements that the Australian military does need to fulfill.

This has been a hugely intensive thing from a resource perspective. That's important. That ought to continue. That ought to be fully funded and resourced. But I think there are concerns in Washington that the government has cannibalized defense spending in other areas to pay for a caustic and that there are really important things like airfield upgrades and infrastructure, missile defense capabilities that maybe won't be receiving the level of resources that they need that are important for defending Australian troops, defending US troops.

So, my personal view is that just looking at a percentage of GDP defense spending tends to be counterproductive. But there are important capability areas where we do need to study, see Australian investing. And I'm not sure we've seen that yet. And what I heard in Canberra is well certain folks in the national security apparatus would like to spend more on defense. It's a very fiscally difficult environment. There's a lot of other needs.

My reaction to that is welcome to every democracy in the world. And I'm not sure that's going to fly as an excuse as to why the Australian military should not be fulfilling its requirements. So, we all have tough issues around social programs and social spending. We all have a lot of demands. And I think there is a question of whether the Australian government is going to be making tough choices and is going to be putting on those table and wrestling with this. And to date, I think the answer to that is probably not.
And can you color that in what circumstances are you talking about what's the scenario in which this is an issue?
Well, the scenario in which it is an issue is if and when Australian forces, but also US forces, need to be able to operate from Australia.

We are in the process of developing a huge number of force posture initiatives throughout Australia. All I should say very carefully conducted under the condition of Australia is very important sovereignty policy.
But nonetheless, those forces are here in part to defend Australia, but in part also to project power up into the South China Sea or up into the Taiwan Strait or Northeast Asia.

Such that the United States does not have choke points around its traditional major military bases in South Korea in Japan, which had been the traditional way of getting forces and sustaining forces in the region, having more points of access and access at further distance from China create much stronger logistics, force flow, and more resilient US military presence in the region.

So we are facing a very significant and growing threat we're facing an ambitious rival in the investments and deterrence are going to be way cheaper than the investments in dealing with the consequences of crisis and conflict.
So we ought to be doing the prevention right now rather than dealing with the disease once it manifests.
Well, Kylie, quite a lot there to unpack. I mean, it will certainly not be lost on listeners that message to allies, maybe wobbling, maybe wavering, take a look in the mirror.
What does it say about your country that you are nervous because of what Trump's doing?
And when I tried to challenge him on that and say, come on, it's not just us who are nervous, look at all of our traditional allies who also feel the same way.
This is based on something we're seeing before our eyes. He may have understood it, but all the same.
The messaging around President Trump's foreign policy was just hold on, this will change, just bear with us, stay strong in the alliance.
Let's keep building Beijing is there, nothing has changed in terms of the threat from Beijing and that's what we should be focused on.
And he talked about, I guess, his dream scenario of more points of access, joint command centers.
And he talked about he's been addressing military leaders and talking to other kind of strategic thought leaders and the conversations that are going on.
But I think also he acknowledged that at a population level, not every Australian voter will necessarily be feeling confident enough to go further down that path with the Americans.

Well, I suppose interestingly that scenario, joint commands, joint operating commands, does assume not necessarily the sovereignty is seated as such, but it assumes a certain position that Australia would be on the same side as America.
And you know, I suppose there might be people listening that say, look, we haven't forgotten the history.
Actually, Australia has stood side by side with America ever since World War One.
Australia has gone into those explorationary conflicts in the Middle East.
It hasn't necessarily worked out well. And I do think Australians, rightly or wrongly, have a different view of China.
But we're in the Asia region. Our geography is different. Big Chinese diaspora here in Australia.
Very successful migrant communities from all over Southeast Asia.
This changes the shape and even the psychology and the mentality of a nation.
So maybe when we do look in the mirror, maybe we see something slightly different to what Americans see when they imagine us looking in the mirror.
If you have any feedback, remember, please keep it coming. Don't forget to write to us. We love your questions.
Our email is global.roamingatabc.net.au
Thanks for our producers, Aston Brown and Shane Anderson.
Tomorrow, Jerry and Latika will be here. They're going to look a bit deeper, peel back the layers of the rest of Andrew Mountbatten Windsor.
The implications of this for the Royal Family, the British institutions and public.
Catch it 11 a.m. or 9 p.m. on Radio National any time on ABC Listen.
Rome, Freely and Wildly Kylie. I'll see you next time.
Thanks, Hamish. See you.
