episodes.title: How Marco Rubio became MAGA's friendly face in Europe
episodes.description: At last year's Munich Security Conference, Vice President JD Vance shocked the world with his fiery attack on Europe.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music and more. Anthony Burke here, host of By Design on ABC Radio National. A show about the clever ideas and human stories behind the spaces, systems and objects shaping everyday life. Whether you're curious about architecture, interior design, fashion or anything in between, we reveal why design matters in a rapidly changing world. By design on ABC Listen. Okay Geraldine, here's the setup. Marco Rubio, Ursula Von Der Lein and Velodomizelenski walk into a bar in Munich. Will they leave with a new world order? I'll very clever. All that is the question we're all asking after this year's Munich Security Conference. But there is someone crucial missing from your lineup because you were there too, Latica. Just as a mere observer Geraldine, but you know who else wasn't there? The infamous star of last year's conference, JD Vance. Yes, relief all round. Is the US trying to win back the Europeans? Or is it all part of their act? I'm Geraldine Duke. And I'm Latica Burke. This is Global Roaming, reporting back from the Munich Security Conference. Yes, so what was it like, Latica, this year's Munich Security Conference? Crazy, mental, exhausting. It is the premier security defense discussion in Europe. There's no doubt about that, Geraldine, but it has become a very unwieldy beast. And so it's a very difficult conference to access. Journalists get yellow badges and if you want to go into the building, you have to be escorted by a military escort. You'll watch the entire time where you conduct an interview and then marched back on out. If you're lucky enough to get a green badge, which you can get, you're allowed to go certain places and talk to people. If you're lucky enough to get a blue and a white badge, you can almost do anything and go into the hall and watch the big wig speeches. Luckily this year I had one of those. Did you feel a different tone like last year? I mean the JD events last year was received in silence. People were so shocked, we'll just play a little bit of it for people to remember. But while the Trump administration is very concerned with European security and believes that we can come to a reasonable settlement between Russia and Ukraine, and we also believe that it's important in the coming years for Europe to step up in a big way to provide for its own defense, the threat that I worry the most about VISAV Europe is not Russia, it's not China, it's not any other external actor. And what I worry about is the threat from within the retreat of Europe from some of its most fundamental values, values shared with the United States of America. Last year I was with a bunch of Europeans watching that speech up on the Mizzini level in the coffee lounge and everyone was just shell shocked. No one is asking that question anymore, it's not just JD events. I think the real Rubicon that was crossed was Greenland. And that's really the frame that everyone approached this year's Munich. I think two things happened. The Europeans were ready for the tough talk, for the tough love, for the hard conversations. Some chose to talk about the action they're taking and others like Friedrich Mertz who opened with his speech actually had a real needle at Mager and said, look, keep your culture wars over there, this is not for us, thank you very much. The culture of the culture of the Mager movement in the USA is not our. The other thing I think that happened is that there is a very clear divide between what Europeans are saying out loud and what they're really thinking and doing and feeling and saying privately to anyone who's not American. And that divergence in diplomacy terms, I think that's always been there, but this year I think that absolute has them widened and deepened and I'm not really sure the Americans have clocked that. Very interesting. We'll look at it's a perfect reason to talk to Ravi Agraval. He's been a guest on Global Roaming before. He joins us from New York. He's just returned from the conference as well in his role as editor in chief of foreign policy. And he also hosts its podcast, F.P. Live. So here he is now. Ravi Agraval, welcome back to the show. Great to be back. How do you think people will reflect, will look back on this year's conference? Well, I think that the conference is very much a continuation from last years. Everyone this year was really waiting to see what the Americans would say. And so Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State, gave a speech that actually wasn't that different in substance but was much nicer in tone. It's because we care deeply. We care deeply about your future and ours. And if at times we disagree, our disagreements come from our profound sense of concern about a Europe with which we are connected, not just economically, not just militarily. We are connected spiritually and we are connected culturally. And so he got around of applause when he was speaking. But broadly, Europeans, I think, are back to square one where they were last year, which is to say they don't really trust the United States. They don't think the United States will help them when they truly need help. Long term, they very much need to boost their defense spending, defense infrastructure. But they're very aware that that will take many years. So there's no immediate fix. And Europeans are living in a state of relative crisis. Ravi, what do you think Marco Rubio set out to do at this year's Munich? And what do you think he achieved? I think he set out to be very clear about the way in which the United States sees Europe. He was riffing on a lot of shared cultural history. We want Europe to be strong. We believe that Europe must survive. Because the two great wars of the last century serve for us as history's constant reminder that ultimately our destiny is and will always be intertwined with yours. Because we know. Now, all of that said, and those are reassuring words, he did, of course, riff on a shared civilizational history, which some have interpreted as a racial unity. It came across in some parts as maybe harkening back to an era of colonization. But by and large, I think Rubio set out to present a friendly American face. And yet one in which the substance of US foreign policy hasn't changed much from the last year. Look, this is a little aside, but I heard that it was standing room only like hanging from the rafters for the Rubio speech. But the Wang Ye speech, the very important and significant Chinese foreign minister, his speech had lots of empty chairs in it, which was fascinating. And the assumption was, it just doesn't resonate. Did that strike you, Ravi? It did. I was in the room, but I was upstairs literally in the rafters for both of those speeches. With the Chinese, you can assume that they don't diverge from the script. The Chinese rift off of very familiar themes of talking about how the UN does function. It's not dead. They like to sort of play off of the idea that China's defending the international system, whereas the United States is not. So that was very much the theme of Wang Ye's speech. He did though really remark on how angry the Chinese were and about the, some of the comments of the new Japanese prime minister, and I take a itchy with a real warning to everyone else. This is not good for Asia. So, you know, that was an interesting addendum, which doesn't seem to have got much coverage. It was an interesting addendum. He pointed out that the Japanese haven't quite recovered from Pearl Harbor. And they still have colonial instincts and that the Taiwanese shouldn't be scared of China. They should instead be scared of Japan because Tokyo might have designs on Taiwan, which of course no one believes. But I did speak to some of the Chinese mid-tier officials later in the conference. And one explanation I got for the very tough stance that Wang Ye took on Japan was that the Chinese are very worried about Japan potentially gaining nuclear weapons. And that for them is a big no-no. China sees itself as surrounded by nuclear powers, whether it's North Korea, the Russians of course, India, Pakistan. And for them, the very notion that Japan could acquire nuclear weapons is one that is unthinkable for them. So that's part of where some of that hawkish tone from the Chinese is coming from. I think the Chinese may have misfired there because in the context of Ukraine, Japan is actually seen as one of the leading lights of the Indo-Pacific in terms of commitment to European security, don't you think? Oh yeah, absolutely. I think this was very much a domestic lens and I think it would have played very well at home. But of course, Japan is a very strong US ally under the new government, but for China, I think they needed to make that message. You had the chance to speak to Elbridge Colby, Ravi, he's the current undersecretary of defense policy. And Australians know him very much as a key Trump whisperer and sort of ambivalent about Orcas, possibly pushing to scrap it. We're just not sure. But there was a fascinating moment where you asked him to define what America first is. I would say America, and I think a little bit of the hack for America first is the common sense approach. I think common sense. The president talks about common sense. But my common sense is different from your common sense. Okay, so I mean, it's not a scientific theorem, but it's basically saying are things working out for regular Americans, right? And I think that obviously people are going to contest what that means and that's actually good. It also sounds like foreign policy for the middle class. Well, I think people are contesting. I mean, Arkansas is that we're doing a lot better job. I must admit, I was in the room for this. I was in the room for this, Ravi. And when you responded with that, I did laugh out loud. I don't know if you heard, but it was very amusing. Yes. And I remember seeing you in the room as well. Look, I mean, he came back by saying that common sense isn't a scientific theorem, but it's basically saying are things working out for regular Americans. To which again, I had to point out that that isn't very different from the Biden administration's foreign policy for the middle class. So in some senses, not much has changed in US foreign policy, at least in the language that successive administrations have used. And that really is the beauty of America first, because they can define it any which way they want. Just by saying that we're acting in our self interest first and foremost. But who doesn't do that every administration in every country has has always do that. So it was a good but feisty interview with Elbridge Colby. And he is of course the Pentagon's top policy maker was very influential in drafting the national security strategy and the national defense strategy, both of which have come out in the last three months. And has kind of set the stage for how the United States will have a posture. It's defense posture across Europe, Latin America and the Asia Pacific. You know, the other thing that came up a fair bit with Colby was just whether the US military is stretched because of course they are also quite interested in what's happening in the Middle East. They could potentially attack Iran at any point. They just had that military action in Venezuela. Colby of course would point out that under the Trump administration, if they do use force, it tends to be sharp, sharp bursts of force. But they're not interested in getting mired in a longer term conflict, the way the United States did and was in Iraq and Afghanistan. What struck me in your interview is this all this emphasis on Americans as if they were the only sort of participants in NATO. That's what it sounded to me like. And I noticed that there was at the same time a bunch of 16 former senior figures, men who had been basically ambassadors to NATO or commanders of NATO forces said this is not just about America. So this is from their formal statement. It's not an act of American generosity. It is a strategic bargain that ensures the US remains the world's most powerful and economically secure nation at a fraction of the cost. So in a very, very out there saying, hey, hey, come on, Elbridge Colby, another's like you. This is not just about Americans. Now, you know, was that permeating at all? Oh, it was. I mean, Article five of NATO, which is the famous line that says if you attack one of us, you attack all of us. And so every member is duty bound to defend another NATO member if it invokes Article five. And so the only time Article five has ever been invoked, by the way, was by the United States after 9-11. And as we know, every European NATO member came to the defense of the United States. Now, I pushed Colby on whether if a European NATO country was attacked, let's say by Russia, whether he could guarantee that the United States would come to their aid. And he was a little bit wishy-washy on that. You know, we see not a retreat of the United States from insoliances, but a kind of moderate approach that puts it on a much more sustainable path. So, bridge, that was a great answer. But it was a yes, no question. He wouldn't give me a clear yes or no answer, which was very telling. And I imagine quite disconcerting for Europeans. The president points out he is prepared to use military force decisively to back up his pledges to work with our allies, like our model ally Israel. And we train, we ready our forces, we are more in the delivering results and readiness business than in the cheap talk business. We are doing more and we are going to be ready, but we're putting things on a more sustainable basis. And I think that's the best answer I can give. If I were a European leader, I would be quite worried right now about the health of NATO and whether Article V is as strong as it once was. On Europe, though, what are the European reactions really caught your eye this year? Who made waves in your view? I think the opening speech at the conference by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, where he said the international order no longer exists was as strong a line as you can imagine. I thought the British Prime Minister Kirstama made a remarkable statement where he said that he didn't think there was a rupture. He instead was making a call for a radical renewal of order, which gives you a sense of how the UK is on the one hand trying to be very chummy and paly with the United States, while still also saying that this is not the Britain of the Brexit era. This is a Britain that wants to join hands with Europe and and fight for a common cause. I thought you might say, Merz saying because the US is not powerful enough to go at a loan in the world. I thought, wow, that's the Germans being punchy. That was a punchy line, I agree. And look, it's a reminder of the fact that again, Article V, the only time it was invoked was in defense of the United States. And God forbid, we won't have a 9-11 again, but it's not unthinkable to imagine that the United States will need its allies to step up. Look, this is not just hard military, this is also cyber attacks. There's a range of things that the United States cooperates with Europe on and to call and to question the unshakeability of that alliance is something Europeans are worried about. And I think it's smart of them to point out that it's not just Europe that will be weaker if the transatlantic relationship isn't strong, but the United States as well. Ravi, it's interesting we've gotten this far and haven't really talked about Ukraine. And I feel that that too is a bit of an indictment or metaphor for what's been happening at Munich, which is all this focus on the transatlantic alliance and the rupture between Europe and the White House. It does feel a bit like Ukraine is slipping. Did you get that sense too? I did, and much like Davos, where all of us were fretting about Greenland, I think Munich was much the same where there was a lot of fretting about the transatlantic alliance without enough talk, actual substantial talk about the future of Ukraine. I was at one private Ukrainian dinner where the foreign minister of Denmark actually got up and said, look, I'm sorry. I'm sorry that we spent all this time talking about Denmark when we should have been talking about Ukraine for these past two months. And that was very much the theme where for all the bravado of European leaders saying that they will help Ukraine and that Ukraine has the strongest fighting force in the world, there's still some years away from any of those things coming to a throesion. And of course, in the meanwhile, Russia is continuing to attack Ukraine. It's killing civilians. One big movement, however, in the last month or so, is the US-India trade deal. India, over the last four years now has become a big purchaser of Russian crude oil. And one of the components of the US-India trade deal was that India would gradually stop buying Russian crude. And if that actually happens, then Russia is much more isolated than it was before. China, of course, will pick up a lot of that slack, happy to buy cheap oil from Russia. But it does isolate Russia more than before. And that could have some bearing on the war in Ukraine longer term. Just to go back to the Australian, what we derived from this, Jennifer Parker here in Australia, formally, she was the Australian Navy. She's very involved in the build for Orcas. She thought that the whole tone of the Americans, the Rubio speech, etc, was a reminder. And I'm quoting her that alliances endure, but expectations evolve. You know, that in a way, the rules-based order will be filtered increasingly through the national interests in US policy. And so that Australia, we here in Australia, we need to demonstrate how our contributions advance US interests in the Indo-Pacific, which is really quite a shift, I think, in tone. Now, do you think that that is a right sort of inference to draw? Well, as it turns out, I also had a panel discussion with Bridge Colby in which we were joined by a few other ministers, and those included the Japanese Foreign Minister, the Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Miles, and also the New Zealand Defence Minister, Judith Collins, and Orcas came up quite directly. Obviously, because they were on stage with an senior American policymaker, they, I think, were quite guarded. From an Australian point of view, we are very much about working with the United States and other partners like Japan to try and put forward deterrence within the Indo-Pacific, so that we can maintain peace and stability and prosperity if we're in open Indo-Pacific. We've continued to do that over the last 14 months, and we're very comfortable with the language that's played out. But there was a general acknowledgement that, like the Europeans, they needed to spend more on defence. And some of it was couched as not just defence spending to stay in line with the American expectation of 3.5% of GDP spent on defence. It was also about climate change. It was also about resilience, if you're a country like New Zealand. So there was a real sense of all of these countries coming on board with the American General Ethos of sharing the burden in the Indo-Pacific. Ravi, if I had to ask you to look at your crystal ball, comparing the difference in Europe from last year's Munich, where it was shell-shock after JD Vance, where do you think we'll find the Europeans in the state of the transatlantic alliance next year? And do you think it really is under destruction? I think the rules-based order is absolutely under destruction. I think Europeans are past the state of shock from last year. They know what reality is in the transatlantic relationship. They're very much in the doing phase. And I think there's a cold, hard reality that they're waking up to, that now that they're relatively on their own, they just have to up the defence spending. And tough decisions have to be made domestically for every member country. The problem is, as I've been saying, that takes time. And it's not just the time factor, but it's also the case that as you spend more in defence, the money does come from somewhere. And all of these European countries over the last 80 years, they basically relied on Russia for energy. They relied on China for export-driven growth. And they relied on the United States for defence protection. Each of those three things now is in jeopardy. And when you build a welfare state off the base of giving those three things, or leaning on those three countries for those three very important things, the social contract with its people where you have a lot of high pensions, great healthcare, great security, great benefits, all of that then comes into question. And so, longer term, I think European leaders will be very aware that they're opening themselves up to the rise of the right. They're opening themselves up to dissent and popular revolts internally. And that's their biggest problem. They know what to do. What they don't know, as the great Jean-Claude Youngcourt used to say, is how to get re-elected once they've done what they need to do. Ravi Agrabile, terrific as usual. Thank you very much for joining us for that overview. My pleasure, as always. And it was great to see you in Munich, Ravi. Likewise. Well, Geraldine, I've got to say, as someone at that conference, that wasn't absolutely bang on snapshot of what it was like, what was said. And some things I hadn't picked up myself, including that fantastic anecdote of the, was that the Danish foreign minister standing up and apologizing for not talking about Ukraine enough. I mean, I thought that really did capture the zeitgeist. Yes, I had heard that the Ukrainians were quite emotional talking about the, the sort of days and days of 30 degree below temperature and the Russians knocking out the electricity. And they, I think, was a lensk at a big sort of audio visual behind his speech. And that had made quite a powerful impact. It's almost like the rest of the European suit had, you know, good central heating, where embarrassed, was sort of terribly affected. Now, nevertheless, both you and Ravi, I noticed, sort of said that Ukraine was slightly sideline. That was really awful to hear. Yes, but I think this is part of a trend that has been going on for some time now. And this really is because the entire transatlantic relationship is at stake, not just the eastern security of the continent. I think maybe one other factor, and this is really in house, but I think it may add is the actual geography of how this conference was laid out over the road they had Ukraine house for the first time. Now, to get into Munich, it's very secure as we discussed at the start. Ukraine house was a place where those with less secure badges could go. And I do wonder if concentrating so much of the Ukraine chatter, the appearances by the senior Ukrainians in Ukraine house as opposed to the main conference venue may have actually just lowered the footfall, lowered the eye contact people had with Ukrainians, lowered the ability to get in and out and have those discussions. What Ravi was emphasizing was this, I suppose, this complete effort to analyze the American personality as it came across. And so you had the two sides, you know, a nicer, more polite, you know, talking about the enlightenment for goodness sake, certainly wasn't something that Trump and events would have done. Did you get the feeling that something was shifting within America after that rather dramatic outing last year? I think what's interesting and what Ravi didn't canvas was who from America came and there was a very strong line of Democrats. Now, there were the regulars who always come. These are congressional members of the various committees that deal with defense and security and foreign relations. But this year you had AOC, you had Gavin Newsmon center stage AOC was on a smaller side stage. And I think some of these younger Democrats showing up was quite important. Having said that, Geraldine, I wasn't particularly, and I don't think any European there was particularly persuaded or comforted by what these Democrats had to say. I mean, AOC herself used the word restraint that the US needed a foreign policy that works for the middle class and was restrained. That's as Ravi said, not too far distant from this America first by an S.C. policy. So you can see, I think a long term trend in how the Americans are thinking about foreign policy, even though the very spectacle of some of these younger Democrats turning up was supposed to be a sign of reassurance. OK, now time for just a little bit of your feedback and thank you for some very nice feedback about our Arctic check with Klaus Dodds. There was appreciation to Latika of yours and Kylie's interview with Joel Witt, which I must say scared the pants off me about nuclear proliferation. And Michelle wrote, having this unbiased and open conversation on your program is what we need more of throughout mainstream media. I think I agree with Andrew here who has written in to ask for an entire episode on the subject of deterrence, especially with Australia's national defense strategy about to be released. I think that's a cool call. We're very open, as you know, here at Global Roaming to suggestions, so please keep them coming. Now, don't forget to write to us and your questions and feedback really do matter. Our email is global.roamingatabc.net.au. Latika and Kylie will be back tomorrow and you can listen at 11 a.m. or 9 p.m. on Radio National or any time, of course, on ABC. Listen, thanks to our executive producer, Kylie Morris and producer Shane Anderson. Thank you to you, Latika, bye bye for now. See you, Geraldine. You've been listening to an ABC podcast. for the tough love, for the hard conversations.
Some chose to talk about the action they're taking and others like Friedrich Mertz
who opened with his speech actually had a real needle at Mager
and said, look, keep your culture wars over there, this is not for us, thank you very much.
The culture of the culture of the Mager movement in the USA is not our.
The other thing I think that happened is that there is a very clear divide
between what Europeans are saying out loud and what they're really thinking
and doing and feeling and saying privately to anyone who's not American.
And that divergence in diplomacy terms, I think that's always been there,
but this year I think that absolute has them widened and deepened
and I'm not really sure the Americans have clocked that.
Very interesting. We'll look at it's a perfect reason to talk to Ravi Agraval.
He's been a guest on Global Roaming before.
He joins us from New York. He's just returned from the conference as well
in his role as editor in chief of foreign policy.
And he also hosts its podcast, F.P. Live. So here he is now.
Ravi Agraval, welcome back to the show.
Great to be back.
How do you think people will reflect, will look back on this year's conference?
Well, I think that the conference is very much a continuation from last years.
Everyone this year was really waiting to see what the Americans would say.
And so Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State, gave a speech that actually
wasn't that different in substance but was much nicer in tone.
It's because we care deeply. We care deeply about your future and ours.
And if at times we disagree, our disagreements come from our profound sense of concern
about a Europe with which we are connected, not just economically,
not just militarily. We are connected spiritually and we are connected culturally.
And so he got around of applause when he was speaking.
But broadly, Europeans, I think, are back to square one where they were last year,
which is to say they don't really trust the United States.
They don't think the United States will help them when they truly need help.
Long term, they very much need to boost their defense spending, defense infrastructure.
But they're very aware that that will take many years.
So there's no immediate fix. And Europeans are living in a state of relative crisis.
Ravi, what do you think Marco Rubio set out to do at this year's Munich?
And what do you think he achieved?
I think he set out to be very clear about the way in which the United States sees Europe.
He was riffing on a lot of shared cultural history.
We want Europe to be strong. We believe that Europe must survive.
Because the two great wars of the last century serve for us as history's constant reminder that ultimately our destiny is
and will always be intertwined with yours. Because we know.
Now, all of that said, and those are reassuring words,
he did, of course, riff on a shared civilizational history, which some have interpreted as a racial unity.
It came across in some parts as maybe harkening back to an era of colonization.
But by and large, I think Rubio set out to present a friendly American face.
And yet one in which the substance of US foreign policy hasn't changed much from the last year.
Look, this is a little aside, but I heard that it was standing room only like hanging from the rafters for the Rubio speech.
But the Wang Ye speech, the very important and significant Chinese foreign minister,
his speech had lots of empty chairs in it, which was fascinating.
And the assumption was, it just doesn't resonate. Did that strike you, Ravi?
It did. I was in the room, but I was upstairs literally in the rafters for both of those speeches.
With the Chinese, you can assume that they don't diverge from the script.
The Chinese rift off of very familiar themes of talking about how the UN does function. It's not dead.
They like to sort of play off of the idea that China's defending the international system,
whereas the United States is not. So that was very much the theme of Wang Ye's speech.
He did though really remark on how angry the Chinese were and about the, some of the comments of the new Japanese prime minister,
and I take a itchy with a real warning to everyone else.
This is not good for Asia. So, you know, that was an interesting addendum,
which doesn't seem to have got much coverage.
It was an interesting addendum. He pointed out that the Japanese haven't quite recovered from Pearl Harbor.
And they still have colonial instincts and that the Taiwanese shouldn't be scared of China.
They should instead be scared of Japan because Tokyo might have designs on Taiwan,
which of course no one believes. But I did speak to some of the Chinese mid-tier officials later in the conference.
And one explanation I got for the very tough stance that Wang Ye took on Japan was that the Chinese are very worried about Japan potentially gaining nuclear weapons.
And that for them is a big no-no. China sees itself as surrounded by nuclear powers, whether it's North Korea,
the Russians of course, India, Pakistan. And for them, the very notion that Japan could acquire nuclear weapons is one that is unthinkable for them.
So that's part of where some of that hawkish tone from the Chinese is coming from.

I think the Chinese may have misfired there because in the context of Ukraine, Japan is actually seen as one of the leading lights of the Indo-Pacific in terms of commitment to European security, don't you think?
Oh yeah, absolutely. I think this was very much a domestic lens and I think it would have played very well at home.
But of course, Japan is a very strong US ally under the new government, but for China, I think they needed to make that message.
You had the chance to speak to Elbridge Colby, Ravi, he's the current undersecretary of defense policy.
And Australians know him very much as a key Trump whisperer and sort of ambivalent about Orcas, possibly pushing to scrap it. We're just not sure.
But there was a fascinating moment where you asked him to define what America first is.
I would say America, and I think a little bit of the hack for America first is the common sense approach.
I think common sense. The president talks about common sense.
But my common sense is different from your common sense.
Okay, so I mean, it's not a scientific theorem, but it's basically saying are things working out for regular Americans, right?
And I think that obviously people are going to contest what that means and that's actually good.
It also sounds like foreign policy for the middle class.
Well, I think people are contesting. I mean, Arkansas is that we're doing a lot better job.
I must admit, I was in the room for this. I was in the room for this, Ravi.
And when you responded with that, I did laugh out loud. I don't know if you heard, but it was very amusing.
Yes. And I remember seeing you in the room as well.
Look, I mean, he came back by saying that common sense isn't a scientific theorem, but it's basically saying are things working out for regular Americans.
To which again, I had to point out that that isn't very different from the Biden administration's foreign policy for the middle class.
So in some senses, not much has changed in US foreign policy, at least in the language that successive administrations have used.
And that really is the beauty of America first, because they can define it any which way they want.
Just by saying that we're acting in our self interest first and foremost.
But who doesn't do that every administration in every country has has always do that.
So it was a good but feisty interview with Elbridge Colby.

And he is of course the Pentagon's top policy maker was very influential in drafting the national security strategy and the national defense strategy, both of which have come out in the last three months.
And has kind of set the stage for how the United States will have a posture.
It's defense posture across Europe, Latin America and the Asia Pacific.
You know, the other thing that came up a fair bit with Colby was just whether the US military is stretched because of course they are also quite interested in what's happening in the Middle East.
They could potentially attack Iran at any point.
They just had that military action in Venezuela.
Colby of course would point out that under the Trump administration, if they do use force, it tends to be sharp, sharp bursts of force.
But they're not interested in getting mired in a longer term conflict, the way the United States did and was in Iraq and Afghanistan.
What struck me in your interview is this all this emphasis on Americans as if they were the only sort of participants in NATO.
That's what it sounded to me like.
And I noticed that there was at the same time a bunch of 16 former senior figures, men who had been basically ambassadors to NATO or commanders of NATO forces said this is not just about America.
So this is from their formal statement.
It's not an act of American generosity.
It is a strategic bargain that ensures the US remains the world's most powerful and economically secure nation at a fraction of the cost.
So in a very, very out there saying, hey, hey, come on, Elbridge Colby, another's like you. This is not just about Americans.
Now, you know, was that permeating at all?
Oh, it was. I mean, Article five of NATO, which is the famous line that says if you attack one of us, you attack all of us.
And so every member is duty bound to defend another NATO member if it invokes Article five.
And so the only time Article five has ever been invoked, by the way, was by the United States after 9-11.
And as we know, every European NATO member came to the defense of the United States.
Now, I pushed Colby on whether if a European NATO country was attacked, let's say by Russia,
whether he could guarantee that the United States would come to their aid.
And he was a little bit wishy-washy on that.
You know, we see not a retreat of the United States from insoliances, but a kind of moderate approach that puts it on a much more sustainable path.
So, bridge, that was a great answer. But it was a yes, no question.
He wouldn't give me a clear yes or no answer, which was very telling. And I imagine quite disconcerting for Europeans.
The president points out he is prepared to use military force decisively to back up his pledges to work with our allies, like our model ally Israel.
And we train, we ready our forces, we are more in the delivering results and readiness business than in the cheap talk business.
We are doing more and we are going to be ready, but we're putting things on a more sustainable basis.
And I think that's the best answer I can give.
If I were a European leader, I would be quite worried right now about the health of NATO and whether Article V is as strong as it once was.
On Europe, though, what are the European reactions really caught your eye this year? Who made waves in your view?
I think the opening speech at the conference by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, where he said the international order no longer exists was as strong a line as you can imagine.
I thought the British Prime Minister Kirstama made a remarkable statement where he said that he didn't think there was a rupture.

He instead was making a call for a radical renewal of order, which gives you a sense of how the UK is on the one hand trying to be very chummy and paly with the United States, while still also saying that this is not the Britain of the Brexit era.
This is a Britain that wants to join hands with Europe and and fight for a common cause.
I thought you might say, Merz saying because the US is not powerful enough to go at a loan in the world.
I thought, wow, that's the Germans being punchy.
That was a punchy line, I agree.
And look, it's a reminder of the fact that again, Article V, the only time it was invoked was in defense of the United States.
And God forbid, we won't have a 9-11 again, but it's not unthinkable to imagine that the United States will need its allies to step up.
Look, this is not just hard military, this is also cyber attacks.
There's a range of things that the United States cooperates with Europe on and to call and to question the unshakeability of that alliance is something Europeans are worried about.
And I think it's smart of them to point out that it's not just Europe that will be weaker if the transatlantic relationship isn't strong, but the United States as well.
Ravi, it's interesting we've gotten this far and haven't really talked about Ukraine.

And I feel that that too is a bit of an indictment or metaphor for what's been happening at Munich, which is all this focus on the transatlantic alliance and the rupture between Europe and the White House.
It does feel a bit like Ukraine is slipping. Did you get that sense too?

I did, and much like Davos, where all of us were fretting about Greenland, I think Munich was much the same where there was a lot of fretting about the transatlantic alliance without enough talk, actual substantial talk about the future of Ukraine.
I was at one private Ukrainian dinner where the foreign minister of Denmark actually got up and said, look, I'm sorry.
I'm sorry that we spent all this time talking about Denmark when we should have been talking about Ukraine for these past two months.

And that was very much the theme where for all the bravado of European leaders saying that they will help Ukraine and that Ukraine has the strongest fighting force in the world, there's still some years away from any of those things coming to a throesion.
And of course, in the meanwhile, Russia is continuing to attack Ukraine. It's killing civilians.
One big movement, however, in the last month or so, is the US-India trade deal.
India, over the last four years now has become a big purchaser of Russian crude oil.
And one of the components of the US-India trade deal was that India would gradually stop buying Russian crude.
And if that actually happens, then Russia is much more isolated than it was before. China, of course, will pick up a lot of that slack, happy to buy cheap oil from Russia.
But it does isolate Russia more than before. And that could have some bearing on the war in Ukraine longer term.
Just to go back to the Australian, what we derived from this, Jennifer Parker here in Australia, formally, she was the Australian Navy. She's very involved in the build for Orcas.
She thought that the whole tone of the Americans, the Rubio speech, etc, was a reminder.
And I'm quoting her that alliances endure, but expectations evolve.
You know, that in a way, the rules-based order will be filtered increasingly through the national interests in US policy.
And so that Australia, we here in Australia, we need to demonstrate how our contributions advance US interests in the Indo-Pacific,
which is really quite a shift, I think, in tone.
Now, do you think that that is a right sort of inference to draw?

Well, as it turns out, I also had a panel discussion with Bridge Colby in which we were joined by a few other ministers, and those included the Japanese Foreign Minister, the Australian Deputy Prime Minister Richard Miles,
and also the New Zealand Defence Minister, Judith Collins, and Orcas came up quite directly.
Obviously, because they were on stage with an senior American policymaker, they, I think, were quite guarded.
From an Australian point of view, we are very much about working with the United States and other partners like Japan to try and put forward deterrence within the Indo-Pacific,
so that we can maintain peace and stability and prosperity if we're in open Indo-Pacific.
We've continued to do that over the last 14 months, and we're very comfortable with the language that's played out.
But there was a general acknowledgement that, like the Europeans, they needed to spend more on defence.
And some of it was couched as not just defence spending to stay in line with the American expectation of 3.5% of GDP spent on defence.
It was also about climate change. It was also about resilience, if you're a country like New Zealand.
So there was a real sense of all of these countries coming on board with the American General Ethos of sharing the burden in the Indo-Pacific.
Ravi, if I had to ask you to look at your crystal ball, comparing the difference in Europe from last year's Munich, where it was shell-shock after JD Vance,
where do you think we'll find the Europeans in the state of the transatlantic alliance next year?
And do you think it really is under destruction?
I think the rules-based order is absolutely under destruction.
I think Europeans are past the state of shock from last year. They know what reality is in the transatlantic relationship.
They're very much in the doing phase. And I think there's a cold, hard reality that they're waking up to, that now that they're relatively on their own,
they just have to up the defence spending. And tough decisions have to be made domestically for every member country.
The problem is, as I've been saying, that takes time. And it's not just the time factor, but it's also the case that as you spend more in defence,
the money does come from somewhere. And all of these European countries over the last 80 years, they basically relied on Russia for energy.
They relied on China for export-driven growth. And they relied on the United States for defence protection.
Each of those three things now is in jeopardy. And when you build a welfare state off the base of giving those three things, or leaning on those three countries for those three very important things,
the social contract with its people where you have a lot of high pensions, great healthcare, great security, great benefits, all of that then comes into question.
And so, longer term, I think European leaders will be very aware that they're opening themselves up to the rise of the right.
They're opening themselves up to dissent and popular revolts internally. And that's their biggest problem. They know what to do.
What they don't know, as the great Jean-Claude Youngcourt used to say, is how to get re-elected once they've done what they need to do.
Ravi Agrabile, terrific as usual. Thank you very much for joining us for that overview.
My pleasure, as always.
And it was great to see you in Munich, Ravi.
Likewise.
Well, Geraldine, I've got to say, as someone at that conference, that wasn't absolutely bang on snapshot of what it was like,

what was said. And some things I hadn't picked up myself, including that fantastic anecdote of the, was that the Danish foreign minister standing up and apologizing for not talking about Ukraine enough.
I mean, I thought that really did capture the zeitgeist.
Yes, I had heard that the Ukrainians were quite emotional talking about the, the sort of days and days of 30 degree below temperature and the Russians knocking out the electricity.
And they, I think, was a lensk at a big sort of audio visual behind his speech.
And that had made quite a powerful impact.
It's almost like the rest of the European suit had, you know, good central heating, where embarrassed, was sort of terribly affected.
Now, nevertheless, both you and Ravi, I noticed, sort of said that Ukraine was slightly sideline. That was really awful to hear.

Yes, but I think this is part of a trend that has been going on for some time now. And this really is because the entire transatlantic relationship is at stake, not just the eastern security of the continent.

I think maybe one other factor, and this is really in house, but I think it may add is the actual geography of how this conference was laid out over the road they had Ukraine house for the first time.
Now, to get into Munich, it's very secure as we discussed at the start. Ukraine house was a place where those with less secure badges could go.

And I do wonder if concentrating so much of the Ukraine chatter, the appearances by the senior Ukrainians in Ukraine house as opposed to the main conference venue may have actually just lowered the footfall, lowered the eye contact people had with Ukrainians, lowered the ability to get in and out and have those discussions.

What Ravi was emphasizing was this, I suppose, this complete effort to analyze the American personality as it came across. And so you had the two sides, you know, a nicer, more polite, you know, talking about the enlightenment for goodness sake, certainly wasn't something that Trump and events would have done.
Did you get the feeling that something was shifting within America after that rather dramatic outing last year?
I think what's interesting and what Ravi didn't canvas was who from America came and there was a very strong line of Democrats. Now, there were the regulars who always come.

These are congressional members of the various committees that deal with defense and security and foreign relations. But this year you had AOC, you had Gavin Newsmon center stage AOC was on a smaller side stage.

And I think some of these younger Democrats showing up was quite important. Having said that, Geraldine, I wasn't particularly, and I don't think any European there was particularly persuaded or comforted by what these Democrats had to say.

I mean, AOC herself used the word restraint that the US needed a foreign policy that works for the middle class and was restrained. That's as Ravi said, not too far distant from this America first by an S.C. policy.

So you can see, I think a long term trend in how the Americans are thinking about foreign policy, even though the very spectacle of some of these younger Democrats turning up was supposed to be a sign of reassurance.
OK, now time for just a little bit of your feedback and thank you for some very nice feedback about our Arctic check with Klaus Dodds.
There was appreciation to Latika of yours and Kylie's interview with Joel Witt, which I must say scared the pants off me about nuclear proliferation.
And Michelle wrote, having this unbiased and open conversation on your program is what we need more of throughout mainstream media.
I think I agree with Andrew here who has written in to ask for an entire episode on the subject of deterrence, especially with Australia's national defense strategy about to be released.
I think that's a cool call. We're very open, as you know, here at Global Roaming to suggestions, so please keep them coming.
Now, don't forget to write to us and your questions and feedback really do matter.
Our email is global.roamingatabc.net.au. Latika and Kylie will be back tomorrow and you can listen at 11 a.m. or 9 p.m. on Radio National or any time, of course, on ABC.
Listen, thanks to our executive producer, Kylie Morris and producer Shane Anderson.
Thank you to you, Latika, bye bye for now.
See you, Geraldine.
You've been listening to an ABC podcast. Discover more great ABC podcasts, live radio and exclusives on the ABC Listen app.

episodes.title: Prof Brian Cox on whether Elon Musk owns the moon
episodes.description: As Artemis II prepares for launch, our first trip near the moon since the 1970s, a successful voyage could bring a lunar colony closer to reality.
episodes.transcript: ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music, and more. Hey, I'm Sana Kadar, host of All in the Mind on ABC Radio National, and I have a question for you. Have you ever wondered what is going on inside someone else's head? They're thinking that they need to do the impossible, which is to be perfect and flawless. I think about this a lot, because on All in the Mind, we cover psychology, mental health, and why people behave the way they do. So if you like the sound of that, check out All in the Mind on the ABC Listen app. It's not all that easy being an optimist these days, but safe to say, our guest on this episode is a glass half full kind of guy. His name is Professor Brian Cox. That's right, I think, whether that glass in Professor Cox's case is on top of a rocket or deep underground inside a particle collider, it definitely seems to be on the fuller side, which is refreshing. So in this episode, we're leaving the planet and heading where only tech billionaires, astronauts, and sometimes pop stars, dear to venture, we're heading into space. I'm Hamish McDonald, and I'm Jonathan Webb. This is Global Raming. Well, I'm delighted to welcome Dr Jonathan Webb back to Global Raming. You were on last year, briefly, as a guest, Jonathan, when we were talking about the war on science. And of course, listen to us now, you from lab notes and all the other amazing stuff you do on radio and national space. Are we going to end up with war in space? I don't know about war, but the space race is back on. This very much seems to be the vibe in 2026, and indeed has been for a while, whether it's between nation states or between big companies, the race is back on. Even before the Trump administration came in, NASA were pretty explicitly saying that for these Artemis missions that are happening in the moment, wanting to get back to the moon, it was all about a race specifically, fairly specifically with China in terms of setting up a lasting presence on the moon again, and then looking further to Mars. Yeah, and so maybe it would be helpful for listeners if you could kind of lay out how all the private enterprise in space sits either alongside or up against the more traditional approach, which is countries exploring space. Like obviously we hear a lot about mask and a lot about Jeff Bezos. They're not the only ones, but they're kind of the dominant players. How does that all fit together as a sort of jigsaw puzzle? For a long time, as you mentioned, and back in the first space race, it was very much nation states putting in the money, sending up the rockets over time, even back in the space shuttle era that did involve contractors. So there were big companies that an agency like NASA would use to build parts of its kit for getting people and other things up into space satellites. Then over time, we've ended up with these big players like SpaceX and Blue Origin, that's Jeff Bezos' company, the Amazon owner, that have their own completely independent activities. They can send up their own satellites. They've built in the case of SpaceX, their own reusable rocket technology, which is something that NASA itself never really mastered, that is this sort of hybrid mode that we're in at the moment. There was an interesting moment in US politics and in the kind of NASA back end just recently actually, because NASA has to have it sort of authority renewed. This is called reauthorization. It's a bill that has to go through US Congress. There were a couple of tweaks to the kind of terms of how NASA is run. The most notable one that I've seen a few kind of specialist commenting on was around this privatization thing. The vision with Artemis was definitely that it was going to be NASA's own technology. So this very expensive giant rocket was built and an Orion capsule, which was built by Lockheed Martin and there's other contractors involved as well. But in the new reauthorization, there's an amendment that says they will be able to procure operational services to carry cargo and crew to and from deep space destinations. So places like the Moon and Mars, they won't necessarily keep going with this expensive Artemis program. They might just say, all right, give us your bits. Who's going to send our next NASA mission? Put it out to tender. Yeah, but not just like who's going to build this component of the rocket. Literally, who is going to send our astronauts to Mars? That's the potential. So there's a geopolitical dimension to all of this and in part, it's one so interested to talk to our guests this episode. Professor Brian Cox has actually just been appointed as the UN's champion for space. And what's interesting is that part of that role is to promote the peaceful exploration of space for the good of all humankind. And what I think we're going to get to in this conversation, Jonathan, is in part his view that space in a way forces us to kind of lift up and above some of the kind of geopolitical contexts and issues around sovereignty and borders and actually work together. It's a fascinating time to be in that role, I imagine. And a great appointment to the role, I've got to say, I looked this up. He's not the first. The first time I've heard of this role, I think previously it's been held by Scott Kelly, the American astronaut turned politician among others. But the fact that we're talking about it, you're talking to Brian Cox about it suggests it's a great appointment in terms of global visibility. So in this interview, we're going to explore a bit about who owns space. Can we actually all cooperate together across countries and borders and corporations like Musk and Bezos and sort of achieve something for the betterment of all? I do want to say too, infinity and beyond with Professor Brian Cox, but is that too much, Jonathan? Brian Buzz Lightyear, maybe a little much. Here he is. Professor Brian Cox, welcome. Good morning. I was really interested in reading some of the detail around your, you were recently appointed as a UN champion for space, but what struck me was the language in terms of what the intention of this was to help foster greater understanding of the transformative potential of space technology in addressing, and this is the key bit, global challenges, including climate change, disaster management and sustainable development. And what stood out to me was the hopeful nature of this. When I suppose when I read about space at the moment, it's less enthusiastic, it's less about possibility, it's about conflict, it's about which corporations dominate space, it's a little scarier than that. Yes, I mean, just to put it into context, what you said, the importance of it, is it so that in the UK, I have the number for the UK, it will be similar for Australia, is the 18% of our GDP depends on space-based infrastructure, 1.8, 18. The reason for that, of course, it's obvious things like satellite navigation and the way that we use that for transport and so on, but also timing in financial transactions and things like that, it all comes from space-based infrastructure. So we all use it and it makes our lives better in that sense. But you're right that one of the key points now is this is one of the most, the rapidly expanding area of the global economy. There are tremendous opportunities and you listed some of them, the ability to better manage resources here on earth to understand what's happening to the earth and also to move outwards and access new resources and new ideas that are out there in space, it's very exciting. But as we all knew worlds, there are the risks, it can seem like the Wild West. So I think one of the challenges is to manage this tremendously exciting and rapidly growing part of the global economy, but also it cannot be managed by a single country or corporation because if you think about it, orbit, right, so who owns orbit, you know, if there's something in your airspace, it's in your airspace for five minutes and then it's in somebody else's airspace. So the challenges are by definition international and the solutions are by definition international. You're forced to cooperate. It's not entirely naive to say that because in the past and even now space is one of the places that we do collaborate well. I remember one of the first things I remember was the Apollo Soyuz docking in the 1970s and I remember that and it was unbelievable. It was revolutionary at the time that the United States and the Soviet Union then was collaborated to dock in space and the technologies that were developed then are still used. So I think there's a possibility for optimism because of the challenges that we face. A possibility for optimism. Are we drawing a distinction in between? In between actual optimism. Yeah, well, because you know, I mean to be realistic, you know, there are obviously any rapidly growing area of the economy. There's a lot of competition. Yeah. There's a lot of competition. But that's the point. That's the point of things like the United Nations. If you walk in there in New York, there's a quote on the wall. It's one of the directs of generals of the United Nations back in the early days and it says that the organization isn't there to take humanity to heaven. It's there to prevent it from descending into hell. That's quite wise. Yeah, that's worth reading a few times, isn't it? How do you prevent conflict in space then? Like if you have nations or presidents saying we need a space force, we've got to be ready for taking on our enemies in space. What would space conflict look like? How do you avoid it? I think, again, if you were looking for reasons to be optimistic, it's the same sort of character as nuclear deterrence, which is that it's unthinkable, hopefully, because of the damage it would do. Because as I mentioned, that infrastructure up there on which we all rely is very fragile. Nobody wins. If you start to destroy satellites, then you run the risk of destroying, it's unpredictable. The consequences are almost unthinkable. And so I hope that because the consequences are unthinkable, that will force cooperation. Do you think the people that operate in space do so responsibly in the interests of humankind? Like I'm thinking about, a few years ago, there were terrible floods in a part of Australia. It took too long for the government, for the military to get in there. Phone lines weren't restored. And I ended up reporting up in some of these mountainous areas where the local community had banded together. And the thing that they were really reliant on in that moment of crisis was that they had starlink. And they could access communications via starlink, which of course comes from Elon Musk. And people have very mixed views about Elon Musk. And then now we read about him applying for permission to send a million satellites up into space to crowd out the skies that we already see crowded by some of his satellites. And I guess when I put those two things next to each other, find it hard to land on a clear answer. Yes. And actually what we referred to there, we had a meeting about this morning actually, about the access to space dark and quiet skies. And the initiative is coming from astronomers, optical astronomers, radio astronomers. But when you start to think about the impacts of destroying the night sky, then there are profound cultural impacts. I mean, of course, as you know in Australia, the sky is central. episodes.description: The debate over immigration, border control and social cohesion hardened this week, after a group of women and children in northern Syria attempted to return to Australia.

The debate over immigration, border control and social cohesion hardened this week after an attempt by a group of Australian women and children, so-called ISIS families, to come home. They've been stuck at a camp in Northern Syria for seven years. Some 70 or 80 ISIS fighters, their wives and kids have already returned to Australia over the years under the previous coalition government and the Labor government. But now both sides of politics are adopting much tougher rhetoric. Certainly in the wake of the bomb-niterrest attack and these heightened concerns over social cohesion. I have contempt for them, said the Prime Minister. Shut the door to them, said the opposition leader. But what can Australia do? What powers are there to stop this cohort? And what obligations does Australia have to its citizens, particularly children? Even if their parents have done a terrible thing. I'm David Spears, I'm Nunnable Country at Parliament House in Canberra. Welcome to Insiders on Background. Abel Rizfi is a former deputy secretary of the Immigration Department and now an expert commentator on all things immigration. Abel, good to talk to you again. Thanks for joining us. Thank you, David. So what are Australia's obligations to its citizens when it comes to allowing them back into the country? Fundamentally, all countries have an obligation to accept back their own citizens. There are powers to keep them out at least temporarily. The two powers are in the Passports Act and the second power is in the Tempere Exclusion Order legislation. The government has chosen to use the Tempere Exclusion Order legislation rather than the Passports Act. That's understandable because the Passports Act does not allow the government to exclude procedural fairness as the part of the process of refusing the passport. Just explain what that means because the opposition has been raising this, saying the Passports Act allows the Minister for Foreign Affairs to deny a passport if there's a threat to Australia's security. What is that point you're making about procedural fairness, mean? So if a competent authority, and in this instance it would be ASEO, makes a request to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade to deny someone a passport, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade must provide the applicant with procedural fairness. That is, the applicant must be shown the evidence against them and allowed to comment on that before a decision to refuse is made. And that's difficult when you're talking about ASEO intelligence. Absolutely. ASEO would not want to give them procedural fairness. So this would only ever really apply if it's the sort of evidence that can be made public. And that would be either a sort of court conviction or something like that in a foreign country. Oh, that's right. Something like that. Okay. So if it's simply, this is interesting. If it's simply intelligence on an individual, that's not going to be enough to stop them being issued a passport. No, and I don't think ASEO would want to go down that route. Okay. So then the other option that you referenced is the temporary exclusion order. This is a more recent mechanism that governments can use. And they have used it in the past. How exactly does that work? A key difference with the temporary exclusion order legislation is that it allows the government to make a decision without providing the target of the decision procedural fairness. So that don't have to be shown the evidence against them. They don't get the opportunity to comment on the evidence. There are three steps associated with a temporary exclusion order. The first step is ASEO gathers the relevant evidence and submits a recommendation to the minister for immigration. The minister for immigration considers that evidence and may or may not decide would usually decide to just go with the ASEO recommendation. And I understand in one instance that has occurred. Finally, that decision must then be scrutinized by a judge to ensure that the decision was valid. And those three steps are difficult steps to pursue. They require the evidence that ASEO has gathered to be tested by a judge. And if the judge finds the evidence unsatisfactory, the temporary exclusion order is set aside. Can the minister also issue an order without ASEO advice? No. He must have ASEO advice. That is fundamental. Because this is a point the oppositions raised that under the act for these temporary exclusion orders, the minister can make a decision without ASEO advice. Well, I can't imagine how he would do that. Remembering that the basis of the decision the minister makes must be reviewed by a judge. If the judge says, well, you just made this decision arbitrarily or capriciously, he would overturn the judge would overturn the temporary exclusion order. I just can't see how you could make it with the minister just acting voluntarily. And so once the order is issued, the person that applies to can ask for a permit, is that right to enter Australia, which then triggers a 12 month process? Can you explain how that works? So the person would then request a return permit and provide evidence that their return would not pose a risk to Australia's national security. The minister would consider that in conjunction with ASEO advice. And then would make a decision on the return permit and any conditions that would be applied to that return permit. These conditions can go to things like control orders once they're here in Australia, which can require them to report so often to a police station or other conditions around what they can and can't do. That's correct. That's correct. Remembering, of course, when these people returned to Australia, the women, at least the adults, would also be subject to scrutiny by law enforcement bodies and evidence would be taken. And if the evidence showed a charge can be sustained, that would proceed. So the fact that only one of this cohort of 34 has been issued with a temporary exclusion order by the minister. Does that tell us that the other 33 women and children aren't deemed to be a threat? Well, ASEO may have suspicions, but it's got to have enough evidence to sustain those suspicions to the minister and to a judge. For the others, I imagine the situation is ASEO simply does not have the evidence that it needs. Okay. So the other question I think a lot of people are asking is the kids. They've done nothing wrong as far as we know. They've been dragged into this horrible situation. Can or should Australia be bringing them home without their parents, without their mothers, or is that really complicated? Oh, I think separating mothers from children hasn't got a great history. I don't think any government would want to go there. I mean, arguably, when kids are in a dangerous domestic situation, they can and are removed. This is a situation in a foreign country, though, that is the complication here. They would need ASEO in the mother's permission for them to be separated. I think that's right. And they would need satisfactory care arrangements back in Australia. I think usually when children are separated from their parents, it's usually because of some domestic violence associated issue, rather than I'm not aware of any domestic violence sort of issue in this space. Well, there was previously legislation that the coalition had introduced that enabled the minister to initiate a cancellation of citizenship. The high court overturned that legislation. So it's a judge that decides whether there is sufficient grounds for citizenship to be cancelled. There are a number of conditions that that legislation requires. Often, in most instances, violent crimes, the minister, if the minister considers that there is sufficient evidence to warrant a citizenship cancellation, the minister can make that recommendation, but must be taken to a judge and a judge must decide whether there is sufficient evidence to warrant cancellation. My understanding was that a number of them were actually born in Australia. Right. Okay. To say, we're not lifting a finger, we're not helping them at all, but I assume someone's gone to do either DNA checks or confirm that they are Australian or entirely Australian citizenship. There would have been some level of assistance at that end. Well, it depends on how you define assistance. Where the government agency is doing what it's required to do by the law, that's in my view not assistance, that is simply obeying the law. And I'm not aware of anything that any government agency has done, which is outside the scope of what they are required to do to obey the law. So for example, if they arrange for DNA tests, that is entirely appropriate because you need to be sure that the children are indeed who the mothers claim they are and the DNA test helps with that. And presumably that would have made officials going to the camp in northern Syria to do that sort of testing. It could have been that or it could have been through another agency, usually a UN agency or someone like that doing that sort of work. Okay, so look just before we move off this issue, your expectation is, as we've seen in the years gone by, this group will eventually one way or another. If they can get out of that camp, be allowed back into Australia. That's right. And I don't think once a citizen with a passport seeks to re-enter Australia, there's not a lot the government can actually do to prevent that. The law prevents basically hamstrings the government. Now look, this sits against the backdrop of this fairly heightened debate around immigration and keeping Australia safe and so on. A lot of this has been driven by higher than normal levels of immigration post-COVID. The net overseas migration number has been coming down over the last year or so. The last financial year it came in, it just over 300,000 this year, it's forecast to be 260,000. Not sure if they'll hit that number. But is this trend, this downward trend going to continue? Because I assume the government right now would be starting the process of working out what forecast to put in the May budget that's coming up. What would be going on behind the scenes? So there are two things going on behind the scenes. The first is that the government would be undertaking a consultation process with state governments, with industry bodies, with an associated range of stakeholders on the setting of the 2627 migration program. In addition, the government would be getting advice on the size of the backlogs that it's facing for permanent migration. At the moment, some of those backlogs are of an eye-watering size and the government will eventually have to deal with those backlogs because those applications have a legal right to be processed. These are the family reunion category. Both family reunion as well as mainly partners and dependent children. But also there is a massive backlog of employer sponsored visa applications, as well as the government being under intense pressure from state governments to maintain the visas that the state governments say they need to meet their skill needs. Okay, so they've got that backlog to clear, but the pressure is there to keep that number coming down. So what does that mean they end up with in terms of a number, do you think, for the next financial year? Well, there are two numbers that are relevant here. There is the migration and humanitarian programs. Those are the permanent residents visas issued. And the government will be under pressure to expand the permanent program to accommodate the backlog. Secondly, it wants to keep net migration coming down, but the challenges there are the government itself increased the allocation for student visas for 2026, and is now seems to have been having second thoughts on that. The second challenge is a very, very strong labour market and bringing net migration down in that context is very difficult. Just explain to me what they did with foreign students for 2026 and why you think they might be reversing course on that. Right, so for 2025, the government said we will allow 270,000 new commensments of overseas students in higher education and the vet sector. A number of sectors were excluded. For 2026, it announced in the middle of 2025 that it would increase that by 25,000. I have a suspicion that the government did not think of the consequences of that decision for either net migration or for the long term implications for the permanent program. It has now seen a sharp rise in offshore student applications in the second half of 2025. It has looked at those and thought, wow, that is now going to push net migration upwards and that has worried them. So what they have done is turned around and ramped up refusal rates. It's left the universities in a very awkward situation because they were initially told they were going to have all these extra places, and now they're being told that refusal rates are being ramped up and they may not get to the places that they were allocated. So the universities have offered places they now have to rescind? They are budgeted for places that they now must rescind. Okay. Well, putting all that together, what do you think will end up with a lower net overseas migration forecast than 260,000? I would be surprised if for 2526 Treasury loaded, it would be more likely given the policy changes that have been put in place. Yeah, the politics is tricky, but then if we don't have enough of the skilled migrants given what unemployment is at the moment, there's a need for workers, that has a risk of pushing up inflation, doesn't it? episodes.description: Angus Taylor has emerged as the new Liberal leader, beating Sussan Ley 34 votes to 17. The new Liberal leader says the party is facing a "change or die moment" and has promised to "protect the Australian way of life."

Did he make a case for how he would lead the party in a different way to Susan Lee? I think over the coming months, what we are going to hear a lot from Angus Taylor is this phrase that he has, you know, if a journalist is already staying, you get sick of it. Labor has undermined our standard of living and has failed to protect our way of life.
