So that's kind of the overarching, I guess, catch phrase, if you will, of the Angus Taylor ticket. Underneath that in his first press conference, he set out sort of a series of values, propositions, a lot of what we have heard before from many leaders of the Liberal Party, Susan Lee among them. The couple that stood out to me as being of a slightly different tilt, he talked about immigration in a very specific values context about ensuring that the types of people that are allowed into Australia essentially are not those who hate Australia. It wasn't an argument about bringing in the right skills mix, making sure that the number of people come in don't overwhelm resources, infrastructure, housing. It was all about ensuring that people with hate who come here with hate, who hate Australia don't aren't allowed. And he was actually asked, well, how do you know and stop people with hate coming into the country? We can get a full some policy response, but I thought that in particular was an interesting merging of this sort of distilling of this idea that is being put very forcefully by one nation that there is an immigration problem in this country. It's one that to an extent even Labour have acknowledged by trying to address the growth in immigration. And really, as I said before, focusing on specific skills and things like that, but it was his first big pitch in a way on that main issue that seems to be the concern for a lot of liberals with regards to that risk of one nation. As you sort of asked about, there is clearly the sort of existential push and pull going on to the liberal party. We're talking a lot about one nation at the moment, but as you rightly point out, PK, there's also a pull to the left to the middle because half of the moderates not in the party room anymore. Jane is one of the few that are left. Yeah, and that's right. And some people have questioned, oh, is she a moderate anymore because she's supported Angus Taylor now in two leadership battles. The second one, he obviously won the first he didn't and Susan landed up demoting her. I kept saying on air all day if people have seen our coverage on ABC News that she fought to keep net zero by 2050 loudly and and warned about the risk in the city. So I do think she's a moderate and she's pretty passionate about some of these issues. And so I actually think she's going to play a key role in providing that ballast and balance to Angus Taylor as they try to balance these two messages. Now you can't anymore in a world where, you know, like messages spread on our phones instantly speak to two different audiences. And this is their conundrum how they appeal to till voters and appeal to one nation voters. I can tell you though, because I know a little bit about their plan that the first plan for Angus Taylor is to deal with the bleeding to the rush. That is a priority because they think, well, we're already bleeding to the moderates, you know, to the till. And now we're actually losing the other side too. So he wants to stem that bleeding. That's why you're hearing a tough line on immigration. It won't just be Susan Lee's unannounced policy. He will look at it again. I know he's already had conversations about it and that will be a focus. But he also when I asked him in the press conference, I tried to really got myself in there. Actually, I was couldn't help myself. I asked a few questions about whether they were going to be one nation light. He said no. Right. We are not seeking to be one nation light. Absolutely not. But we respect the fact that those voters who might be thinking about one nation have reasons for wanting to do so. And we have to restore their confidence in us. So wants to be more appealing, but at the same time knows that he cannot chase one nation down a cul-de-sac. So he's trying to be the old conservative leader that stands for values that he can articulate strongly, rather than being wishy-washy, which is what they say Susan Lee was. He I'm not saying he's told me this, but that's the view whether he can do it, though, whether he's the right messenger. I still think is yet to be tested. But it is. It's a big job, Claire. I can't see how they do it easily. No. And the one thing that really stood out to me is apart from that real honing in on the values component. A lot of what he was talking about was not a huge departure from where Susan Lee set herself to the things they wanted to focus on home ownership, young people, multi-cultural Australia. These, you know, the mortgage bell making sure that people have a fair go that they get their money back. All of these kinds of touch points of the liberal party kind of platform that have existed in perpetuity really under any leader under Dutton, under Morrison, and those that came before. So I do think that maybe Susan Lee, if she was watching the press conference, I hope she wasn't. I really do hope she was out the pub. I wonder if she was. I really hope. I would find out now. It would be a bit of a head scratcher and I agree with you that it was a very classy speech from her after the results. She didn't take any questions. I did know the one kind of drive by, if you will, which was that in announcing that she'd be resigning from politics. She said that she thought that leaders deserved clear air, not that they always get it. It is important that the new leader gets clear air, something that is not always afforded to leaders, but which in the present moment is more important than ever. I will be spending the next couple of years. I think that was a not so subtle reference to the reality, which is that she has not had a lot of clear air over the last nine months. Sometimes buffeted by circumstances, but often dealing with things driven by people in her own party room and in the broader coalition, whether it's the splits, doing zero on the NATS timeline, there were these constant kind of inflection points in her own timing of when she wanted to do things. How she wanted to do things that were disrupted. I think one of the things that I found quite interesting was this idea that she needed to have announced policies faster and been more strong. There was a constant complaint of the detractors that appeared over the last 48 hours publicly saying that they were going to be backing Angus Taylor. As if everyone had forgotten that a big part of people's unhappiness with how Peter Dutton had run the party room in the previous turn was that he wasn't consulting. As she set up these back bench committees, she set up these processes to listen and learn and reflect and make sure that the policies were reflecting what the party room wanted, what the public wanted. It wasn't fast enough. You can't win sometimes. No, I think they saw Peter Dutton as two top down and then Susan Lee as two wishy-washy. I'm using it again and two consultative looking at where the wind was going all the time before she made a call. Now, let's see, Angus Taylor, it's a hard line. Will he walk that careful line? Look, I think one of the main things he's going to do, I know he's spending some time with David Little Proud this weekend. He's called the Nats Whisperer by some, like that he has that great relationship with the nationals. I think the nationals treated Susan Lee terribly. I think David Little Proud treated her with very little respect, but clearly he's trying to rebuild the coalition in that old-style, old-school way to try and make them more competitive with one nation. He is, though, in a very wickedly difficult position. What I didn't hear from his vision was how he was going to win back Metropolitan Australia. He said with the mere culpr on the taxes that he wants to go back to the coalition having strong economic credentials. I actually think that's wise. I think it was very strange in the last election that they went saying essentially that their taxes would be higher, like they would repeal a tax card, like mental. What is the point of them? That is one of their main brand values. Now he wants to return to that. He hopes that rebuilds them in the cities. I've got to say, Claire, I think one of the only things that will help him is labour-imploting. Now, don't discount that happening to governments. They do. The vision stuff is going to have to be really well executed, and we know that new opposition leaders are pretty accident-prone sometimes. Yes, Angus Taylor himself has a bit of baggage in that regard, having obviously been a minister and been in a prominent role last term as Shadow Trezra. Labour had attack ads literally ready to go the second that the result out of that party room was published. They feel very confidently that there is a wealth of material to draw on from his own past. It will be difficult. I don't think he's going to get a honeymoon grace period, or if he does, it will not last for very long. I agree with you about articulating how they're going to win back voters in the cities. He was specifically asked, does the party need to move to the left to the right? I know, as you've just said, that he's obviously got a prioritising the right. But he basically just said, I don't see it like that. I don't really think of it as left to right. I see it. I think of it as focusing on Australians and the hardworking... The challenges that hardworking Australians are facing every single day, the challenge that they are struggling to pay their bills, the challenge that they can't see a pathway for their kids to own a home. We're going to take the Liberal Party forward, not left, not right. We're not moving towards any one party. We're taking our party and the people that we want to represent forward. It's hard to say we have a problem as a party, existential, the polls are terrible. I think he said if an election was held today, we may not exist. That's a pretty major problem to have identified. To not be able to come up with what might be a solution, they've diagnosed a problem. The solution sounded a lot like, we're going to keep going how we've always gone and we're going to get back to it. I think that there are a few past Liberal leaders over the last decade who might say, we also had that idea and look how it worked out for us. I do think the point of difference that I really pick up from Angus Taylor is that the small government lower taxes, lower interventions, anti-tariffs, pro-globalisation. That actually makes him very old school, very small, liberal economically. That is a point of distinction. It is very different though than the big spending, that kind of economic nationalism that others would like to see. It's a gamble, but it is back to their knitting, if you like. Believe it or not, he might be a leading conservative, but he has told his colleagues his where that there is a line and that it is about values, whatever that means, Australian values, who comes through the door, but equally, just being careful about not overreaching. My assumption in that framing of people who hate for the country shouldn't come here is probably a way of nod to this idea that there are obviously a lot of people in their base who feel that the migration mix is not what they want to see. But potentially, and this would be a difficult message to sell, but it seems to be the one who is going to attempt, is saleable to even migrant communities because you essentially start to set up this idea that, oh, the majority of you are great. You are good. You don't hate us. Well, he told us about cappuccinos. Yes. And we are just talking about this very narrow subset of migrants who even you don't necessarily want in your community. And many migrants do want to shut the door behind them. It's a nuance that I would be interested to see how it plays out. I think the other point that you raised about him being a traditionalist in a lot of these economic issues will also be a challenge because is the electorate still there? Does the electorate still care deeply about having a budget in surplus, paying down debt so that the children, their children don't have to pay it? Or do they expect a little bit more from government these days? Is Andrew Hastie right to people expect the government to intervene and save their jobs and do these kinds of, have these kind of populist or high spending economic policies that give them the services and the other kinds of benefits in life that they've come to expect? That will be a tough argument, I think, for him to make. But one that, you know, he obviously is going to have a crack at. There's a bit of talk that, you know, we could be back here in six months talking about a Tim Wilson versus Andrew Hastie. A leadership challenge. For my own sake, I hope not. I'm exhausted after this week alone. Never say never. I used to do them every five minutes. Well, yes. Well, I've been in Canberra nearly seven years and this is my first spill and a major party that's fantastic. Well, in my decade here, I can tell you it was like, you know, another day, another challenge. His first test is obviously going to be very soon. It's going to be the farrow by election because we know that Susan Lee is going to be stepping down in a couple of weeks. That's going to be a very tricky contest. Yeah, because there you'll get probably a nationals candidate, a liberal candidate. Remember Susan Lee actually was the liberal upset after Tim Fisher, who was a nationals leader, resigned from the seat. So there's always been a little, little dislike that she was successful there. And she's always been very proud of winning that set for the liberals. And now one nation will run. So, you know, there's a lot of talk about one nation's polling. Well, well, well. In the seat of Farrah, it will be tested the way they run that campaign. Now Pauline Hansen hasn't missed. She's been up talking about, you know, this is basically they're still flogging a dead horse even with a new salesman in Angus Taylor. So one nation will, it's almost like they are the rival at the moment, rather than the Labour Party to the liberals. Again, that's a danger though. Absolutely. And the other factor in Farrah is just last year at the election and independent run and got 20% of the vote, the primary. You know, that sort of orange rural, you know, they're not quite in teal, but the the Helen Hans kind of mold of a rural independent. It is very possible that we could see a four horse race and the preference flows will ultimately determine who ends up winning that seat. And that is also going to be interesting because as we've talked endlessly about since this one nation surge in the polls, we don't have a lot of data on what happens to preferences after people put one nation or this many people put one nation first. So it will be quite an interesting test case. And if the liberals do fare poorly, I think it will be very hard for Angus Taylor to distance himself from that result. And that's not what you want in your first couple of weeks and months as a new opposition later. What a parting gift from Susan Lee. Here is my regional electorate where I already knocked off the nationals. Now it will be contested by a wider field of right wingers and you Angus Taylor must defend the brand good for you. Good luck. I wonder if there might be even I don't know a backlash. You know, you could really run a campaign of they got rid of your local member because they they knife to I can imagine all sorts of shenanigans going on. Okay, Claire, you say this is your first and seven years. How's it been for you? It's been kind of as you thought it. I mean, the best and all worst part was being crammed into a tiny pen of couple meters by a couple meters with about 50 of my colleagues and a facial fresh gallery screaming up all is as they walk past. No, it's been it's been instructing has been instructive. I'm clearly losing my ability to speak. I might but I think there will be a vindication of sorts of Susan Lee when the period that she took over the liberal party is reflected on in the broader context of wherever the party lets up that she identified the groups that the party needed to win back in terms of, you know, the very obvious. She identified them. She set them out. Did she get a chance to do it? No. If we see a resurgent liberal party who ultimately reaches out to those groups. I think she could be vindicated. But obviously she's sailing off in the into the sunset to enjoy a bit of free time with her kids and grandkids. Yeah, and she has big family and I'm sure they want her home and I'm sure this has been a very bruising part of her career, although she's been in politics for a very long time since the Howard government. But you know, let like you got a you got a hand at her. She smashed a very thick glass ceiling in the liberal party and that will you can't take that from her. That's it for politics now for today. But it's just a little reminder Claire reminding you Claire and also our listeners that on Monday night. I've got my four corners on the realignment of the right. I mean timing is everything isn't it. You know, it's a much bigger story about the changes in right wing politics and what it's all about and what people find appealing that is on ABC TV Monday night. David Spears will be back in the feed for insiders on background tomorrow speaking with liberal party vice president Fiona Scott. Fran and I will be back together on Sunday for the Madigraf Fair Day show in Sydney. It's at 1pm at Victoria Park. If I haven't collapsed as I'm finishing my four corners, you will see me. I hope to be standing. Say, Claire. Say yeah.

We can get a full some policy response, but I thought that in particular was an interesting merging of this sort of distilling of this idea that is being put very forcefully by one nation that there is an immigration problem in this country.

It's one that to an extent even Labour have acknowledged by trying to address the growth in immigration. And really, as I said before, focusing on specific skills and things like that, but it was his first big pitch in a way on that main issue that seems to be the concern for a lot of liberals with regards to that risk of one nation.

As you sort of asked about, there is clearly the sort of existential push and pull going on to the liberal party. We're talking a lot about one nation at the moment, but as you rightly point out, PK, there's also a pull to the left to the middle because half of the moderates not in the party room anymore. Jane is one of the few that are left.
Yeah, and that's right. And some people have questioned, oh, is she a moderate anymore because she's supported Angus Taylor now in two leadership battles.

The second one, he obviously won the first he didn't and Susan landed up demoting her. I kept saying on air all day if people have seen our coverage on ABC News that she fought to keep net zero by 2050 loudly and and warned about the risk in the city.

So I do think she's a moderate and she's pretty passionate about some of these issues. And so I actually think she's going to play a key role in providing that ballast and balance to Angus Taylor as they try to balance these two messages.

Now you can't anymore in a world where, you know, like messages spread on our phones instantly speak to two different audiences. And this is their conundrum how they appeal to till voters and appeal to one nation voters.

I can tell you though, because I know a little bit about their plan that the first plan for Angus Taylor is to deal with the bleeding to the rush. That is a priority because they think, well, we're already bleeding to the moderates, you know, to the till.

And now we're actually losing the other side too. So he wants to stem that bleeding. That's why you're hearing a tough line on immigration. It won't just be Susan Lee's unannounced policy. He will look at it again. I know he's already had conversations about it and that will be a focus.

But he also when I asked him in the press conference, I tried to really got myself in there. Actually, I was couldn't help myself. I asked a few questions about whether they were going to be one nation light. He said no. Right.

We are not seeking to be one nation light. Absolutely not. But we respect the fact that those voters who might be thinking about one nation have reasons for wanting to do so. And we have to restore their confidence in us.
So wants to be more appealing, but at the same time knows that he cannot chase one nation down a cul-de-sac.
So he's trying to be the old conservative leader that stands for values that he can articulate strongly, rather than being wishy-washy, which is what they say Susan Lee was.
He I'm not saying he's told me this, but that's the view whether he can do it, though, whether he's the right messenger. I still think is yet to be tested. But it is.

It's a big job, Claire. I can't see how they do it easily. No. And the one thing that really stood out to me is apart from that real honing in on the values component. A lot of what he was talking about was not a huge departure from where Susan Lee set herself to the things they wanted to focus on home ownership, young people, multi-cultural Australia.

These, you know, the mortgage bell making sure that people have a fair go that they get their money back. All of these kinds of touch points of the liberal party kind of platform that have existed in perpetuity really under any leader under Dutton, under Morrison, and those that came before.
So I do think that maybe Susan Lee, if she was watching the press conference, I hope she wasn't. I really do hope she was out the pub. I wonder if she was. I really hope. I would find out now.

It would be a bit of a head scratcher and I agree with you that it was a very classy speech from her after the results. She didn't take any questions. I did know the one kind of drive by, if you will, which was that in announcing that she'd be resigning from politics. She said that she thought that leaders deserved clear air, not that they always get it.
It is important that the new leader gets clear air, something that is not always afforded to leaders, but which in the present moment is more important than ever.
I will be spending the next couple of years.
I think that was a not so subtle reference to the reality, which is that she has not had a lot of clear air over the last nine months.

Sometimes buffeted by circumstances, but often dealing with things driven by people in her own party room and in the broader coalition, whether it's the splits, doing zero on the NATS timeline, there were these constant kind of inflection points in her own timing of when she wanted to do things.
How she wanted to do things that were disrupted. I think one of the things that I found quite interesting was this idea that she needed to have announced policies faster and been more strong.
There was a constant complaint of the detractors that appeared over the last 48 hours publicly saying that they were going to be backing Angus Taylor.
As if everyone had forgotten that a big part of people's unhappiness with how Peter Dutton had run the party room in the previous turn was that he wasn't consulting.

As she set up these back bench committees, she set up these processes to listen and learn and reflect and make sure that the policies were reflecting what the party room wanted, what the public wanted.
It wasn't fast enough. You can't win sometimes.
No, I think they saw Peter Dutton as two top down and then Susan Lee as two wishy-washy.
I'm using it again and two consultative looking at where the wind was going all the time before she made a call.
Now, let's see, Angus Taylor, it's a hard line. Will he walk that careful line?
Look, I think one of the main things he's going to do, I know he's spending some time with David Little Proud this weekend.
He's called the Nats Whisperer by some, like that he has that great relationship with the nationals.

I think the nationals treated Susan Lee terribly. I think David Little Proud treated her with very little respect, but clearly he's trying to rebuild the coalition in that old-style, old-school way to try and make them more competitive with one nation.
He is, though, in a very wickedly difficult position.
What I didn't hear from his vision was how he was going to win back Metropolitan Australia.
He said with the mere culpr on the taxes that he wants to go back to the coalition having strong economic credentials.
I actually think that's wise. I think it was very strange in the last election that they went saying essentially that their taxes would be higher, like they would repeal a tax card, like mental.
What is the point of them? That is one of their main brand values.
Now he wants to return to that. He hopes that rebuilds them in the cities.
I've got to say, Claire, I think one of the only things that will help him is labour-imploting.
Now, don't discount that happening to governments. They do.
The vision stuff is going to have to be really well executed, and we know that new opposition leaders are pretty accident-prone sometimes.
Yes, Angus Taylor himself has a bit of baggage in that regard, having obviously been a minister and been in a prominent role last term as Shadow Trezra.
Labour had attack ads literally ready to go the second that the result out of that party room was published.
They feel very confidently that there is a wealth of material to draw on from his own past.
It will be difficult. I don't think he's going to get a honeymoon grace period, or if he does, it will not last for very long.
I agree with you about articulating how they're going to win back voters in the cities. He was specifically asked, does the party need to move to the left to the right?
I know, as you've just said, that he's obviously got a prioritising the right.
But he basically just said, I don't see it like that.
I don't really think of it as left to right. I see it. I think of it as focusing on Australians and the hardworking...

The challenges that hardworking Australians are facing every single day, the challenge that they are struggling to pay their bills, the challenge that they can't see a pathway for their kids to own a home.
We're going to take the Liberal Party forward, not left, not right. We're not moving towards any one party.
We're taking our party and the people that we want to represent forward.
It's hard to say we have a problem as a party, existential, the polls are terrible. I think he said if an election was held today, we may not exist.
That's a pretty major problem to have identified.
To not be able to come up with what might be a solution, they've diagnosed a problem.
The solution sounded a lot like, we're going to keep going how we've always gone and we're going to get back to it.
I think that there are a few past Liberal leaders over the last decade who might say, we also had that idea and look how it worked out for us.
I do think the point of difference that I really pick up from Angus Taylor is that the small government lower taxes, lower interventions, anti-tariffs, pro-globalisation.
That actually makes him very old school, very small, liberal economically. That is a point of distinction.
It is very different though than the big spending, that kind of economic nationalism that others would like to see.
It's a gamble, but it is back to their knitting, if you like.
That is specific and that is something he brings. The way he offsets it to those who would like a more populous approach is on values, on immigration, being tough on that.

I know privately when they were canvassing for who should be the right-wing candidate, for instance, between him and Andrew Hastie, part of the discussion was that he was not going to go quite as hard on immigration as an Andrew Hastie.
That was part of the pitch because they are worried about migrant communities. That is the other side of this story that you can go too far and alienate.
That is the cul-de-sac thing. The one nation, it is a smaller group. He wants to go hard on it, but he probably not as hard as others that would have in the party.

Believe it or not, he might be a leading conservative, but he has told his colleagues his where that there is a line and that it is about values, whatever that means, Australian values, who comes through the door, but equally, just being careful about not overreaching.

My assumption in that framing of people who hate for the country shouldn't come here is probably a way of nod to this idea that there are obviously a lot of people in their base who feel that the migration mix is not what they want to see.

But potentially, and this would be a difficult message to sell, but it seems to be the one who is going to attempt, is saleable to even migrant communities because you essentially start to set up this idea that, oh, the majority of you are great.
You are good. You don't hate us.
Well, he told us about cappuccinos.
Yes. And we are just talking about this very narrow subset of migrants who even you don't necessarily want in your community.
And many migrants do want to shut the door behind them.
It's a nuance that I would be interested to see how it plays out.
I think the other point that you raised about him being a traditionalist in a lot of these economic issues will also be a challenge because is the electorate still there?
Does the electorate still care deeply about having a budget in surplus, paying down debt so that the children, their children don't have to pay it?
Or do they expect a little bit more from government these days?

Is Andrew Hastie right to people expect the government to intervene and save their jobs and do these kinds of, have these kind of populist or high spending economic policies that give them the services and the other kinds of benefits in life that they've come to expect?
That will be a tough argument, I think, for him to make.
But one that, you know, he obviously is going to have a crack at.
There's a bit of talk that, you know, we could be back here in six months talking about a Tim Wilson versus Andrew Hastie.
A leadership challenge. For my own sake, I hope not. I'm exhausted after this week alone.
Never say never.
I used to do them every five minutes.
Well, yes.
Well, I've been in Canberra nearly seven years and this is my first spill and a major party that's fantastic.
Well, in my decade here, I can tell you it was like, you know, another day, another challenge.
His first test is obviously going to be very soon. It's going to be the farrow by election because we know that Susan Lee is going to be stepping down in a couple of weeks.
That's going to be a very tricky contest.
Yeah, because there you'll get probably a nationals candidate, a liberal candidate.
Remember Susan Lee actually was the liberal upset after Tim Fisher, who was a nationals leader, resigned from the seat.
So there's always been a little, little dislike that she was successful there.
And she's always been very proud of winning that set for the liberals.
And now one nation will run.
So, you know, there's a lot of talk about one nation's polling. Well, well, well.
In the seat of Farrah, it will be tested the way they run that campaign.
Now Pauline Hansen hasn't missed. She's been up talking about, you know, this is basically they're still flogging a dead horse even with a new salesman in Angus Taylor.
So one nation will, it's almost like they are the rival at the moment, rather than the Labour Party to the liberals.
Again, that's a danger though.
Absolutely. And the other factor in Farrah is just last year at the election and independent run and got 20% of the vote, the primary.
You know, that sort of orange rural, you know, they're not quite in teal, but the the Helen Hans kind of mold of a rural independent.
It is very possible that we could see a four horse race and the preference flows will ultimately determine who ends up winning that seat.
And that is also going to be interesting because as we've talked endlessly about since this one nation surge in the polls,
we don't have a lot of data on what happens to preferences after people put one nation or this many people put one nation first.
So it will be quite an interesting test case. And if the liberals do fare poorly, I think it will be very hard for Angus Taylor to distance himself from that result.
And that's not what you want in your first couple of weeks and months as a new opposition later.
What a parting gift from Susan Lee. Here is my regional electorate where I already knocked off the nationals.
Now it will be contested by a wider field of right wingers and you Angus Taylor must defend the brand good for you.
Good luck. I wonder if there might be even I don't know a backlash.
You know, you could really run a campaign of they got rid of your local member because they they knife to I can imagine all sorts of shenanigans going on.
Okay, Claire, you say this is your first and seven years. How's it been for you?

It's been kind of as you thought it. I mean, the best and all worst part was being crammed into a tiny pen of couple meters by a couple meters with about 50 of my colleagues and a facial fresh gallery screaming up all is as they walk past.
No, it's been it's been instructing has been instructive. I'm clearly losing my ability to speak.

I might but I think there will be a vindication of sorts of Susan Lee when the period that she took over the liberal party is reflected on in the broader context of wherever the party lets up that she identified the groups that the party needed to win back in terms of, you know, the very obvious.
She identified them. She set them out. Did she get a chance to do it? No. If we see a resurgent liberal party who ultimately reaches out to those groups.

I think she could be vindicated. But obviously she's sailing off in the into the sunset to enjoy a bit of free time with her kids and grandkids. Yeah, and she has big family and I'm sure they want her home and I'm sure this has been a very bruising part of her career, although she's been in politics for a very long time since the Howard government.
But you know, let like you got a you got a hand at her. She smashed a very thick glass ceiling in the liberal party and that will you can't take that from her. That's it for politics now for today.

But it's just a little reminder Claire reminding you Claire and also our listeners that on Monday night. I've got my four corners on the realignment of the right. I mean timing is everything isn't it.
You know, it's a much bigger story about the changes in right wing politics and what it's all about and what people find appealing that is on ABC TV Monday night.
David Spears will be back in the feed for insiders on background tomorrow speaking with liberal party vice president Fiona Scott.

Fran and I will be back together on Sunday for the Madigraf Fair Day show in Sydney. It's at 1pm at Victoria Park. If I haven't collapsed as I'm finishing my four corners, you will see me. I hope to be standing.
Say, Claire. Say yeah.

I guess I thought that he was not as interested in fame as he turned out to be. But I believe family did this technology and I am willing to take the criticism for thing. Gene editing holds huge promise to cure disease and alleviate suffering. But changing our genes comes with huge ethical considerations too. Per Jean-Coy did something that crossed the line that every country in the world has decided shouldn't be crossed. He made changes to the human genome that could be inherited. There are issues to do with things like playing God is it ethically appropriate for us to be manipulating the human genome in a way that's going to be passed on to future generations. Hi, I'm Peter DeCryfe. I'm a ABC Environment reporter. For Science Friction on ABC Radio National, a bonus episode of Artificial Evolution. My series on how gene technologies are reshaping the world around us. And I'm joined by Health Report Producer Shelby Trainer who has been looking into human gene editing. Shelby, welcome. Nice to be here. You know, we've covered gene editing of animals for conservation, food and organ transplants on the show. But we haven't really touched on human gene editing. Yeah, it's kind of the elephant in the room of artificial evolution that we haven't mentioned human gene editing. So we've been able to map the human genome for decades, which has meant we've gotten way better at screening for genetic diseases. But we also have ways of changing our genome. This year's prize is about rewriting the code of life. In 2020, researchers Jennifer Daudner and Emmanuel Chapintiere won the Nobel Prize in chemistry. For the development of a method for genome editing. Every one of ourselves contains a copy of our DNA, which can be thought of as the instruction manual our bodies need to be bodies. What these researchers had developed was called CRISPR, a set of genetic scissors capable of cutting away or changing parts of this instruction manual, with the goal of changing how the body behaves. We have 3 billion A's, C's, G's and T's in sequence in our cells that encode the entirety of our genetic information, our legacy that we will pass down onto our children. Professor John Rasko is a leading researcher in gene therapy using techniques like CRISPR to treat genetic causes of disease. Gene editing was possible before CRISPR, but those techniques weren't as simple or precise. So this new technology allows the possibility of us genetically adding, editing or removing sequences of DNA that are then potentially permanently modified and can propagate into all of the cells that that particular target cells divide into. And this year there was a promising breakthrough that tested the specificity of these genetic scissors. You might have seen the headlines about the CRISPR baby. Did you receive the first infusion of his drug on February 25th, 2025? This is the first time that a patient has received a personalized gene editing drug. The story of KJ Muldoon, this little baby, was born with a genetic condition that affected his liver in particular and meant that he couldn't process proteins and would get ammonium toxicity and an early demise. This baby was kept alive and within two weeks of birth, the geneticists who were looking after him already knew the precise genetic abnormality. And the team in Philadelphia in collaboration with a company started to create a bespoke genetic scissor, the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology to target the specific mutation in this baby's liver. See, this isn't the first time humans have received CRISPR gene therapy, but it is the first time it was personalized. So when the infusion starts, most of the drug actually gets into the liver and is taken up by the cells almost immediately after it's gotten into the bloodstream. CRISPR gene editor enters the nucleus of the cell. And in this case, we programmed it to go to the site of the genetic variant that is actually causing the disease in KJ. The drug is really designed only for KJ, so the genetic variants that he has are specific to him. It's personalized medicine. This little baby became the poster baby for a bespoke precision medicine that was targeting a unique mutation in this baby's genome for the first time on the planet. When this happened, I remember seeing a post about it on X from Chinese scientist Hirzhang Kwe. And he called the case of baby KJ a double standard. Hirzhang Kwe was released from prison in 2022, having served three years for editing the genomes of babies. But there's a big difference between what he did and what the scientist in Philadelphia did for KJ. The changes to KJ's DNA seemed to be keeping him healthy, but they're changes to his somatic cells, meaning they won't be passed down to his kids. Hirzhang Kwe was imprisoned for attempting to make changes to germline cells, which are passed down from one generation to the next to the next. If we modify the germline, we open an ethical minefield because we're not just modifying the target person that carries these germline cells, but all of their descendants forever. Yeah, hello, my name's Matthew Portius. I'm a professor of pediatrics and stem cell biology at Stanford University. Professor Portius has been involved in gene editing research for decades. And so he cross paths with Hirzhang Kwe a few times. I first met Hirzhang Kwe at a small meeting of about 15, 20 people, but didn't really think much of it until sometime later he said that he was going to be in the area and look forward to meeting with me and talking to me about some of the work he was doing. It was a pretty standard meeting. Hirzhang Kwe talked about his attempts to use CRISPR to edit the germline cells of non-human primates. According to Professor Portius, it didn't seem to be working all that well. And then at the end of that hour long conversation or towards the end, he mentioned that that plans to now use this in humans. Really said, look, I don't think your science justifies it. I don't think your rational justifies it. And I think that if you do this, it will be a real setback for the field. I think he and his student were a bit shocked because I don't think it hurts such clear negative feedback on what he was doing from others. This was a Friday, so the rest of his lab was out enjoying happy hour. And I came stomping out and like, you cannot believe what I just heard and this and that. And so, yeah, I was human. Professor Portius thought after his negative reaction, there was no way Hirzhang Kwe would go through with the plan to edit human embryos. What he didn't realize at the time was that Hirzhang Kwe had already edited the embryos and they had already been implanted in the mother. Didn't hear anything from him until I got off the plane in Hong Kong for the second international summit and met people in the hallways who said, have you heard? And I was like, have I heard what? And they said, have you heard what Hirzhang Kwe is done? And it's like, and when we met at Stanford, I said, look, I respect the confidentiality of your research and I won't talk to anyone about it. In retrospect, I now think that was my mistake. I really should have talked to others. And because I had asked him, well, I think you should talk to others. Clearly, he was, but he wasn't necessarily getting the same feedback that he was getting from me. I said, well, I've heard a little bit about what do you mean? And then heard his plan announcement that he had edited two human embryos and they had implanted them and babies had been born and so on and so forth. This was all happening at the second international summit on human genome editing. World leading experts were gathered all in one place, maximum impact. Most people believe that his main goal in doing this was to be the first on the planet to do germline gene editing. Hirzhang Kwe did have a therapeutic goal in mind. He wanted these babies to be protected from HIV infection. The fathers were HIV positive. Now, the principle of his idea was that we know there is a mutation called CCR5 gene mutation, which leads to resistance to HIV when it occurs in both of the copies of the genes that we all carry. Now, this is a relatively rare mutation, but it is observed naturally. And in the natural state, we know that these individuals who happen to be born with this mutation of the CCR5 gene are highly resistant to HIV infection. So his goal was to artificially introduce this mutation to the CCR5 gene of these embryos. And then use IVF to impregnate the mother without exposing her to HIV. But it failed on so many levels. It was, frankly, a scientific and clinical debacle. But the extent of that debacle was unclear until Hirzhang Kwe was allowed half an hour to present to the summit. You know, we listened to his presentation. He came from a genomics background. I thought that the data that was presented was actually very messy, very hard to interpret, but clearly demonstrated that the attempt at making mutations at the CCR5 gene was not efficient and certainly not clear that the genetic change that was intended had even been made. One of the babies was born with only one of the copies of the genes changed and the other copy was intact so there would never have been a possibility of a resistance to HIV. And the other baby had a change in the gene that was unintended, so the so-called off-target effects. So it was scientifically a failure in the first place and the cells should never be implanted in the womb of the mother to carry the baby's to term when he knew from the get-go there was improper targeting. While Hirzhang Kwe was answering audience questions, Professor Portius noticed something else. He was being very cagey about whether the trial was ongoing. While he had announced the birth of twins Lulu and Nana, he hadn't disclosed whether he'd edited human embryos since. And that's what prompted me to ask him, wait a second, there's a gap now between where we are and what was done and that's when he acknowledged that there was another baby on the way who hadn't been born yet. This baby is known as Amy, but for obvious reasons we don't have a lot of information about any of these children. Many scientists have called for them to be closely monitored in case the edits to their genomes have unintended consequences. And to monitor their offspring as well to see if these changes are passed down to their children and their grandchildren. This was a complete ethical, clinical and scientific debacle. He did this secretly, he did it without ethical approval and he did it without proper consent of the parents and make no mistake, that is something that is illegal in pretty much every jurisdiction on the planet, including China. Her Zhang Qui was found guilty of illegal medical practices. The court declared he and his two collaborators had crossed the bottom line of ethics in scientific research. But why does germline gene editing cross a line? According to Professor Portius, we have to ask this question because as technology improves, it will come up again and again. One day the technology is going to be, we're not going to have off targets. And the breach was that he did it, not that he did it when it wasn't safe. The question is should we even do it at all? I'm Peter DeCrythe, I'm an ABC Environment reporter. The science fiction is an artificial evolution on ABC radio national. My series on how gene technologies are reshaping the world around us. This week, an extra episode from Health Report Producer Shelby Trina on the ethical minefield of human gene editing. There are issues to do with things like playing God. Is it ethically appropriate for us to be manipulating the human genome in a way that's going to be passed on to future generations? Professor Diane Nicholl is at the Center for Law and Genetics at the University of Tasmania. She says a big issue is consent because changes to a person's germline will be passed onto that children, that grandchildren and so on into perpetuity. How can an individual that's the grandchild of a person possibly consent to things that are being done to the egg cells from two generations ago? Then there's the issue of designer babies. In Australia, laws came into effect in 2002, restricting what can be done to human embryos. And it was largely in response to concerns about human cloning. Dolly the sheep had happened a few years before and at the same time researchers were exploring the use of embryonic stem cells to treat disease? So you've got that tension between things that are considered to be morally abhorrent, through to the moral imperative to treat human suffering. And this legislation draws a line between those two things. It says that certain things should be absolutely prohibited, one of which is human cloning, another of which is any techniques that make heritable, that's things that can be inherited, heritable changes to the human genome. There was of course Samantha Taylor and her supporters sitting on one side of the court, but in the same row all the way at the other side of the court right next to the door were the Sylvanis.
And I saw Joe Sylvani Tom's mother actually twist her body to look at the victim a couple of, during a couple of points while those remarks were being read out.
I mean, there's so much interest in this case in Victoria, Alex, as we've been talking about through this episode.
What was it like once the proceedings finished because it's your job to get out there and get statements from the various parties involved here if there's anything they need to say?
I mean, you know, it's not just you. There's dozens of journalists following this trial. I mean, there must have been just kind of absolute scenes outside.
Yeah, that's right. Pretty much. Well, as I said, the Sylvanis were sitting right next to the door. As soon as proceedings finished, they got up and walked out the door.
The journalists pretty promptly followed, but by the time I'd gotten out the room, they were nowhere to be seen.
So we ran down the stairs and it was only really a couple of journalists who were able to catch up to them to ask them for comment.
They didn't respond to any requests for comment, but Joe Sylvani did tell the journalists who had made it there to go away.
And she did at one point even push one of the journalists away.
Yeah, right. I mean, we heard from the Sylvanis following the conviction of Tom that they would be fighting this.
What have we heard about that? They have now filed an appeal on Tom Sylvanis rape conviction on what grounds are they trying to pull this apart?
It's a little bit technical. There are two grounds and both linked to the prosecution's evidence involving that phone call that Tom Sylvanis victim made to him in the days after the rapes.
Yeah, this is what we spoke about earlier where Tom Sylvani told her not to pursue this any further, right?
Yeah. So in these appeal documents that we've seen, Tom Sylvani's lawyers argue that the judge,
heard in determining statements that Tom Sylvani made during that call, constituted as incriminating conduct.
And they also said that the judge, heard in his directions to the jury concerning how the jury was meant to use that evidence to form their verdict.
Yeah, interesting. I mean, again, thinking about who is involved in this, someone with access to a lot of resources.
Have already heard that? I had a couple of lawyers representing them throughout this whole process as well.
And previously, when I've seen appeals filed, often they're left until the last possible day of the appeal window.
This one has come what seems to be quite quickly in this process as well. So what happens from here?
Well, for now, we're waiting to see if this appeal gets up, but Tom Sylvani remains in jail.
Okay, Alex, thank you so much for joining us on the case of.
Thanks, Toky.
If you have any questions about this trial or anything else that we are working on, please get in touch.
You can send us an email at the case of at abc.net.au.
On Thursday this week, following a number of your emails about the retrial of Greglin,

episodes.title: 06 Kumanjayi Walker | Six years on, what's changed?
episodes.description: It's been six years since Kumanjayi Walker was killed by Constable Zachary Rolfe, and six months since Coroner Elizabeth Armitage found that racism was a factor in Kumanjayi's killing.
episodes.transcript: New Year, new me! Woohoo! Forget it. And ladies, we need to talk. We're keeping it real. We're calling out wellness industry nonsense, ozempic and its influence, and how our relentless striving for perfection is actually bad for us. So join us for the anti-new year's resolution and start 2026 on the right foot. Search Ladies We Need to Talk on the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts. ABC Listen, podcasts, radio, news, music, and more. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander listeners are advised that in this episode, we're going to be discussing an Aboriginal person who has died. It's been six months since the coroner made the explosive finding that racism was a contributor to Kumajai Walker's death. Then recommended significant reforms to try and change the culture in the NTPL East Force. We'll dig into whether anything has changed and answer your questions. I'm Stephen Stockwell. This is chapter six of the case of Kumajai Walker. Constable Zachary Rolf fatally shot the 19-year-old. Sometimes I think about how he must have felt in his last moments. Was he scared? And I can promise you, consequences will flow. Constable Rolf has pleaded not guilty to one charge of murder. Prosecutors took the case to the high court. There's been a huge outpouring of grief. An organisation with significant hallmarks of institutional racism. When we are going to get justice, when? Throughout this series, looking at the shooting of Kumajai Walker, we have had so many questions and reflections from all of you as well as our own. So we're going to answer some of them and find out whether anything is changing when it comes to policing and governing in the Northern Territory to help us, as always, with this in this series, is ABC reporter and presenter Melissa McKay. Welcome, Melissa. Hey, Stocky. Mel, we announced six months on from the handing down of this inquest report. Where are we at? Well, a lot has changed in the last six months the Northern Territory police force has finally got a full-time permanent police commissioner. Now, Martin Dole had been acting in the role when these findings were handed down. He has now been made the commissioner of police. The anti-police force has also released its anti-racism strategy, which was a really big recommendation by the coroner in relation to Kumajai Walker's death. Okay, so I mean, it sounds like there is a little bit of progress happening. There are things changing, which is, you know, maybe I'm a bit cynical, but it's maybe a little bit more than I was expecting. Is it all been kind of smooth sailing though? I mean, there's certainly been, you know, this appetite for change within the upper echelons of the Northern Territory police force, and we haven't yet seen a formal response from the Northern Territory government yet. They haven't legally had to provide a formal response just yet. They've got, you know, under the legislation a certain amount of time to be able to do that. And so we are expecting that to come in the next few months when Parliament returns for the year. But so far, when, you know, the Chief Minister of Nokiaro has been asked about it, you know, the response has largely rested on the cost of this inquest and how long it took to get to this point. There hasn't been this formal recognition yet from the Northern Territory government about this systemic racism that the coroner found within the police force. In fact, I saw a press conference with the Chief Minister not long ago where she was asked about the anti-racism strategy and the racism in the anti-police force. And she sort of rejected the premise of that question. Right. I mean, that's really interesting because, as you say, the anti-police force has been moving forward. I mean, we talked in our last episode about how they already started doing some of this work before the findings were handed down. You know, they were hearing what was being told to the coroner or the Zbathamitij, and they were making actions throughout that process. And one of them, I believe, was the appointment of Leanne Little, an R&D woman to come in and draft an anti-racism framework for the anti-police. Is that all kind of moving ahead going forward? Yeah, it is. Leanne Little has released this anti-racism strategy alongside the police commissioner, Martin Dole, made up of four key priority areas, including eliminating racism and representing and reflecting the Northern Territory as well as, calling for police officers to be more accountable. So part of it is rolling out anti-racism training to police, giving them ways to identify racism, improving processes as well that protect whistleblowers and victims of racism, which is something that was highlighted throughout this inquest. They also are looking to boost Aboriginal employment to 30% across the police force. And this is what Leanne Little, who was the head of cultural reform of the anti-police, told our Darwin ABC colleague, Eline Rousseau, during an exclusive interview in November last year, when she talked about her experience in that role. I can honestly say now that I've seen behaviors shift dramatically and that's due to the leadership in the police force. I've had police officers who have been gifted or taken artifacts from communities that might be 10, 15 years ago, return those items to me because they know that they wasn't there to take. I've seen lots of complaints over my table that I'm now looking at and passing on to other parties to deal with. But that's also not to say that every police officer in the Northern Territory recognises these findings and recommendations. As we've been talking about throughout this series, there was that sort of binary view, right, people who were either pro-Zackery Rolf or pro-Common-Jai Walker and his community, right? There was this sort of this binary that developed quite quickly and I think there are still elements of the police force that may not feel as though there is a problem or may not feel as though there is as much of a problem as the coroner has made out to be in her findings and recommendations. But from what we've heard from the commissioner, from Leanne Little, there isn't really an option to not make any of these changes. Well, the risk is to go high. We know that when racism is there, that it contributes to suicide, it contributes to hurt and harm. We know it contributes to anti-social behaviour, to alcohol and drug use, to contact with the criminal justice system. We know that it hurts and harms people in ways where it's not their responsibility to own that poor behaviour by those officers. So at the end of the day, this is a risk that we have to take and we can't fail. That's Leanne Little, an R&D woman who is basically the anti-racism framework architect within the Northern Territory Police. In this episode, we're going to talk through some of the changes that we've seen since the findings were handed down, we're going to explore the fallout. Also, answer your questions that have been sent through to the case of at abc.net.au. We've had so many questions sent through, and also some really beautiful and thoughtful reflections as well. So we'll get to them throughout this episode. Mel, when I want to start with though, is actually a suggestion that was sent through to the inbox. Someone asking if we could give the context of the name Kumanjai. Why is that a name we hear used for different Aboriginal people? Kumanjai is a name used after someone has passed away in wopry culture. So there are different substitute names for different cultures, but within Kumanjai walkers family and his community, Kumanjai is sort of this substitute name that is given to someone after they have passed away. They don't speak his first name anymore now that he has died. So we use Kumanjai for Kumanjai walker in this context, but it's also a name given to many other wopry people who have passed away. We use Kumanjai and then their surname. Thank you, Mel. You might notice the start of these episodes. We have a warning mentioning we're going to be talking about the name or mentioning the name of an Aboriginal person who has died. And really, we're doing that. So people listening know that we're going to be discussing Kumanjai walker in these episodes, even though we're not using his first name. Have a, not a question from Julie Melbita, a statement that she has sent in. Julie writes that she spent the last six years living and working across 18 remote communities, mostly in the Northern Territory, but also in South Australia and Western Australia. And this included Yundamo, which she left just one week before the shooting occurred. She says, from that experience, I genuinely believe Northern Territory Police have one of the hardest jobs in Australia. They operate with minimal support. Stations are consistently under manned and officers are often working in extremely complex high-pressure environments. In my community, I worked in an eight person station, really had more than two or three officers, physically in the community at any time. Coming from South Australia originally, I had absolutely no idea that parts of Australia function like this. The culture shock is real and confronting. I honestly believe that every Australian should spend at least a month living in a remote community. There are roles for everyone from professionals to shop assistants. And the experience gives a depth of understanding you simply can't get from the outside. Do yourself a favour, see it for yourself, and make lifelong memories and friendships. Mel, you spent time in Yundamo, you spent time in remote communities. Does that outline from Julie kind of ring true? Yeah, it absolutely does. I think Julie is absolutely right in saying that the culture shock is real. And she, like many other Australians, wouldn't have had any idea that parts of Australia function like this, as she said. I think we talked about this in an earlier episode around the difficulty of police officers work in remote communities. And I think we heard about it a lot, particularly in the lead up to Kumajai Walker's death, that the police officers who were working in Yundamo at the time were overworked. They were exhausted. The coroner had a lot of really good things to say about the work of police in remote communities. And you know that they do have a really, really tough job. You know, Yundamo for example is 300 kilometres from Alice Springs. And anyone who's been to Alice Springs would know that even Alice Springs is really, really remote from anywhere else in the country. You know, it's several hours on a plane to get anywhere from Alice. And so remote communities spattered across the Northern Territory, WA, South Australia, Queensland. They are really remote and really different to what anyone who has grown up in somewhere like Sydney would understand. Yeah, Mal, I mean, I've been fortunate in my work to travel through so many parts of Australia, you know, working in Karatha for a couple of years. I've travelled across Northern WA, the Northern Territory, you know, all through Queensland as well. The places are incredibly beautiful. The people are wonderful. But you know, they're not without their challenges. You know, you see some really confronting living conditions for people. You see some really confronting interactions between white people and Aboriginal people in those places as well. And so there's a lot to unpack when you go to those places. But it's, you know, it's a reality of parts of Australia, right? And I mean, one of the recommendations we saw from the coroner was that Northern Territory police should spend time in those communities, you know, that they should spend at least a couple of years at the start of their career working in remote communities in places around the Northern Territory. So they have an understanding of what it's like. Yeah, absolutely. This was something that was that was really important for the coroner to make a point about in terms of police having an understanding of what it's like. Policing in a remote community by comparison to somewhere like Darwin or Alice Springs, you know, the challenges that community members face in a remote community is very different to the challenges that you face living in Darwin. And the challenges as a police officer are very different to what you face in a bigger community. And so in having that experience of, you know, working in a remote community, I think the coroner sort of talked about people needing to have a cultural understanding of the places that they're working in in order to try and tackle these unconscious biases and racism that can develop, as she said, Leanne Little has done a lot of work in that space and she has also acknowledged the difficulty of working in remote communities. Yeah, and, and Mel, I mean, you know, as well as police getting that experience, I mean, it was a finding of the anti-coroner that there's elements of the anti-police that I racist, there's racism that exists within that organization. I mean, it sounds like Leanne Little who we heard from a little bit earlier is working quite hard to not just address that, but also address the kind of the idea that all police are racist. Yeah, absolutely. I think this is something that she is working to try and build a space where police officers also feel comfortable in reporting, you know, racism that they see. You know, the coroner found even, for example, when those racist awards that we heard so much about throughout the inquest were being handed out by the TRG, when that came to light so many years after they had been happening, that there was so many members of the police force who knew that that was happening and didn't say anything. That's something that the coroner found was evidence of this entrenched systemic racism within the Northern Territory Police Force that people likely are little and now trying to grapple with how to change that culture. Yeah, and this is what Leanne told the ABC a couple of months ago about that work. It gets me out of bed every day is the fact that I know that there are good police officers out there who are providing me with a lot of the information that I need to eliminate racism in the police force. People who are brave and courageous who bring that information to the table because they don't want to work in a system that's racist. I want those bad racist police officers to be the minority and I want the good police officers to be able to be in a space where they can call out that bad behaviour and report it and know that we will do something about it. Yeah, reminds me, Mal, of what David Morrison said over a decade ago when the defense force was dealing with sexism and abuse within itself saying that the standard that you walk past is the standard you accept. So, you know, Leanne sounds like she's trying to build a similar culture in the in the anti police force as well. And Mal, I mean talking about the recommendation of anti police spending time in community, all this work that's being done around that. I mean, we spoke in the last episode about how strong Elizabeth Armageddon's findings were. You know, she really didn't hold back, you know, basically finding that exactly where off was racist, you know, finding the elements of racism with the anti police, you know, all of these, you know, really damning findings around, you know, anti government, anti health, all of that. But then the recommendations all felt very achievable. They were all very matter of fact, they all seemed quite straightforward. I mean, do you think they were written by Elizabeth Armageddon knowing that they were going to be going to a conservative CLP government that probably wasn't going to be that responsive? Look, it's difficult to, you know, get into the head of the coroner and, you know, it's her job to be impartial and and to write and make these findings and recommendations that, you know, she feels will lead to genuine change. But yeah, like you said, you know, and we talked about in the last episode, there was sort of a bit of a language shift, I think, from the findings, you know, those, those hundreds of pages of findings to those 33 recommendations, which, you know, were targeted predominantly at the police force, but also at various other government agencies for change. And a lot of the recommendations that she made seemed fairly straightforward, I suppose, you know, working with remote communities seems fairly obvious, right? And coming up with strategies to work with elders in these remote communities, you know, in a lot of these recommendations that she made were also not necessarily things that we hadn't heard before. We've had the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Desceng custody, which made so many recommendations, which again sort of seemed in a lot of ways fairly obvious. So, yeah, you might be onto something there, Stokey. We've got a heap of questions that I want to get to in this set, Mellas, we go through. So I'm going to start running through some of them with you now. First one is a question from Jennifer, who's been listening to the pod from the UK. She's got a question about the jury in Zachary Rolf's murder trial, which is what we covered in episodes two and three of this series. And Jennifer asks, considering a jury is supposed to be representative of the community, whether any Aboriginal people on the jury is there an effort to actively include Aboriginal communities in jury selection? This is a really, really big question in the Northern Territory in particular. And something that came up quite a lot throughout this process. We can't actually say for sure whether or not there were any Aboriginal people on the jury because of the legislation in Australia that protects the identities of jurors. The only information that we actually get from the court about the makeup of a jury is the gender split. How many men and women make up that number of 12? We heard from members of the community that there were no yapa, no Walpuri people that they were aware of that were on the jury. But we don't know for sure what the actual makeup was. There isn't sort of a specific push to try and include more Aboriginal people on Northern Territory juries. Yeah, thank you, Mel. And a wonderful question, Jennifer. So thank you for writing to the case of at abc.net.au. Another one here, Mel from SNF on the Gold Coast was Zachary Roff's police partner required to give evidence or be questioned. Surely their testimony would have been helpful. Yeah, we did hear from people who had worked with Zachary Roff. We also heard from, you know, his partner, Adam E. Burl, those who were there on the night of the shooting. Particularly throughout the coronal inquest, we heard a lot of evidence from people who were there on the night. And yeah, their evidence was helpful in in terms of giving, you know, a broader picture of what people saw and experienced on the night of the shooting. Yeah, thank you, Mel. And Steph, wonderful question. So thank you for writing to the case of another one here, Mel from Janet, who's listening to the pod in Madrid in Spain. She writes, I'm wondering about why they left Comunjai Walker to die in the police station. The court actually heard that police officers who were there in the police station in Yuntamur on the night did the best that they could to try and keep Comunjai Walker alive. They performed CPR, but they had very little, you know, training for those sorts of things and very little equipment as well. We know Comunjai Walker was taken to the police station rather than the health center because there were no nurses in Yuntamur at the time. Police didn't give mouth to mouth to Comunjai Walker on that night, but the court also heard that they didn't necessarily have to and that that may not have actually assisted in any way. Yuntamur was so far away from a hospital that it would have been very difficult to save Comunjai Walker's life that night given the extent of his injuries. Yeah, thank you, Mel. And thank you for the question as well, Janet. One he from Taya Mel, Taya writes, as Zachary Rolf was found not guilty, is he able to return to his role as a police officer or is there some kind of regulation preventing that? Zachary Rolf did return to his role as a police officer after the trial after he was acquitted of murder, manslaughter and engaging in a violent act causing death. He had returned to work in Darwin. He wasn't in uniform or sort of out on the on the bait he was working some kind of office job for several months before he then returned to leave when the inquest resumed or when the inquest started. He is no longer working as a Northern Territory Police Officer. Zachary Rolf was dismissed from the force during the coronal process, not for any disciplinary matters related to the night of the shooting, but for writing an open letter, which was published in a Northern Territory publication called the anti-independent where he sort of criticized the coronal process, the upper echelons of the Northern Territory Police Force. The investigation into the shooting, that was a breach of the Northern Territory Police's sort of media and public commentary guidelines. So he was dismissed from the force because of that. I should note he has flagged that he would appeal that decision to dismiss him, but he is now no longer working. Thank you, Mel. Thank you, Taylor, for that question as well. Mel, as we get towards the end of this series, I want to take you to an email we got at the start of this. This is an email from Greg and it's not so much a question. It's more of a statement and he writes, hi there. I'm a dedicated listener. I love the podcast. I've cried, learnt and been fascinated in the thrall. I've looked and seen your next topic and immediately got teary. I'm hesitating to listen so I'm e-mailing you instead. What happened in Yundamoo was felt so viscerally, not just in Yundamoo, but in every remote community in the NT. I'm a non-Indigenous linguist who has spent a career working in and around remote NT. The idea that remote homes were no longer safe, the police could enter an Aboriginal person's home and shoot a man dead. I believe something shifted in the collective psyche of remote Indigenous Territoryans because of that day. And what was lost has never been recovered. I'm so scared to listen. Six years is not long. So many hearts still hurt, not just for what happened, but for bearing witness to the power of the white man and his and I use the male pronoun intentionally here, institutions. I work as an interpreter, often with police and the justice system. I see injustices and ignorance and misunderstandings and disadvantage all the time. Come and Joe Walker's case still feels like an open wound. Keep up the great work. But I listen to this come and Joe Walker series. It's not you. It's me. Mel, is this still an open wound? Yeah, absolutely it is, stocky. And I think Greg's really hitting the nail on the head there by saying that he believes something shifted in the collective psyche of remote Indigenous Territoryans on that day. There's still so much pain and trauma. Six years isn't that long to heal from from the death of a loved one for anyone, let alone to heal from the death of a loved one in such a traumatic and and public way. And come and Joe Walker isn't even the most recent death in custody in the Northern Territory. There's been several more since come and Joe Walker died. And in the lead up to the coroner's findings being handed down, there was the death of come and Joe White, another young, well pre man who died on the floor of a supermarket in Alice Springs during an attempted arrest by off duty police officers in the center of town. And I can't speak for for come and Joe Walker or come and Joe White's family, but I went back to Alice Springs to cover come and Joe White's death as a reporter. And I was speaking to members of his family who I already knew from my work covering the death of come and Joe Walker, you know, we sat on the same grass out the front of the same police station listening to the same people speaking. But speaking about the death of a different young man and so it's so clear that there hasn't really been this chance to heal from the death of come and Joe Walker before family within grieving the death of come and Joe White. And we don't have the details yet around the circumstances of come and Joe White's death. That's going to be another coronal inquest that the community is is going to have to go through. Thank you, Mel. And thank you Greg for writing to the case of Mel. Thank you so much as well for for taking us through this whole story for taking us to Yundemu that night in 2019 and through the criminal trial and through the inquest really appreciate having you here on the case of to tell this story. Thanks, Rocky. And if you want to read some more, there's some wonderful books around the moment as well, you know, during the production of this series we read Steven Schibitz book, Death in Yundemu. Yeah, and also Kate Wilde's book The Red House. Kate is also a former ABC journalist and she held my hand throughout a lot of this case as well. So there's a lot of really incredible reporting and further reading that people can do on this case. Yeah, absolutely. I'd encourage you if you've learned something through this, if you want to read more, look around. There's plenty out there that you can check out to learn more about this story. And thank you for following through on the case of come and Joe Walker. The case of come and Joe Walker is produced by ABC audio studios and ABC News. It's reported by Melissa McCay and presented by me, Steven Stockwell. Our supervising producer is Greg Muller and our executive producer is Claire Rollinson. Thank you to senior lawyer Jasmine Sims to senior cultural advisor, Murin Corolla and to editorial policies advisor Bridget called Well Bright for their help making this series. This episode was produced on the land of the Gadigal and War Entry people.

chapters.title: CEO's Death and Initial Crisis
chapters.summary: Quadriga CX announces CEO Gerald Cotton's death amid financial instability and withdrawal delays.

chapters.title: Key Access Revelation
chapters.summary: Court reveals Cotton held sole access to $250M in cold storage, sparking panic among users.
