episodes.title: Paul Roos' Grand Final forecast
episodes.description: The Brisbane Lions have touched down in Melbourne and the city is filled with finals anticipation. Roosy reminds us of Brisbane's Fitzroy roots and the team vote that sparked its move north.
episodes.transcript: This is an ABC podcast. ABC AFL Daily with Poppy Penny and Paul Brews. Hello and welcome to the ABC AFL Daily podcast. My name is Poppy Penny and with me as always is 2005 Premiership Coach and 7-time Australian Paul Brews, Rosie. Hello. Poppy, I've been really living the glory days. Apparently Wednesday was 20 years exactly. So on Instagram, we're going nuts on Instagram. So it's a big week for me as well. I'm just pretending I've won it again this year. I've seen that. There's a lot of, there's a lot of young Paul Brews from 20 years ago in my Instagram feed. So they are really living the glory days at Sydney. I forgot how big the parade was. There was one came up and I just reposted it. I forgot how big the Sydney parade was. I do remember thinking when we got on, on no one will turn up and it'll be me and Hall he's just waving at each other and the players behind it. I remember it was big but it was the, it's crazy when you go back and look at it. Was that kind of a realization of what the Premiership means to not just the playing group but to the wider community and what, you know, so Jolong and Brisbane will be hoping to experience in a couple of days? Well, I think so and I think it was just probably cemented the connection between South Melbourne and Sydney because it was pretty rocky 81. I think it was when they went up there. So yeah, we knew it was going to be big in South Melbourne because a lot of people sort of got back on board, you know, we played in 96, plight were coming up and all those sorts of things. But we probably weren't ready to win the flag in 96 but the momentum of Tony and then some great players coming up and Hawley and then winning it in 05. Yeah, I think it, I think it just showed that, you know, we'd made it in Sydney in a small way but big enough that we could own a slice of the sporting landscape, never push our way in. I think that was one of the great things that the swans did, never tried to push our way through rugby or rugby league, rugby union, you know, we coexisted really well and but I think that was the culmination of South Melbourne, the excitement of South Melbourne. We had the Sunday at Lakeside A, which we knew was going to be big. I was surprised at how big it was in Sydney. So you talk about that sort of move from South Melbourne to Sydney, which is kind of a similar path to what the Brisbane Lions have plotted to end up where they are now. And I want to, before we maybe get too far into the game, since you've sort of mentioned that there, is I want to talk about that story because there will be some younger Brisbane Lions fans who maybe have only seen four premierships in the last 25 years, which, you know, seems under for Brisbane Lions fans, but they may not understand the connection that that club has to Fitzroy and to Melbourne. So I wondered given that, you know, you played 269 games for the club and capped in them and won a number of fest and ferrisks there, you could give us a little bit of a history lesson as to how we got from Fitzroy to the Brisbane Lions. Yeah, sure. I mean, it sort of started in 1986. We were, I don't know where we were with seven rounds to go, but we had a meeting on Wesley College on the tennis courts on a Sunday morning. And the President Leon Wigard said, we've got three options. We can fold. We can merge with the Melbourne-based club or we can relocate to Brisbane. So the remainder of that season, I was meeting with the consortiums with the consent of the club. It wasn't like we're going behind because we didn't know what was going to happen. We all voted to stay together on the tennis courts. We all voted to go, if that was going to be the best option, players staying together, going to Brisbane. And then a company called Hecron Baylor just out. We won six of our last seven games. We played in the preliminary final that year. And then it was sort of a slow burn from there, you know, like we had Gary Pertleaving, Richard Osborne leaving, Paul Brotrick, Michael Gail, Alistair Lynch, and then myself in 90, then the 94 going to Sydney. And then by 1996, I think it was, it was just a club bereft of certainly money. Now the AFL didn't support the clubs as they do now because they did want a club to go to Brisbane. And then it was going to be North Melbourne slash Fitzroy. But the preference was for Fitzroy to go to Brisbane and merge with the Brisbane lines. And I thought it was the best thing. I thought we should have gone in 86. And I can't be clear on this, but in 86, the two Germans, Martin Leslie and number of South Australians will link to the Brisbane lines. And Charles is a really good friend of mine. I think if we had gone and had the caliber of team that we had in 86 going into 87, we could have won a Premier League. She'd been 87, 88, 89 as the Brisbane lines. But yeah, that's the history of the club. And another story which is a little bit similar to the Sydney one. I was working for Channel 7 as a boundary rider in 201 and Lynch, good mate of mine was playing, had chronic fatigue and I had to walk on the field after game. It was so exciting. And I remember walking back to the hotel, I think it was staying at the Hilton or the Hider, whatever it was and all the Fitzroy sports. Well done, Rusey. Congratulations. It's an amazing day. And I'm like, actually, I didn't play, but it was so exciting for the Fitzroy faithful that did stick around. I know that some didn't and I know some left. But yeah, you're right. For those young Brisbane line supporters that don't really understand and some of the players, I suspect Fakes has done a really good job of integrating their old, you know, Kevin Murray is one of the greatest people I've ever met in my life. I've got a lot of iconic Gary Wilson's over here and I'm watching the game with him on Friday night. Gary will come over and watch it at the house and we'll be bericking for the Brisbane lines. Yeah, not that we've got much skin in the game now. But yeah, there's a strong connection, great history. Some of the best players I've ever seen, well two of which are Bernie Quinlan and Gary Wilson. A lot of Brisbane line young fans would never have heard of them, which is a shame because they are exceptional players. It is a great iconic history of the Fitzroy Football Club. Yeah, and I think that last year when they won the Premiership, they actually took the Premiership Cup and did their first celebration. Obviously they went back to Brisbane and did a big one, but they did their first celebration in Fitzroy, which I think does tie it all together and you're right. There would be younger players who don't really fully understand that, but the fact that they take it back to Fitzroy and they still have FFC on the back of their football players for the Fitzroy Football Club, I think that they do a really nice job of tying it all together. Looking back on your grand final experience and I'm going to start in 96 and then we'll move on to the good times in 2005, but I want to talk about as a player, what are the nerves like this week? Yeah, there's two things as a player where there's only one as a coach and I'll go into the coach in a minute, but there's two things. There's the fear of losing in the excitement of winning and the second one is not playing well yourself. There's two things going into the grand final. Clearly you want to win and you don't want to play poorly. You've got two things on your mind. You're really preparing yourself individually as best you can and you're thinking team as best you can. There's a combination of the two. I've got to play my role. I want to play really, really well not to let the team down, a family down, the fans down, etc. And we want to win the game. It is a very different feeling going into a grand final as a player than it is as a coach. What are the nerves like then if you're a coach? What are the things that you're thinking about? What is the nervous feeling that you're trying to suppress maybe? You only win or lose as a coach. You can't play well. You sort of can because you don't want to get belted. It's not like people go, you know, GZ Coach well and they've lost by a point or two points or three points you lose. Whereas people are remembered for great grand final performances, Gary Abelett, senior nine goals or eight goals or whatever it was. People do remember you playing well in a grand final. They never remember you coaching well in a grand final. That's probably the biggest difference. The other thing it's not about yourself at all. You don't think about yourself. All you're thinking about is the team. How do I get the team ready to play? So there's significant differences as a player and as a coach. Results aside, did you enjoy the build up to one more than the other like player or coach? Yeah, it's a hard question to answer because you can't talk about the build up without the result. That's the hardest thing. So clearly, O5 is so much better than 96. But I do remember as a player because I was always one that wanted to take in the surrounding. So I was able to do that. Some players get really, really nervous before the game and some players throw up before the game. Some people, you know, they're really tunnel vision. But I was a certain player that could take in the surrounding. I wanted to do that. I do remember running around warming up, looking at the crowd, thinking I'm normally in the grandstand. And I think that helped enjoy the experience even though we lost because there was some really good memories from the grand final. But when you lose, like it's, yes, it's your best footy day and worse rolled up into one day, you know, in three hours. So it's hard to differentiate, you know, the, yeah, I was playing against my good mate, Johnny Blake. Yeah, Dennis Pagan was like a cult, the pagan cult. They wouldn't look at us, scouting the parade on yelling at him and he's, you know, he's head down and he wouldn't, wouldn't look at us. They weren't glad to wear sunnies. And, you know, so you remember things like that, which is pretty funny. We talk about that now, but they won. They, they, they deserve to win. They were the best team, yeah, that year. And yeah, we had a chance during the game. But yeah, you, O5 is so much better because you win the game. Yeah, I imagine the result does color everything that went before it because you just think, well, all of those nerves were worth it because you ended up winning a flag in 2005. Just very quickly, I want to touch on the fact that Joel, Sirwood and Jonathan Brown will be the representatives to hand over the cup should their team win, which I think are both really good choices. I feel like we've had sort of older champions hand over the cup in recent years. And these are two who the younger generations will remember watching play. And I think that's a, there's a really nice tie there. And obviously Joel, Sirwood, they've had a difficult year as a family. And Jonathan Brown is a champion of that club and is so synonymous. I think even when I picture the Brisbane Lions, I think I still picture Jonathan Brown wearing the Lions jumper. That's sort of my affiliation of him is not working in the media, but it's 100% playing at full forward for the Brisbane Lions. So I think both fantastic sort of choices to hand over the cup.
